title: Utilizing a GPT-based exam assistant to support practice and assessment in higher education: an exploratory study on learner engagement and perceptions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Abstract Instructors increasingly use chatbots to reduce their workload and to support students with individualized learning opportunities. However, there is still limited knowledge about how students engage with chatbot-based formats for practice and assessment compared to similar human-authored formats. This study examines whether chatbot-supported instruction can achieve similar outcomes with respect to students’ engagement, perceived fairness and perceived usefulness while reducing the workload associated with creating practice and assessment activities. We developed an Exam Assistant (EA) that delivers exam-like open-ended questions, including short case studies, provides immediate feedback, and supports automated scoring with instructor review (human-in-the-loop). The EA was implemented in a real classroom setting with N = 30 undergraduate business students at a German university. Students used the EA for practice and for a graded assignment in the first course phase, while in the second course phase, these activities were delivered via conventional Moodle quizzes. This ensured alignment between practice activities and assessment across both instructional formats . Using learning analytics, chatbot interaction logs from 224 sessions with the EA, and post-assessment surveys, we conducted a descriptive, exploratory comparison of students’ engagement patterns and fairness perceptions. Results show comparably high levels of practice intensity and perceived fairness across both instructional modes. Students demonstrated greater engagement with EA than has typically been reported in prior research on educational chatbots. Nevertheless, students perceived Moodle quizzes as more suitable for future graded assessments, a difference that appears to be driven by question format rather than by fairness concerns. Overall, the findings suggest that thoughtfully chatbot-supported practice and assessment may offer a promising pathway to reduce instructors’ workload without evident disadvantages in student engagement or perceived fairness.

analysis.discussion: This study examined how students engage with chatbot-supported practice and assessment across different instructional formats implemented in consecutive course phases. Practice intensity (RQ1) was comparable across the chatbot-supported and conventional Moodlebased modes and overall, relatively high. On average, students practiced with the EA about seven to eight times during the first course phase, with a large share of practice occurring on the day before the graded exam. About 40% of all practice attempts were fully completed. This finding contrasts with prior research showing that approximately onethird of students did not use the chatbot-based learning mode at all, and that those who did engage with the chatbot typically did so only for a few minutes across several days, exhibiting an initial peak followed by a gradual decline (Hellas et al., 2024; Martins et al., 2024) . One possible explanation is that, unlike the chatbot deployments examined in prior work, the EA was not introduced as an optional learning tool but was closely aligned with the graded assessment, which may have motivated students to engage more seriously with the EA during self-study. Interestingly, despite offering virtually unlimited practice opportunities and immediate feedback, students did not make markedly more practice attempts than in the Moodle condition. This suggests that practice intensity may be constrained by overall workload and competing study demands rather than by the availability of additional exercises. From an instructional perspective, however, achieving comparable practice intensity with substantially less authoring effort is itself a relevant benefit. This advantage may be greater than indicated by the estimates in Sect. "Instructor workload for authoring practice and assessment activities", because the EA also provided immediate individualized feedback on open-ended and case-based responses, which would be costly to deliver manually at scale. Regarding students' perceptions of fairness, the EA-based and Moodle-based assessments performed very well and at similarly high levels in both informational and procedural fairness evaluations by students. This also suggests that including the course reader as a domain-specific knowledge base in the EA setup, as suggested by earlier research, may have supported good alignment between AI-generated tasks and course content, as students did not report major issues related to hallucinations, off-topic content, or subjective bias. Overall, our results suggest that the AI-supported assessment format did not compromise students' perceptions of fairness compared to traditional, human-authored Moodle quizzes. In contrast to previous studies, which found a reluctance toward automated grading among as many as half of the students (Schei et al., 2024) , reluctance toward the EA appeared to be less pronounced in our context. As suggested before, the reasons for these differences are likely attributable to the general design of the instruction, which led to a very tight integration of the EA within the course. Students were invited to point out caveats with respect to the EA, which even led to major reconfigurations of the tool after an in-class introductory EA session. The participatory implementation process may have fostered a general atmosphere of trust and fairness with regard to the EA, including assessment practices. A notable difference between the two modes was that more students experienced time pressure when completing the tasks and questions presented by the EA during the graded exam, as compared to the Moodle quiz. First of all, students may have experienced additional stress due to technical issues encountered during the EA-based assessment. Moreover, the EA required free-text responses to all questions presented, whereas in the Moodle mode, this question type only made up about one-fifth of the questions, and the remaining questions used closed-response and interactive item formats. Because free-text answers typically take longer to formulate than closed-format questions, this likely resulted in increased time pressure, especially for slower writers. The differences in question formats may also provide a plausible explanation for the somewhat counterintuitive finding that, although students considered both modes to be equally fair, most students favored Moodle quizzes over the EA when asked about their preferences for future courses, particularly with respect to graded assessments. Apart from considerations of fairness, students may simply prefer a mix of predominantly clickable question formats with only a small proportion of open-ended responses over fully text-based question-answer interactions with a chatbot-especially in graded exams that must be completed under strict time constraints. Although this initial exploratory study has several limitations that should be addressed in future research on chatbot-supported practice and assessment, the absence of marked differences in student engagement and perceived fairness between the EA and Moodle formats provides an important starting point. The findings suggest that chatbot-supported practice and assessment can be integrated into higher education without evident disadvantages in these outcomes while reducing instructor workload associated with authoring. An important insight is that chatbot-supported practice seems to be particularly promising when closely aligned with assessment procedures, purposefully integrated into the course structure, and linked to graded assessments. This suggests that alignment-a well-established principle of instructional design-should also be a key consideration when designing educational technologies, rather than offering them as an optional add-on. Practically speaking, the finding that chatbot-based formats were perceived as comparable to traditional, human-authored Moodle-based practice and assessment in terms of learning experience suggests that the choice between these formats primarily becomes a workload decision. In our study, we showed that chatbot-based tools for practice, feedback, and assessment, such as the EA, can be implemented using off-the-shelf tools and without technical expertise. The primary challenge for instructors lies in developing a structured system prompt that incorporates conceptual design considerations, such as task logic, rubrics, and feedback principles. However, instructors have to take into account these issues also when creating quiz questions and interactive tasks manually in Moodle or other learning management systems. When large numbers of practice and assessment questions are required, or when course content changes, creating such items entirely manually results in a high workload on the instructor side. In contrast, once a chatbot-based setup is stable, updating or extending the practice and assessment based on changes to the course content is as simple as replacing the domain-specific knowledge base. This implies that the same EA-like tool can be reused across courses with different content, requiring only minor adjustments. At the same time, it should not be overlooked that students were somewhat less comfortable with EA-based graded assessments than with conventional Moodle quizzes, even if they perceived them as similarly fair. analysis.limitations: A first set of limitations concerns the study design. Blended-learning formats like ours make it difficult to disentangle the effects of the two practice modes from those of other parallel instructional activities, such as lectures. Moreover, the two formats were implemented in a fixed sequence and covered different topics (Organizational Behavior vs. Human Resource Management). The lack of counterbalancing may have introduced order effects, although greater familiarity with the course and assessment procedures in the later Moodle phase would arguably have favored Moodle. Conversely, because prior knowledge and topic familiarity were not controlled, the potentially greater accessibility of the Organizational Behavior content may have favored the EA phase independently of the instructional format. These differences, together with the lack of formally established reliability and validity of the assessments, prevented a meaningful direct comparison of learning outcomes. At the same time, a coarse review of assignment scores and pre-post self-assessments during data analysis did not raise concerns that the use of the EA was associated with any noticeable negative effects on learning outcomes. Finally, because all participants shared the same classroom experience, their responses may not have been fully independent, further limiting the interpretation of individual-level comparisons. Additional limitations affect the comparability and precision of the available evidence. The system failure required an unplanned switch to a different LLM and platform during the graded EA assessment. As a result, data from both systems were analyzed together without formally testing their comparability. Second, detailed information about usage patterns was only available for the EA mode, but not for the Moodle mode. As a result, we were not able to directly compare how students actually practiced in the respective modes, for example how far they progressed through the questions, how extensively they responded, and where they discontinued practice. Still, the detailed insights into students' use of the EA made it possible to compare the observed usage patterns with those of prior evaluation research on educational chatbots, suggesting a higher level of active use for practice than is commonly reported. Finally, workload estimates in Sect. "Instructor workload for authoring practice and assessment activities" for authoring both formats were retrospective and should be interpreted as approximate. Moreover, the study's small, context-specific sample and the particular instructional setting limit the generalizability of the findings. As the study was carried out in a single undergraduate business course, students in other disciplines or learning environments may respond differently to the EA and Moodle activities. In addition, the extensive support offered by instructors, the cooperative, open atmosphere between instructors and students and students' involvement in testing and refining the EA may not be replicable in largerscale teaching contexts and may partly explain the favorable perceptions of the EA phase. Lastly, although one of the main promises of chatbot-based teaching tools is individualized feedback at scale, this study did not look at how students used or perceived the EA's feedback. Conclusions about how AI-generated feedback affected subsequent learning or practice behavior cannot be drawn from the data currently available, indicating a crucial area for further study.

verified_article_review.provenance: Original paraphrases from the checked HTML article
verified_article_review.methods: Thirty business undergraduates at a German university practiced organizational behavior with a GPT tutor. It asked four questions and then presented a case. In one example, students had to explain how they would handle conflict in a newly reorganized team. The tutor gave written feedback after each response. In the next unit, the same class studied human resources with instructor-written Moodle quizzes, including an exercise on calculating wages. The researchers examined practice records and surveyed students after each unit.
verified_article_review.results: The first question appeared in 224 chatbot sessions. Students typed an answer in 118 sessions (52.7%). The final case appeared in 146 sessions and drew an answer in 91 (40.6% of all launches). Students could practice repeatedly, so these counts describe sessions. Most survey respondents reported 30 minutes to two hours of weekly practice with either tool. Among the 23 who took the second survey, over half preferred the chatbot for practice or considered either format suitable. Most preferred Moodle for graded work.
verified_article_review.discussion: A teacher looking only at the 224 launches would count opening the exercise and working through the case in exactly the same way. The written answers let the authors distinguish those actions. They suggest that students may have returned to rehearse the kind of question they expected on the exam. The logs cannot show how much students learned from reading the tutor’s feedback.
verified_article_review.limitations: All students used the chatbot first and Moodle second. The subject changed between units, and the chatbot exam was supervised while the Moodle exam was taken at home. Moodle recorded 181 practice attempts without showing which questions students actually answered. The researchers could compare reported practice time, but could not tell which tool produced more active practice or better learning.
verified_article_review.review_scope: Read the publisher's full HTML article, including the practice counts, survey results and limitations.

title: Beyond the Pyramid: Bloom’s Taxonomy Meets Generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

analysis.discussion: GenAI has not simply added one more tool to the educator's kit; it has unsettled the very hierarchies that underwrote models like Bloom's Taxonomy. By revising, inverting, or 'UnBlooming' those models, the approaches in this article argue for designs that foreground recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth as the real work of learning, especially in an age where GenAI is marketed as doing the 'thinking' for us. The future of learning is not arriving later. It is already here, unevenly distributed across classrooms, disciplines, and institutions. The educators who will shape that future are those willing to revise their most cherished frameworks, revisit their assessment practices, and keep asking questions about the kinds of thinkers, makers, and citizens we want our students to become. As we write, and as we advocate for this change, we are keenly aware that faculty at our Higher Education institutions already carry a heavy burden with teaching, researching, and public engagement. There are a finite number of hours in a day, and faculty do not have the time to stop and redesign courses almost weekly as GenAI changes and morphs. We make a point to call for change, but we know this change cannot happen overnight. It will require the dedicated commitment of administrators to find the funding and time for faculty to make these changes. Designing for recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth means little if only a subset of students and faculty have the material and institutional support to engage in that work. GenAI cannot be framed primarily as a compliance or efficiency problem because it is a fundamental change in the way teaching and learning happen. Right now, for example, many programs and professional standards have been rigidly structured to Bloom's Taxonomy, making authentic education suffer in the Age of AI (Gonsalves 2024) . Taken together, these post-AI frameworks reframe Bloom's Taxonomy not as a ladder to be climbed, but as a historical starting point-inviting educators to design learning that prioritizes metacognition, agency, and ethical judgment in a world where answers are instant but understanding is not. As Table 3 summarizes, Bloom's/Revised Bloom's, Fink's Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom's, and UnBlooms™ do not represent interchangeable models; rather, they mark a movement from hierarchical cognition, to relational learning, to AI-era inversion, and finally to recursive, judgment-centered pedagogy. Instructors and institutions must design new structures and assessment systems to account for the reality of GenAI. This does not mean being a full-on AI adopter, but it does mean that they will need to be 'AI aware' (Watkins 2024) . Ultimately, that is why we published this article: we needed to better understand how learning works in the Age of AI and build from there. In comparing selected pre-AI and post-AI pedagogical frameworks according to how they conceptualize the relationship among process, product, cognition, agency, and metacognitive reflection, we have demonstrated how learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks can be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning. Although Bloom's Taxonomy endures, we must see Bloom's as a point to begin the revision rather than an endpoint or script. If our institutions, educators, and students are to thrive in the Age of AI, we need to begin the inquiry into what pedagogy should look like with GenAI, what we are trying to accomplish, whose learning counts, who benefits, and who is left out of the future we are building. It is an ongoing conversation, one that we are privileged to be a part of, but also one we understand must move quickly into the future as our technology, institutions, and educational priorities change (hopefully) for the better.

title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

analysis.discussion: Generative AI disclosure should not be treated as a transparent reconstruction of manuscript production. Authors may accurately report particular operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional descriptions such as language polishing, structural editing, or idea generation remain retrospective classifications whose causal significance may not be fully recoverable. The distinction between observable actions, interpreted functions, and intellectual contributions places limits on what disclosure can establish, even when authors report their practices sincerely and in considerable detail. These limits matter because provenance information can influence scholarly evaluation. The readerly distraction model developed here distinguishes justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently connected to the disclosed operation or its plausible epistemic consequences. Such monitoring may redirect attention away from a manuscript's claims, evidence, and reasoning, and under some conditions may contribute to negative perceptions of authorial competence, originality, or trustworthiness. However, attentional displacement and evaluative stigma remain analytically distinct. Their relationship is an empirical question that can be examined through comparisons of function-specific disclosures, generic disclosures, and equivalent forms of human mediation. The appropriate policy response is epistemically proportionate reporting rather than either exhaustive provenance reconstruction or the abandonment of disclosure. Methodological reporting should make consequential research operations examinable; governance reporting should identify how adopted outputs were assessed and controlled; and production-provenance disclosure should communicate relevant circumstances of composition without claiming to reconstruct every intellectual influence. Reporting requirements should correspond to the role of an operation, the risks created by reliance on its outputs, and the evidence needed to evaluate the resulting claims. Authorship, in turn, cannot rest on nominal responsibility alone. Accountable judgment requires understanding, appropriate verification, meaningful decision authority, and answerability that can be exercised when justified challenges arise. These capacities cannot be certified infallibly, nor must every contributor personally reproduce every specialized procedure in collaborative research. Nevertheless, claims about responsible authorship can be examined through role-specific explanations, relevant verification records, and substantive responses to criticism. The distinction is between responsibility merely attributed to an author and judgment that can be meaningfully questioned and defended. The central ethical task is therefore not to determine what proportion of a manuscript originated with AI, but to establish what information is necessary for evaluating its claims and who can justify the scholarly decisions embodied in them. A defensible publication policy should make consequential operations visible without allowing technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning. The objective is neither perfect transparency nor unquestioned human authority, but scholarly judgment

title: Performance without capability: generative AI and the validity of assessment in higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has altered how assessment supports learning and evidences achievement in higher education. Early institutional responses concentrated on academic integrity, detection, and task redesign, while a rapidly expanding empirical literature documents the contingent benefits and trade-offs of AI-mediated learning. This conceptual paper develops an assessment-specific framework organised around two dimensions: the distribution of learning-relevant cognitive responsibility and the visibility of student process. GenAI can operate as an engagement amplifier when it supports cognitive and metacognitive activity while preserving student responsibility for the intellectual work that matters, or as a cognitive substitute when it displaces that work while enabling successful task completion. The framework distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable capability, whether demonstrated independently or with GenAI, and connects this distinction to the validity of inferences drawn from assessment evidence. Rather than proposing a universal solution to what has been called the wicked problem of AI and assessment, the framework offers an evaluative lens for judging how particular assessment configurations distribute cognitive responsibility and make student thinking visible, and whether the resulting evidence can support defensible claims about achievement. This reframing informs assessment judgements without prescribing a single model for all higher education contexts.

title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments
abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

abstract_text: Abstract The application of artificial intelligence technology in education is becoming increasingly widespread, but there is no consensus yet on its impact on learners’ critical thinking. To gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationship between the two, this study adopted the meta-analysis structural equation modeling method and systematically integrated data from 31 empirical studies worldwide in this field. The results show that the use of artificial intelligence is not directly associated with the improvement or decline of critical thinking, but rather appears to operate through two different psychological mechanisms. On the one hand, frequent use of artificial intelligence can easily lead to technological dependence, and this tendency of dependence can harm the development of critical thinking. On the other hand, the proper use of artificial intelligence tools can stimulate learning motivation, thereby promoting the cultivation of critical thinking skills. These two opposite indirect effects coexist and nearly offset each other; the net indirect effect was not statistically significant, whereas the direct association of AI use with critical thinking remained positive and significant. Further analysis suggests that this dual effect may vary across groups: the motivational pathway appeared especially pronounced among college students, whereas the group difference in the inhibition pathway was not statistically significant. This study, from a theoretical perspective, reveals the dual paths through which artificial intelligence influences critical thinking, providing an important reference for how to effectively utilize artificial intelligence tools in educational practice and also offering new directions for future related research. However, causal interpretations are limited by the predominantly cross-sectional nature of the included studies.

title: Generative artificial intelligence dependence and academic performance: serial mediation through attentional control and physical fitness and moderation by grade level
abstract_text: Objective This study examined the association between generative artificial intelligence dependence (GenAID) and academic performance (AP) among adolescents, whether attentional control (AC) and physical fitness (PF) mediated this association individually and in sequence, and whether grade level moderated these pathways. Methods Participants were 1,461 Chinese adolescents. PF was assessed using standardized fitness tests; GenAID and AC were measured by questionnaires; and standardized scores in Chinese language, mathematics, and English served as indicators of AP. Structural equation modeling and related analyses were conducted using AMOS 24.0 and SPSS 26.0. Results GenAID was negatively correlated with AC, PF, and AP ( p &lt; 0.01), whereas all other pairwise correlations were positive ( p &lt; 0.01). All direct predictive paths among the variables in the serial mediation model and the predictive paths from the interaction terms to AP were statistically significant ( p &lt; 0.01). GenAID significantly predicted lower AP through three indirect pathways: AC (95% CI [−0.067, −0.031]), PF (95% CI [−0.190, −0.003]), and AC followed by PF (95% CI [−0.009, −0.002]). Grade level significantly moderated the AC–AP and PF–AP paths: the standardized coefficients for Grade_AC_inter and Grade_PF_inter were −0.101 ( p &lt; 0.001) and −0.164 ( p &lt; 0.05), respectively. Conclusion GenAID directly predicted lower AP and also predicted lower AP indirectly through AC, PF, and AC followed by PF. The findings indicate interrelationships among GenAID, AC, PF, and AP. Grade level moderated the serial mediation model, with a weaker negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP at higher grade levels.

analysis.methods: The final sample comprised 1,461 Chinese adolescents aged 12–17 years, including 735 boys and 726 girls. Of the 2,000 questionnaires distributed, 1,638 were returned; after invalid responses were excluded, the usable-response rate among returned questionnaires was 89.19%. According to the grade-level categories specified in the Education Law of the People’s Republic of China, the sample included 361 students in Grade 7, 350 in Grade 8, 410 in Grade 10, and 340 in Grade 11. Students in Grades 9 and 12 were excluded because these graduating cohorts may differ substantially in psychological stress, emotional fluctuations, and academic pressure, thereby increasing sample heterogeneity. Participation was voluntary, and legal guardians were informed about the study and provided written informed consent. The Ethics Committee of Sichuan Normal University approved the study (2026LSTY01). Questionnaires were classified as invalid if they contained substantial item-level missingness, could not be linked to standardized academic examination scores, or could not be linked to valid PF scores. PF records were treated as invalid when indicator scores were markedly inconsistent with the participant’s actual physical condition. The inclusion criteria were adequate proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing in Chinese and written informed consent from a parent or legal guardian. The exclusion criteria were a psychological disorder, physical disability, intellectual disability, developmental impairment, sports injury, or a similar condition. GenAID was measured using the 17-item Student Generative Artificial Intelligence Dependence Questionnaire developed by Yu and Yan (2026) . The instrument comprises three dimensions: cognitive and behavioral dependence, functional dependence, and emotional dependence. Cognitive and behavioral dependence comprises six items (e.g., “When completing learning tasks, I first consider using generative AI to help me complete them”); functional dependence comprises six items (e.g., “I believe that generative AI can meet my learning needs”); and emotional dependence comprises five items (e.g., “I believe that generative AI can understand my emotions and needs”). Items are rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) on a five-point Likert scale. All items are positively keyed and summed, with higher total scores indicating greater GenAID. Cronbach’s alpha was 0.898 in the present sample. AC was measured using the Chinese version of the 21-item Attentional Control Scale revised by Yu (2017) . The instrument comprises five dimensions: inhibitory control (five items), attentional shifting (four items), task persistence (five items), attentional focusing (four items), and divided attention (three items). Items are rated on a four-point scale (1 = never, 2 = sometimes, 3 = often, and 4 = always). Seven items are positively keyed (e.g., “I can concentrate well even when music is playing in the room”), and 14 are reverse-scored (e.g., “When I am studying, I am easily distracted if someone is talking in the same room”). Item scores are summed, with higher total scores indicating better AC. Cronbach’s alpha was 0.862 in the present sample. PF was assessed in accordance with the National Student Physical Health Standard (2014 Revision) across three weighted dimensions: body morphology (15%), physiological function (15%), and physical performance (70%). The indicators were body mass index (BMI), vital capacity, the 50-m sprint, sit-and-reach, standing long jump, the 1,000-m run for boys, the 800-m run for girls, pull-ups for boys, and one-minute sit-ups for girls. The total PF score comprised a standard score and bonus points. The standard score, calculated as the weighted sum of the individual indicator scores, had a maximum of 100 points. Bonus points were awarded for eligible indicators when performance exceeded the 100-point standard, yielding a maximum total score of 120 points. Scores were classified as excellent (≥90.0), good (80.0–89.9), passing (60.0–79.9), or failing (≤59.9). AP was derived from total scores in Chinese, mathematics, and English on large-scale, standardized, in-person examinations administered by the participating schools. Because test difficulty and scoring rules varied across schools and grade levels, raw scores were converted to standardized scores. At both the junior and senior secondary levels, the maximum score for each subject was 150 points. Scores were transformed as follows: standardized score = (raw score / total possible raw score) × 100, producing AP values from 0 to 100 ( Li and Jiang, 2023 ). After obtaining approval and support from the administrators of the sampled schools, the research team distributed informed-consent forms to all eligible students who participated in the questionnaire survey. Students completed the questionnaire only after a legal guardian had signed the form. Data collection was completed within 6 months. PF data were obtained from the test records that each school submitted to the National Student Physical Health Network. School physical education teachers administered the tests and entered and reviewed the records using standardized procedures. Testing protocols, equipment specifications, and operating procedures followed the regulations of the Ministry of Education of the People’s Republic of China and the General Administration of Sport of China. Scores were classified as excellent, good, passing, or failing according to the official criteria. At the junior secondary level, PF results contributed 1 point to the physical education component of the senior high school entrance examination. At the senior secondary level, failure to meet the standard affected eligibility for high school graduation. The questionnaire was administered online, either collectively during information technology classes or outside class time under parental supervision. Completion took approximately 10 min. AP data were drawn from large-scale, standardized, in-person examinations administered by each school and were based on combined scores in Chinese, mathematics, and English. Analyses were conducted in AMOS 24.0 and SPSS 26.0. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, and overall model fit was evaluated using structural-model fit indices. Harman’s single-factor test was used to assess common method bias. Descriptive statistics summarized the study variables, and Pearson correlations quantified their bivariate associations. Path coefficients and direct effects were estimated in AMOS by maximum likelihood. Indirect effects were evaluated using a bias-corrected nonparametric percentile bootstrap proc

Because this value was below the stated 40% threshold, common method bias was within the acceptable limit ( Yu et al., 2026 ). Standardized path coefficients are reported in Table 3 , with larger absolute coefficients indicating stronger modeled paths. GenAID was a significant negative predictor of AP ( p < 0.01). All constituent paths in the serial mediation model were statistically significant: GenAID negatively predicted AC ( p < 0.001) and PF ( p < 0.01); AC positively predicted AP and PF (both p < 0.001); and PF positively predicted AP ( p < 0.001). Bootstrap estimates based on 5,000 resamples showed that the 95% confidence intervals for all three indirect pathways excluded 0 ( Table 4 ); each indirect effect was therefore significant and negative. For Path 1, the indirect effect through AC (GenAID → AC → AP) was −0.048 and accounted for 76.19% of the total indirect effect. For Path 2, the indirect effect through PF (GenAID → PF → AP) was −0.010 and accounted for 15.87%. For Path 3, the serial indirect effect through AC and PF (GenAID → AC → PF → AP) was −0.005 and accounted for 7.94%. These results supported H2, H3, and H4. Figure 3 presents the structural equation model for GenAID → AC → PF → AP and the estimated direct and indirect paths. Both interaction terms had significant negative paths to AP: Grade_AC_inter (standardized coefficient = −0.101, p < 0.001) and Grade_PF_inter (standardized coefficient = −0.164, p < 0.05). These coefficients indicated grade-level moderation. Conditional effects were evaluated using 5,000 bootstrap resamples, and simple slopes were used to depict the interactions. Conditional effects were estimated at grade levels 1 SD below (M − 1 SD) and 1 SD above (M + 1 SD) the mean ( Niu et al., 2025 ). At the lower grade level, AC was a significant positive predictor of AP (effect = 0.429, p < 0.001), whereas its predictive association with AP was not significant at the higher grade level ( Table 5 ). Correspondingly, the indirect predictive association between GenAID and AP through AC (GenAID → AC → AP) was significant and negative at the lower grade level (effect = −0.101, p < 0.001) but not significant at the higher grade level. The confidence intervals for the lower-grade conditional paths excluded 0, and Figure 4 presents the simple slopes. These results supported H5. Conditional direct and indirect effects by grade level. Moderation plots. The positive AC–AP and PF–AP slopes were statistically significant at the lower grade level ( M − 1 SD) but not at the higher grade level ( M + 1 SD). At the lower grade level (M − 1 SD), PF had a significant positive effect on AP (effect = 0.367, p < 0.001), whereas the effect was not significant at the higher grade level (M + 1 SD). At the lower grade level, the indirect predictive associations along GenAID → PF → AP and GenAID → AC → PF → AP were both significant and negative (effect = −0.030, p < 0.001; effect = −0.016, p < 0.001, respectively); neither pathway was significant at the higher grade level ( Table 5 ). The confidence intervals for the lower-grade conditional paths excluded 0, and Figure 4 presents the corresponding simple slopes. These results supported H6.
analysis.discussion: This study tested a moderated serial mediation model. GenAID was a significant negative direct predictor of adolescents’ AP and also negatively predicted AP indirectly through AC and PF. Grade level also moderated the serial mediation model: the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP weakened as grade level increased. The correlation and prediction analyses indicated interrelationships among GenAID, AC, PF, and AP. The association between GenAID and AP is thus part of a broader pattern of relationships involving cognitive functioning and PF indicators. The findings supported H1: GenAID significantly and negatively predicted AP directly, with higher GenAID scores corresponding to lower adolescent AP. GenAID can have contrasting implications for adolescent AP. Cognitive offloading theory holds that sustained overreliance on external tools may diminish deep processing and independent thought ( Risko and Gilbert, 2016 ). Once cognitive outsourcing becomes routine, the apparent reduction in cognitive load provided by external tools becomes a maladaptive transfer of that load, compromising deep processing and disrupting the allocation of cognitive resources. Adolescents may outsource complex thinking processes, including independent thought, decision-making, and information processing, to GenAI. Although this may reduce cognitive load in the short term, the development of dependence can lead to the continued depletion and impairment of cognitive functioning. Previous research suggests that GenAI’s capacity to generate text, images, video, and audio can substantially improve adolescents’ learning efficiency ( Kasneci et al., 2023 ), whereas excessive dependence can reduce independent thinking and impair cognitive functioning ( Zhang et al., 2024 ). Academic emotions and anxiety also shape adolescent AP. Persistent dependence on AI can heighten academic anxiety, prompt doubts about one’s abilities, and reduce academic self-efficacy, adversely affecting AP ( Li et al., 2026 ). A 30-month longitudinal study of 26,811 Chinese students in Grades 7–12 across nine subjects found that AI assistance increased homework scores by approximately 18% and reduced completion time by 30%, while examination scores decreased by 18%–24%. Learning losses were concentrated among approximately 80% of AI users whose behavior was consistent with homework outsourcing, as indicated by exceptionally short homework completion times combined with high homework scores. AI users whose homework completion times were similar to those of nonusers experienced small learning losses ( Strömberg and Lei, 2026 ). These findings support the interpretation that GenAID is negatively correlated with academic performance. GenAID negatively predicted adolescent AP through AC, consistent with H2. The negative indirect estimate through AC was lower than the direct estimate for GenAID predicting AP, suggesting that stronger AC can reduce the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP. Previous research has linked excessive AI use in adolescence to neurobiological changes, including reduced prefrontal-cortex activation and lower hippocampal gray-matter density; these changes may contribute to cognitive-overload symptoms such as distractibility and impaired decision-making ( de Sousa et al., 2026 ). Excessive dependence on AI has also been associated with poorer long-term memory retention and AC ( Deckker and Sumanasekara, 2025 ). AC, in turn, is consistently associated with adolescent AP: impaired AC is related to poorer AP ( Bruce et al., 2016 ), whereas stronger AC is related to better AP ( Ma and Li, 2023 ; Song et al., 2018 ). AI’s predictive relationships with adolescent cognitive functioning and AP differ substantially according to how individuals use it. Research suggests that the learning benefits of AI depend on students’ AI literacy and how they prompt AI and verify its output. Higher AI literacy can positively predict AP through prompting practices, information verification, AI-assisted calibration accuracy, and perceived task cognitive load ( Shen, 2026 ). AI also has the potential to provide students with personalized, efficient learning experiences ( Xuan, 2025 ). In the present study, the negative indirect effect via AC was the largest, indicating that AC constitutes an important correlational pathway in the negative association between GenAID and poorer AP. The observed correlational pattern suggests that AI literacy, cognitive load and AC may co-vary with this association. A parallel pattern emerged for PF. GenAID was negatively associated with PF, whereas PF was positively associated with AP, yielding the negative indirect effect proposed in H3. The negative indirect estimate through PF was lower than the direct estimate for GenAID predicting AP, suggesting that higher PF can reduce the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP. Prior research suggests that excessive AI dependence among adolescents may involve substantial out-of-school time devoted to human–AI interaction, thereby increasing sedentary behavior, reducing time available for exercise, and lowering PF ( Liu et al., 2026 ). Higher PF, by contrast, has been associated with better AP ( Wen et al., 2018 ; Liang and Li, 2020 ). These findings offer a plausible account of the observed indirect effect: by displacing time otherwise available for exercise, GenAID may gradually compromise PF, with downstream implications for AP. Cognitive behavioral therapy interventions can alleviate negative emotions, stress, anxiety, and related psychological problems. Health-risk behaviors in adolescence tend to cluster, and the occurrence of one such behavior often increases the likelihood of others. These interventions can therefore target co-occurring unhealthy behaviors and psychological and behavioral problems in adolescents ( Zhang et al., 2026 ). This pattern raises the possibility that combined cognitive and exercise interventions may be associated with lower digital dependence. The model also yielded the negative serial indirect effect through AC and PF proposed in H4. GenAID negatively predicted adolescent AP through the combined pathway involving AC and PF. The negative estimate for this serial indirect pathway was lower than both the direct estimate for GenAID predicting AP and the estimates for the separate indirect pathways through AC and PF, suggesting that stronger AC and higher PF can jointly reduce the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP. title: Do People Trust AI Assistants Even When They Are Consistently Wrong?
evidence: Preprint; source-checked v1, peer review unverified
abstract_text: People are increasingly using conversational AI systems to make decisions despite concerns around their reliability. How well do people calibrate to AI systems' accuracy in multi-turn conversations? We measure how people's reliance on LLMs' advice changes across repeated interactions, varying whether the AI assistant is helpful (100% accurate), unhelpful (0% accurate), or mixed (50% accurate). Across 4 experiments, we find people learn to trust helpful models more than unhelpful ones (67% vs 21% of the time), but only when they receive external feedback on the models' accuracy. Without feedback, people continue to be persuaded 48% of the time by a consistently unhelpful model (vs 38% for helpful). Rather than gaining trust in helpful models, participant reliance on LLM advisors tended to be high in early trials and only fell with evidence of inaccuracy. Participants trusted LLM advisors more than they trusted human advisors (83% vs 65%, Experiment 4), and LLMs benefited more from having a helpful track record than humans did. In contrast with previous work, we find limited evidence of an advantage for arguing for the truth (versus a falsehood). Truth advantages emerged only when participants were already very confident in their position, and did not emerge at all for static hints. Collectively, the results suggest that people may be swayed by LLM advice, even when it is consistently false, unless they have access to timely ground-truth feedback. Unfortunately, in many domains such feedback may not be available, leading to overreliance on AI.

title: Right Advice, Wrong Reasons: How Decision and Reasoning Alignment Shape Reliance on AI Advisors
evidence: Preprint; source-checked v1, peer review unverified
abstract_text: When people seek advice from AI on social situations, the system may recommend a decision they fully agree with but justify it through reasoning they disagree with. Conversely, it may offer reasoning they agree with, and yet reach a decision they reject. We distinguish decision alignment, whether an advisor recommends the option favored by a user's measured values, from reason alignment, whether its stated reasons align with the user's values. In this work, we ask how these two forms of alignment shape people's preferences for AI advisors and their willingness to use them in different roles. We conducted a within-subjects study (N=121) in which participants evaluated three AI advisors varying in decision and reason alignment across eight everyday moral dilemmas. Participants then chose which advisors they would consult, allow to draft messages for review, or allow to act on their behalf in new tasks. When seeking advice, participants most often preferred an advisor that reasoned through their prioritized values while recommending the opposing decision (40%). However, when participants had to pick advisors for new tasks, their preferences shifted toward advisors that also recommended decisions aligned with their values, rather than those that only shared their reasons. Also, as participants considered tasks that gave AI advisors greater autonomy, they became more likely to opt out of using any advisor, from 12% when consulting to 38% when allowing an advisor to act on their behalf. Our findings suggest that decision and reason alignment shape advisor preferences differently across contexts of AI use, and that alignment with a user's values does not necessarily imply willingness to delegate.

title: People prefer AI to human advice in multi-turn conversations but neither changes incentivised behaviour
evidence: Preprint; source-checked v1, peer review unverified
abstract_text: People increasingly ask AI chatbots for advice, yet large language models (LLMs) are sycophantic, overconfident, and can amplify human cognitive biases. In this article, we investigate how people perceive advice from humans versus LLMs and whether AI advice reshapes incentive-compatible donation decisions. Using Carrier, a new experimental platform, we designed an experiment where participants made a donation decision after discussing it with an AI chatbot advisor, another human, or receiving no advice. Participants judged LLM advisors to be significantly more rational, trustworthy, convincing, and sycophantic than human advisors. Analysis of chatlogs showed that LLMs were more engaged than human advisors: they shared more facts and more often stated their opinion and justified their recommendations. Despite this, donation decisions did not vary across conditions.

title: Human tutoring, generative AI tutoring and independent internet search: A randomised between‐subjects experiment on students' responses to academic challenge
abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

analysis.methods: The study was conducted in a large sixth-form college in England with a well-established digital infrastructure, including a bring-your-own-device policy, a dedicated digital leadership team and prior experience with custom-built educational GenAI tutors. Participants were aged 16-18. A total of 160 students volunteered and took part, representing approximately 5% of the college's population of around 3000. Recruitment was college-wide. The Director of Digital Strategy circulated invitations by email at several points during the academic year and a two-minute video in which the researcher explained the study and invited participation was shown during morning tutor time. Recruitment did not occur through particular subject lessons, although participation was self-selecting. Eleven participants were excluded because technical disruptions resulted in incomplete sessions or unusable data, yielding a quantitative analytic sample of 149. Usable post-task questionnaire responses were available for 154 participants (Human, n = 52; GenAI tutor, n = 52; Internet, n = 50) and were retained in a separate questionnaire dataset. Current A-level subject data were available for 144 of the 149 participants in the quantitative analytic sample. The most commonly studied subjects were Mathematics (n = 94, 65.3%), Psychology (n = 69, 47.9%), Biology (n = 43, 29.9%), Chemistry (n = 38, 26.4%), Physics (n = 37, 25.7%), Further Mathematics (n = 34, 23.6%) and Computer Science (n = 28, 19.4%). Participants could report multiple subjects. To assess baseline comparability following random allocation, participant characteristics were compared across the three conditions. Kruskal-Wallis tests identified no statistically significant differences in perceived socioeconomic status, GCSE mathematics grade, perceived mathematics ability or perceived mathematics ability relative to others (all ps ≥ 0.917). Chi-square tests likewise identified no significant associations between condition and baseline trait challenge-seeking category (p = 0.446), gender among female and male participants (p = 0.307), Mathematics participation (p = 0.606) or Further Mathematics participation (p = 0.871). The study used a single-site, three-condition, randomised between-subjects experimental design. Each participant had only one form of support and remained in that condition throughout. Random allocation was used to reduce the likelihood of systematic baseline differences between the condition groups and thereby strengthen the internal validity of the comparison (Clark et al., 2026) . Participants were individually allocated using a randomnumber generator to one-to-one human tutor, GenAI tutor or independent internet search. The quantitative analytic sample comprised 52 participants in the Human condition, 50 in the GenAI tutor condition and 47 in the Internet condition. All participants were presented with the same fixed sequence within a 90-min session: two 20-min sections of increasingly challenging mathematics problems ( S1 and S2 ), inspired by the PERC task (Porter et al., 2020) , followed by a behavioural challenge-selection task adapted from Rege et al. (2021) . Materials, task order, timings and outcome measures were held constant across conditions. Participants were instructed to use the support for guidance and not to seek direct answers. Participants in the GenAI tutor condition additionally received verbal and written guidance on using the tutor, including instructions not to enter personal data. The two-section structure was designed to examine how students responded when required to return to a new round of challenge after an earlier encounter with substantial difficulty. Effort, perceived difficulty and the number of questions attempted were recorded for each section. Task-related stress was assessed after the problem-solving sections, and behavioural challenge-seeking was assessed through the subsequent selection task. Students attended a single 90-min session conducted in a small teaching room within the college and completed the study individually on their own devices using a standardised Qualtrics platform. After instructions emphasising that tasks were intentionally challenging and optional, participants completed S1 with their assigned support, followed by effort and difficulty ratings, then S2 and the same measures. They then completed the challengeseeking task and a post-task questionnaire. The researcher was present to ensure procedural consistency. As an incentive for participation, all students were entered into a prize draw to win one of five £20 gift vouchers.
analysis.results: Findings are reported first for condition differences in perceived difficulty, effort, attempts and challenge-seeking, followed by task-related stress and changes across the two task sections. Tables 1 and 2 present the descriptive and inferential results, with significant omnibus differences examined using Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons.
analysis.discussion: The capacity of generative AI to independently complete many traditional academic tasks calls into question the educational value of using such tasks as primary indicators of learning (Corbin, Dawson, et al., 2025; Corbin, Walton, et al., 2025) . In response, there is growing consensus that evaluations of AI in education should move beyond grades to attend more closely to how learning is enacted and to the development of higher-order human capacities in human-AI interaction (Luckin, 2018 (Luckin, , 2025;; OECD, 2019 OECD, , 2025;; Wegerif & Major, 2024) . By foregrounding learners' effort, perceived difficulty, behavioural engagement and affective responses, the present study responds directly to these concerns by examining how learning is experienced and regulated under different support conditions. Even with identical tasks, the Human, GenAI tutor and Internet groups differed in their patterns of perceived difficulty, effort and attempts, while stress-response distributions varied descriptively. Consistent with long-standing critiques of performance-based assessment (Bjork & Bjork, 2011 , 2020; Marton & Saljo, 1976; Wegerif & Major, 2024) , the present findings further underscore the value of examining how students travel through learning, not just where they end up. As calls grow to prioritise the development of wider human capacities essential for learning (Luckin, 2025) , understanding these behavioural trajectories becomes critical. The findings did not support the preregistered directional hypothesis overall, as support from the GenAI tutor used in this study did not produce consistently higher effort, a greater number of attempted questions or greater challenge-seeking than the comparison conditions. Given the differences between the preregistered and implemented study, the precise outcome-and section-specific findings are interpreted as exploratory. The variation in effort, perceived difficulty and attempts across conditions suggests that some aspects of students' responses while working through challenge may be shaped by the form of interactive support available during learning, consistent with prior work on the role of framing and interaction in shaping engagement with difficulty (Duckworth, 2016; Duckworth et al., 2007; Dweck, 2006; Hadwin et al., 2018; Young et al., 2024 ). Crucially, these findings extend prior accounts by showing that these response patterns may also differ when support is provided by a GenAI tutor. Students working with the GenAI tutor used in this study reported the highest and most stable effort across sections, although the between-condition difference was significant only in Section 2, when effort was higher than in the Human condition. This higher effort co-occurred with greater perceived difficulty than under human tutoring. One possible interpretation is that the GenAI tutor used in this study helped students continue investing effort despite finding the tasks difficult, suggesting that this form of GenAI support may help sustain engagement during challenging independent work. However, higher effort could also reflect the additional exertion required when difficulty remained unresolved. Self-reported effort is not inherently positive or negative. Higher effort may indicate willingness to persist, but it may also reflect unresolved difficulty or a greater need for exertion. Conversely, lower effort may indicate disengagement, but it may also mean that less exertion was required because support made the task more manageable. The findings therefore cannot determine whether this effort represented productive persistence or difficulty that the support had not adequately alleviated. Effort was therefore interpreted alongside perceived difficulty and attempts, rather than as a standalone indicator of the quality or success of students' engagement. In the separate post-task questionnaire, the GenAI tutor condition descriptively contained a lower proportion of stressed responses than the Internet condition. As no inferential comparisons were conducted, this pattern cannot establish that GenAI tutor support reduced stress, but it is consistent with prior work suggesting that AI-supported struggle may reduce frustration, support motivation and help regulate cognitive load (Bassner et al., 2026) . The GenAI tutor condition also showed the largest descriptive increase in attempts from the first to the second section. Although co-regulation was not measured directly, the combined pattern of reported effort, perceived difficulty, attempts and stress responses is consistent with the possibility that interaction with the GenAI tutor contributed to students' regulation of behavioural engagement and affect as they worked through unresolved difficulty. This interpretation aligns with conceptual accounts that position generative AI as a potential participant in distributed co-regulatory systems (Lodge et al., 2023; Nguyen, 2025) . Consistent with expectations from scaffolding and co-regulation theory (Gaffney & Rodgers, 2018; Hadwin et al., 2018; Vygotsky, 1978; Wood et al., 1976; Wood & Wood, 1996) , the Human condition produced the most favourable difficulty profile, with students reporting the lowest perceived difficulty in both sections. Students also attempted significantly more questions than those in the GenAI tutor condition in Section 1 and the Internet condition in Section 2. Post-task responses also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses and the highest proportion of calm responses in the Human condition, adding an affective dimension to this more favourable profile. While these patterns do not establish greater conceptual progress because response accuracy and learning were not assessed, they may reflect more extensive scaffolding and co-regulatory support under human tutoring. Within this broader pattern, lower effort in the Human condition may indicate that less exertion was required to continue when support made the tasks feel more manageable, rather than reduced engagement. Viewed through this theoretical lens, the pattern observed in the GenAI tutor condition is consistent with accounts of a distinct and partial form of emerging co-regulation, rather than the fuller scaffolding and co-regulatory capacities associated with human tutoring. In contrast, the pattern under human tutoring was more consistent with scaffolding and coregulation operating together. Comparable dissociations have been observed in recent experimental studies of AI-supported learning, where improvements in affective experience under AI support were not accompanied by gains in conceptual understanding (Bassner et al., 2026) , and where AI support was associated with motivational and affective benefits while lacking the social presence and collaborative depth of human interaction (Fan et al., 2025) . Together, these patterns are consistent with positioning generative AI between human support and independent internet search along a continuum of scaffolding and coregulation. Because conceptual progress and learning were not assessed, this positioning concerns engagement with difficulty rather than comparative learning effectiveness. Figure 1 provides a schematic summary of this interpretive positioning. By comparing human tutoring, the GenAI tutor used in this study and internet-based support under controlled conditions, this study contributes empirical evidence relevant to socio-cognitive accounts of challenge and to the idea
analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be noted. The study was a single-session experiment conducted in one high-attaining, digitally confident sixth-form college. Participation was self-selecting and large proportions of the sample studied Mathematics and science subjects. Although Mathematics and Further Mathematics participation did not differ significantly across conditions, this subject profile may limit the generalisability of the findings to students with different academic backgrounds. The findings may also not generalise to contexts in which baseline self-regulation or digital familiarity is lower or to longer-term classroom settings. Effort, perceived difficulty and stress were measured using single-item self-reports, with stress assessed only once, and tasks were intentionally set above curriculum level, which may have amplified challenge-related responses. Regulatory processes were inferred indirectly through behavioural and affective indicators rather than measured directly. The number of questions attempted did not capture the accuracy or quality of students' responses. A higher number of attempts could therefore reflect productive persistence, superficial movement between questions or unproductive floundering. Attempts should consequently be interpreted as a behavioural indicator of engagement across the task, rather than as evidence of successful task progress, conceptual understanding or learning. Interaction logs and transcripts were not included in the analysis, and the frequency, content and quality of support interactions were therefore not compared systematically across conditions. Consequently, scaffolding, co-regulation and learning partnership are used as theoretical lenses for interpreting the observed patterns, rather than as processes demonstrated by the study. Support-specific factors also warrant consideration. As support was provided by a single tutor, his individual style and physical presence may have shaped participants' interactions and responses to challenge. His presence may have offered reassurance or encouraged persistence, while obtaining help required direct social interaction. By contrast, students could consult the GenAI tutor without initiating a direct social interaction whenever they wished. Responses to the GenAI tutor may also have been influenced by novelty (Fryer et al., 2017) , while the Internet condition reflected the variable quality of open web resources. Finally, because the precise underlying model snapshot and behavioural configuration were not available to the researchers, and changes during the data-collection period could not be ruled out, the findings concern Khanmigo Lite as accessed between November 2024 and July 2025. They should not be generalised uncritically to other versions of Khanmigo Lite or to GenAI tutors as a category. Differences between these conditions may therefore reflect both the source of support and how that support was accessed. Despite these limitations, the findings have implications for how challenge is supported and experienced in educational contexts. For teachers, the results suggest that support should be treated as a pedagogical decision that shapes learners' engagement with difficulty, not simply as a means of providing answers. This points to a complementary role for AI tutors alongside human instruction, where AI may support learners in continuing to invest effort during challenging independent work, while teachers monitor whether difficulty is being resolved and provide responsive support when needed. For learners, the study highlights that responses to difficulty are not solely individual traits but are shaped by the support context, underscoring the importance of developing awareness of how different forms of help influence effort, persistence and stress. This suggests value in explicitly teaching helpseeking strategies, including how to engage productively with AI tutors as a way of working through difficulty rather than bypassing challenge. More broadly, the results underscore the value of attending to learners' behavioural and affective responses when evaluating the educational impact of AI.

digest.explain: Students worked through two sets of unfamiliar math problems. The experiment asked how they responded when the work got hard and which difficulty levels they chose afterward.
digest.approach: Researchers randomly assigned students aged 16–18 at one English sixth-form college to a human math tutor, Khanmigo Lite or independent internet search. The main analysis included 149 students. Each set lasted 20 minutes.
digest.finding: On the second set, students using Khanmigo Lite rated the problems harder and reported more effort than students with a human tutor. The human-tutored group started more questions than the AI group on the first set and more than the search group on the second. The researchers found no clear difference across the three groups in the difficulty of the six problems students chose next.
digest.limitation: The experiment covered one session at one school with a single human tutor. Attempts counted questions started. The study did not score answer accuracy, test lasting learning or directly measure attention.
