title: Teacher-regulated generative AI in structured group tasks: independent performance and metacognitive judgements in higher education
abstract_text: Introduction As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in higher education classrooms, an important question is whether it shapes not only students' task performance but also how they judge their own learning. This study examined whether participation in AI-supported structured group tasks was associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration compared with non-AI-supported structured group tasks. Methods A group-randomized, post-test-only classroom design was implemented in two undergraduate classes using Rain Classroom, a digital instructional platform. Students worked in pre-existing groups, and instructional condition was randomly assigned at the group level. In the AI-supported condition, students were permitted to use the platform's built-in AI learning companion during structured group discussion; in the non-AI-supported condition, they were instructed not to use it. After previewing the post-task assessment items, students completed a task-specific judgement form before responding to the assessment itself. The final analytic sample consisted of 126 students. Results Linear mixed models accounting for class and group-level clustering indicated significantly higher independent post-task performance in the AI-supported condition, B = 0.506, SE = 0.188, p = 0.013, 95% CI [0.117, 0.894], with a small descriptive standardized mean difference ( d = 0.196). No statistically significant between-condition differences were observed in predicted performance, confidence judgements, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. Discussion These findings indicate a modest between-condition difference in post-task performance without parallel statistically detectable differences in metacognitive monitoring.

This study adopted a group-randomized, post-test-only classroom design to examine whether AI-supported structured group tasks were associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration compared with non-AI-supported structured group tasks. The study was conducted in two undergraduate classes within the same university course. Students completed the same instructional task under one of two conditions: an AI-supported condition or a non-AI-supported condition. Because the intervention was implemented through group-based classroom activity, instructional condition was randomly assigned at the group level, whereas the main outcome variables were measured at the individual level through a task-specific judgement form and an individual post-task assessment. The design was intended to preserve ecological validity while maintaining reasonable control over the role of AI in classroom learning by embedding AI as a regulated support resource during structured group discussion rather than as an unrestricted answergenerating tool. Because no pre-intervention measures of the study outcomes were collected, the design does not permit direct assessment of baseline equivalence or within-student change over time. Participants were undergraduate students enrolled in a university course taught by the researcher. During the semester, the researcher taught five sections of the course, from which two intact classes were randomly selected for inclusion in the study. The study was conducted in March 2026 in regular classroom settings and was embedded within normal teaching activities. All participants were second-year undergraduates majoring in Business English or Secretarial Studies. Age and gender were not collected as study variables. At the beginning of the semester, students in each class had already formed their own discussion groups for routine classroom activities. Group formation was based on students' free choice, and some students chose to work individually; as a result, group size ranged from 1 to 8 students. Of the 28 pre-existing groups, three were single-person groups: one was assigned to the AIsupported condition and two to the non-AI-supported condition. The remaining 25 groups consisted of two to eight students. These naturally formed groups were retained for the present study in order to preserve the ecological validity of the instructional context and to respect students' original grouping preferences. At the time of randomization, each class consisted of 14 pre-existing groups, resulting in 28 groups across the two classes. The first class included 86 enrolled students, whereas the second class included 67 students. Of these, 139 students initially consented to participate. Participation was entirely voluntary, and students were informed that choosing not to participate would not affect their course grades or academic evaluation in any way. The flow of participants from initial enrolment to the final analytic sample is shown in Figure 1 . Because the instructional intervention was implemented during small-group discussion, the pre-existing discussion groups, rather than individual students, served as the units of randomization. The 28 groups from the two classes were pooled and allocated to the two instructional conditions in SPSS using an overall 1:1 restricted randomization procedure. Class was not used as a stratification factor. This resulted in 14 groups being assigned to the AIsupported condition and 14 to the non-AI-supported condition. In Class 1, five groups were allocated to the AI-supported condition and nine to the non-AI-supported condition; in Class 2, nine groups were allocated to the AI-supported condition and five to the non-AI-supported condition. Because the pre-existing groups varied in size, group-level randomization did not produce equal numbers of individual students across the class-by-condition cells. After exclusions due to withdrawal or incomplete data, the final analytic sample consisted of 126 students, including 62 in the AI-supported condition and 64 in the non-AI-supported Flow of participants through the study. condition (see Figure 1 ). Detailed exclusion reasons and their distribution by class and instructional condition are reported in Supplementary Appendix K. Missing outcome data were not imputed, and the primary analyses were conducted using complete cases. These exclusions left 27 analytic groups (13 AI-supported and 14 non-AI-supported), as one AI-supported group in Class 2 had no remaining analysable participants. The overall exclusion proportions did not differ significantly by instructional condition, χ 2 (1, N = 139) = 0.717, p = 0.397; however, this comparison does not rule out the possibility of attrition-related bias. No exclusions were made on the basis of detected use of the Rain Classroom AI learning companion outside the assigned condition, as no such platform-based violations were identified in the usage records. The instructional activity was implemented through Rain Classroom, a smart teaching platform commonly used in Chinese higher education (Li et al., 2022; Lv et al., 2024) . The platform was used to deliver the case materials, organize the structured group discussion, administer the judgement form, and collect students' responses to the individual post-task assessment. The study was embedded in a course session focusing on life and wellbeing, and the instructional task was designed to align with this instructional theme while remaining standardized across the two classes. The study was conducted during regular 90-min class sessions and followed a standardized procedure across both classes. The five core study stages accounted for 80 min. The remaining approximately 10 min were used for routine procedural instructions and transitions between activities, including access to Rain Classroom and movement between the discussion, judgement, and assessment stages. analysis.results: In contrast to the significant difference in independent posttask performance, the adjusted between-condition difference in predicted score was not statistically significant. Neither confidence in anticipated performance nor confidence in understanding differed significantly between conditions. Thus, although the AIsupported group obtained higher actual post-task scores, the present data provide no statistically detectable evidence that AIsupported discussion also changed students' prospective estimates of performance or their immediate subjective certainty about performance and understanding. One explanation is that performance predictions and confidence judgements are shaped by more than informational support alone (Lichtenstein and Fischhoff, 1977) . In classroom settings, such judgements may reflect habitual self-evaluative tendencies, perceived task difficulty, prior academic experience, and personal standards for determining whether sufficient understanding has been achieved (Nederhand et al., 2021) . A single episode of AI-supported discussion may therefore support task preparation without being sufficient to produce a clearly detectable shift in students' prospective self-evaluations. The timing of the judgement form may also be relevant. Students completed it after viewing the assessment items but before answering them, a procedure designed to capture taskspecific judgements rather than general attitudes toward AI. Their predictions and confidence ratings may therefore have reflected a relatively cautious appraisal of the specific assessment they were about to complete rather than a broader sense of ease or familiarity associated with AI support. In this sense, the measures captured a more immediate task-specific judgement than broader self-report measures commonly used in studies of AI adoption or attitudes (Double, 2025; Schraw, 2009) . From a distributed cognition perspective, it is plausible that access to shared cognitive resources supported task preparation without necessarily changing students' personal estimates of their own performance. Because the study did not measure how individual students appropriated peer or AI contributions, this remains an interpretive possibility rather than a tested mechanism (Aarset and Johannessen, 2022; Atchley et al., 2024; Hollan et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2022 Kim et al., , 2025)) . Taken together, these findings show that higher observed performance in the AI-supported condition was not accompanied by statistically detectable differences in predicted performance or confidence. The confidence intervals around the prediction and confidence estimates all included zero and remained sufficiently wide to indicate uncertainty about the magnitude of any betweencondition differences. Given the limited number of analytic groups and the absence of an a priori power calculation, these non-significant findings should not be interpreted as evidence that the conditions were equivalent; rather, the present study did not detect parallel changes in students' immediate prospective judgements. The study also found no statistically significant differences between the AI-supported and non-AI-supported conditions in either calibration bias or absolute calibration error. The corresponding descriptive effect sizes were small (d = 0.227 for calibration bias; d = -0.144 for absolute calibration error). Thus, although students in the AI-supported condition performed significantly better on the post-task assessment, they did not show statistically detectable greater accuracy in judging their own performance than students in the non-AI-supported condition. This pattern is consistent with the distinction between task performance and metacognitive accuracy (Janssen and Lazonder, 2024; Schraw, 2009) . AI-supported discussion may assist task preparation without necessarily changing the processes students use to evaluate how well they are likely to perform. Performance and accurate self-monitoring should therefore not be assumed to develop in parallel. One explanation is that cognitive calibration requires more than informational assistance or discussion support (Janssen and Lazonder, 2024) . Better calibration may require explicit opportunities to compare judgements with outcomes, reflect on the basis of confidence, and evaluate the limits of one's understanding (Wang et al., 2024) . In the present study, the Rain Classroom AI learning companion supported group discussion but was not designed specifically to prompt metacognitive reflection, confidence checking, or prediction-feedback comparison. The instructional design therefore targeted task engagement more directly than calibration processes. Distributed cognition provides a contextual rather than causal interpretation of this result. The AI-supported task made information and interpretive resources available across peers, task materials, and the AI tool (Aarset and Johannessen, 2022; Hollan et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2022) , but the study did not directly assess whether or how these shared resources were internalized by individual students. It is therefore possible that collaborative resources supported task processing without producing a corresponding difference in individual metacognitive monitoring, but this mechanism remains to be tested directly (Atchley et al., 2024; Qiao et al., 2024) . The short-term nature of the activity may also be relevant. Calibration depends on the alignment between subjective judgement and actual performance and may require repeated cycles of prediction, action, feedback, and revision before measurable change becomes visible (Janssen and Lazonder, 2024; Wang et al., 2024) . A single classroom session may therefore be more likely to reveal an immediate performance difference than a stable change in monitoring accuracy. Because both predicted and actual performance were measured on bounded 0-10 scales, and actual scores showed substantial upper-end concentration, the derived calibration indices also had constrained score distributions, which may have reduced their sensitivity to between-condition differences. The non-significant calibration findings should therefore be interpreted cautiously. They provide no evidence that the present form of AI-supported discussion improved calibration accuracy, while the brief intervention and restricted score variability may have limited sensitivity to detect such differences. If improved judgement accuracy is an instructional goal, additional metacognitive scaffolding may be needed alongside AI-supported task activities. Taken together, this differentiated pattern suggests a theoretically important distinction between externally supported task processing and internally calibrated self-monitoring. In a structured collaborative task, AI may expand the informational and interpretive resources available to the group, but the present findings do not establish whether such support changes individual metacognitive monitoring.
analysis.discussion: This study examined whether AI-supported structured group tasks were associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration. The findings revealed a differentiated pattern across outcomes. Students in the AI-supported condition obtained significantly higher scores on the independent post-task assessment than those in the non-AIsupported condition. However, no statistically significant betweencondition differences were found in predicted score, confidence in anticipated performance, confidence in understanding, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. Taken together, the statistically detectable difference was concentrated at the level of independent task performance rather than extending to students' prospective judgements or metacognitive accuracy. This pattern underscores the importance of examining performance and metacognitive monitoring as related but distinct outcomes of AI-supported classroom activity. This study examined whether AI-supported structured group tasks were associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration in a higher education classroom. Using a group-randomized, post-test-only classroom design implemented through Rain Classroom, the analysis indicated that students in the AI-supported condition obtained higher scores on the independent post-task assessment than those in the non-AI-supported condition. However, no statistically significant between-condition differences were observed in predicted performance, confidence in anticipated performance, confidence in understanding, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. These findings indicate that, in the present instructional context, the AI-supported condition was associated with modestly higher performance on this task-specific assessment, without statistically detectable between-condition differences in performance predictions, confidence judgements, or cognitive calibration. Overall, the findings highlight the value of distinguishing task performance from metacognitive monitoring as separate outcomes when evaluating AI-supported classroom activities in higher education.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations of the present study should be considered when interpreting the findings, with the most consequential relating to study design, measurement, and statistical precision. First, no pre-intervention measures of content knowledge, confidence, or calibration were collected. Consequently, although random assignment occurred at the group level, it cannot be determined with certainty whether the two instructional conditions were fully equivalent on these variables prior to the intervention. This limits the strength of causal inference that can be drawn from the observed post-task differences. Future research could incorporate pre-and post-intervention measures in order to examine more directly how AI-supported structured group tasks influence change over time in both learning outcomes and metacognitive judgements. Second, the post-task assessment was intentionally brief and designed for classroom implementation. Although this format suited the practical constraints of a single class session and aligned closely with the instructional task, it should be interpreted as a task-specific indicator of learning rather than as a fully validated standardized measure. Because the assessment consisted of only four heterogeneous items, score precision may have been limited, and individual items may have had a relatively strong influence on total scores. Because item-level scores were not retained in the analytic dataset, item-specific performance patterns could not be examined retrospectively. The score distribution also showed notable upper-end concentration: 27.8% of the full sample obtained the maximum score, and ceiling concentration was particularly pronounced in the Class 1 AI-supported subgroup, where 69.0% obtained the maximum. This restricted variability may have reduced sensitivity for estimating between-condition differences in performance and, because calibration indices were derived from predicted and actual scores on the same bounded 0-10 scale, may also have constrained calibration-related outcomes. Although inter-rater reliability for the application/transfer item was excellent for the mean of the two ratings, ICC (A,2) = 0.935, 95% CI [0.890, 0.955], the brevity, heterogeneity, and upper-end concentration of the assessment remain important constraints. Future research could employ more extensive outcome measures with greater discrimination at the upper end. Third, no a priori power analysis was conducted. Together with the limited number of analytic groups, this means that the study may have had limited statistical precision for detecting small or moderate between-condition differences in performance predictions, confidence, or calibration. The non-significant findings should accordingly be interpreted as an absence of statistically detectable differences in this sample rather than as evidence of equivalence between conditions. Future studies should use larger samples, prospectively justified sample sizes, and repeated assessments to provide a more precise account of how AI-supported learning relates to both performance and metacognitive monitoring. Fourth, the study was conducted by the researcher acting as the course instructor. Although this arrangement supported implementation within an authentic teaching context, it also introduced the possibility of instructor-related bias. The dual role of researcher and instructor may have influenced instructional delivery, participant expectations, or intervention fidelity in subtle but unmeasured ways. Future research could reduce this source of bias by involving independent instructors, using multiple instructors, or adopting designs in which implementation and analysis are more clearly separated. Fifth, although the study examined performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration in addition to performance, it did not capture fine-grained interaction data on how groups actually used the AI support during discussion. For example, the study did not analyse the specific prompts students entered, the types of responses generated by the AI learning companion, or the extent to which different groups relied on AI in different ways. As a result, the present findings can describe between-condition differences, but cannot identify the detailed mechanisms through which those differences emerged. Future research could incorporate process-oriented data such as prompt logs, interaction traces, discussion transcripts, or response uptake patterns to move beyond whether conditions differ and toward a more precise understanding of how different forms of human-AI interaction relate to performance and metacognitive outcomes. Sixth, the AI support examined in this study was the Rain Classroom AI learning companion, embedded within a specific classroom platform and used under teacher-regulated conditions. The comparison in this study was therefore based on permitted vs. non-permitted use of a platform-embedded AI tool within a structured classroom task, rather than on unrestricted use of external generative AI systems. In addition, the intervention was relatively short in duration, as the study focused on a single classroom-based activity. As a result, the findings should not be taken as applying equally to all forms of generative AI or to more open-ended, sustained, or student-directed AI use. Future research could compare different AI systems, interaction conditions, and intervention durations in order to clarify how different AI affordances and instructional arrangements shape both learning outcomes and metacognitive processes (Atchley et al., 2024; Bauer et al., 2025; Janssen and Lazonder, 2024; Kim et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024) . Seventh, the study was conducted in a specific instructional context, namely a university course session on life and wellbeing, using a single case-based structured group task. Although this context provided an authentic classroom setting for examining AI-supported learning, the findings should not be assumed to generalize directly to other subjects, task types, or higher education contexts. The role of AI support may differ across disciplines, especially in courses characterized by different epistemic demands, problem-solving requirements, or assessment forms (Bond et al., 2024; Qian, 2025) . Future research could therefore examine whether the present pattern of findings is specific to this course theme and task design or reflects a more general feature of AIsupported structured group learning across disciplinary contexts.

title: Editorial: Harnessing AI to support self-regulated learning in educational and workplace settings

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: The Research Topic begins with Achuthan's Artificial intelligence and learner autonomy: a meta-analysis of self-regulated and self-directed learning, which provides a broad empirical examination of the relationship between AI and learner autonomy. Synthesizing 32 empirical studies, 92 effect sizes, and 3,029 participants, the study examines the effects of AI-based interventions on SRL, self-directed learning (SDL), different dimensions and phases of SRL, and learning outcomes. The findings indicate positive effects of AI interventions on overall SRL and SDL, with particularly notable effects during the forethought phase, including goal setting and planning. At the same time, less consistent effects for behavioral regulation point to an important design challenge: supporting learners in knowing what to do and why to do it does not necessarily ensure that they will translate those intentions into effective action. The findings therefore provide encouraging evidence for AI as a scaffold for self-regulation while highlighting the importance of designing support across the full SRL cycle.Building on this macro-level evidence, Agustin's AI as a co-regulator: relational design for strengthening self-regulated learning addresses the theoretical mechanics of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in Winne and Hadwin's COPES architecture, this conceptual paper tackles a core dilemma in educational technology: how can AI assist learners without eroding the cognitive agency and productive struggle essential to self-regulation? Agustin introduces "productive metacognitive friction" -the deliberate structuring of challenge and discrepancy within AI interaction -as a design mechanism to prevent passive reliance. The article presents five relational design principles alongside an evaluation framework prioritizing learner autonomy, interpretability, process integrity, and long-term developmental growth across both formal education and workplace reskilling environments.Moving from meta-analytic synthesis and conceptual frameworks to empirical classroom research, Gu et al.'s Fostering feedback literacy by scaffolding self-regulated feedback: a comparative study of GenAI and human peers examines the operational mechanisms through which GenAI fosters feedback literacya key component of self-regulated learning. In a comparative mixed-methods study of first-year undergraduates in Hong Kong, the authors compare the developmental impact of GenAI-generated feedback against traditional human peer review. Their findings demonstrate that GenAI yields a statistically significant improvement in feedback literacy over human peer feedback alone. Qualitative evidence reveals that this advantage stems from GenAI's ability to scaffold distinct self-regulatory behaviors: providing immediate, non-judgmental spaces for goal setting, structured planning, critical evaluation, and real-time self-reflection. By removing the interpersonal friction and psychological safety concerns common in peer review, GenAI emerges as an effective tool for cultivating student feedback literacy.Finally, Chang et al.'s "Should I tell my teacher?" Student AI disclosure practices, stigma, and selfregulated learning in higher education examines the affective, social, and institutional factors that influence how learners adopt these tools in practice. Focusing on undergraduate students at a Canadian university, the authors explore the intersection of student AI disclosure practices, social stigma, and SRL processes. Their findings illuminate a key tension: while transparent disclosure to instructors correlates with proactive self-regulated learning behaviors (a "transparent-disclosure pattern"), fear of academic judgment and social stigmatization often triggers an "anxious-concealment pattern." Highly anxious students who use AI heavily are more likely to conceal their usage or restrict sharing to peer networks. This study highlights that technical scaffolds cannot succeed in a vacuum; institutional policies and pedagogical environments must account for emotional and social dynamics to prevent secrecy from undermining reflective SRL practices.Considered together, the four articles in this Research Topic illustrate that AI's role in self-regulated learning extends far beyond simple automation or content delivery. Achuthan's meta-analysis provides evidence of AI's potential to strengthen SRL and SDL, while also identifying limitations in behavioral regulation. Agustin's framework addresses this challenge conceptually by positioning AI as a co-regulator that supports learners without displacing their agency. Gu et al. demonstrate how such support can be enacted in feedback processes, whereas Chang et al. show how emotions, stigma, and institutional expectations shape learners' decisions about AI use. This collection highlights that realizing the promise of AI-supported self-regulated learning requires more than personalization or automation. Research and design must examine how AI can scaffold regulatory processes, support learner autonomy and human agency, and safeguard against cognitive over-reliance.

abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of online educational technologies, instructional videos have become a pivotal tool for flexible and efficient learning. The integration of visual aids, such as animations and dynamic elements, aims to enhance the learning experience; however, their effectiveness remains debated. This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static AI-generated images or manually animated versions of those images. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 undergraduate participants ( n = 10 per cell), comparing static versus motion-enhanced presentation conditions across male and female participant groups. Stable Diffusion XL generated the base images, and CapCut was used to add motion; the motion itself was not AI-generated. Participants viewed a 140-s mobile video on mortise-and-tenon structures, completed a 10-item accuracy test, and rated willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and mental effort. The ANOVA results provided no statistically significant evidence of a main effect of motion on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several subjective outcomes. For acceptability, the gender × motion interaction was statistically significant, but Bonferroni-adjusted simple-effect tests supported a gender-group difference only in the static condition. For mental effort, the interaction was also statistically significant; adjusted simple-effect tests indicated higher mental effort among female than male participants in the dynamic condition and higher mental effort in the static than dynamic condition among male participants. Given the small sample and multiple outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

analysis.discussion: Before discussing the implications of our findings, it is important to define the scope within which these results are most directly applicable. This study examined a specific type of instructional contentvisuospatially complex material (mortise and tenon structures) requiring understanding of three-dimensional relationships and assembly processes. The participants were higher education students with no prior domain knowledge, and the instructional videos were brief (140 s) and delivered on mobile devices. Therefore, our findings are most directly relevant to similar learning contexts: technical or procedural knowledge domains, novice learners, and short-format mobile learning environments. The present study investigated the effects of motion-enhanced AI-generated images in instructional videos on learning performance and subjective experience, with a particular focus on genderbased differences. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), this research aimed to elucidate whether dynamic visual presentations differentially impact male and female learners. The findings reveal a nuanced pattern: while motion effects alone did not significantly enhance learning accuracy, gender was associated with differences in objective performance and subjective evaluations. Significant interaction effects between gender and motion effects were observed for acceptability and mental effort, suggesting that responses to dynamic visual information may differ across gender groups; however, these differences should be interpreted cautiously because gender was not experimentally manipulated and relevant covariates were not measured. The present study yielded several noteworthy findings regarding the differential impact of motion-enhanced AI-generated images on male and female learners. A significant main effect of gender was observed, with male learners showing higher accuracy rates than female learners in this sample. However, this difference cannot be confidently attributed to spatial-processing ability, because the study did not measure baseline spatial ability, technology experience, general academic ability, or interest in the subject. Screening for prior woodworking knowledge does not ensure equivalence in these characteristics. Therefore, the accuracy difference may reflect unmeasured baseline differences, and this explanation should be treated as tentative. These findings address Q2 by indicating a difference between gender groups in this sample, but the underlying reasons remain unclear. This exploratory study examined learning performance and subjective responses to static versus motion-enhanced AI-generated images in a short mobile instructional video. No statistically significant evidence was found for a main effect of presentation condition on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several outcomes, but these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of inherent gender-based cognitive differences. For acceptability, a significant gender group × presentation condition interaction was observed. Bonferroni-adjusted simpleeffect tests indicated that female participants reported higher acceptability than male participants in the static condition, whereas the gender-group difference in the dynamic condition was not statistically significant. For perceived mental effort, the interaction was also significant: female participants reported higher mental effort than male participants in the dynamic condition, and male participants reported higher mental effort in the static than in the dynamic condition. The remaining adjusted comparisons were not statistically significant. These findings suggest that the effects of motion-enhanced visual presentation may vary across learners and outcomes rather than producing a uniform benefit. However, the small sample, absence of a formal manipulation check, limitations in measurement validation, multiple exploratory outcomes, and unmeasured learner characteristics constrain generalization. TAM-related perceptions and Cognitive Load Theory therefore serve as interpretive perspectives rather than as a tested integrated model. Future research should use larger samples, validated measures, appropriate analyses for bounded accuracy data, and learner-controlled or adaptive presentation based on measured needs and preferences rather than gender-based design prescriptions.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the findings of this study and should be considered when interpreting the results. First, no formal manipulation check or independent image-quality assessment was conducted. We did not collect expert or participant ratings of visual quality, structural accuracy, semantic consistency, motion salience, or informational equivalence between the static and dynamic conditions. Although images were informally screened for visible artifacts and structural accuracy before inclusion, this screening served only as a material-selection step and does not constitute formal validation. We therefore cannot conclusively verify that participants perceived the static/dynamic distinction as intended, nor can we fully rule out artifact-related confounding. Future research should include manipulation checks and systematic ratings of visual quality, structural accuracy, semantic consistency, motion salience, and informational equivalence. Second, the measurement instruments have several limitations. No formal pilot testing was conducted. The reliability coefficients reported in the original manuscript were drawn from prior source studies rather than calculated in the present sample; sample-specific reliability estimates are now reported in Supplementary material but should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size. The 10-item true/false accuracy test was reviewed for content validity by three experts, but no itemlevel analysis of difficulty, discrimination, or reliability was conducted. The acceptability scale was newly developed for this study and has not been formally validated; its factor structure, convergent validity, and discriminant validity remain unknown. The mental effort measure captures self-reported perceived effort and should not be interpreted as a pure measure of extraneous cognitive load. Future research should pilot-test all instruments, conduct item analyses, validate newly developed scales, and use measures that distinguish intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load more precisely. Third, the study does not test a full TAM model or provide measurement-model evaluation. TAM-related perceptions and Cognitive Load Theory are used as interpretive perspectives rather than as a tested integrated model. Willingness to continue learning is an intention-related evaluation, ease of understanding is perceived comprehensibility, preference is an affective evaluation of the video, and acceptability is a study-specific evaluation. No causal paths, factor structure, convergent validity, or discriminant validity are claimed. Future research should either validate adapted TAM constructs using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling or continue to use them as exploratory interpretive tools. Fourth, the sample size was small (N = 40; n = 10 per cell), and no a priori power analysis was conducted. Small or medium effects may therefore not have been detected. Nonsignificant results are reported as "no statistically significant evidence was found" rather than as proof that no difference exists, and 95% confidence intervals for nonsignificant effects are provided in Supplementary material. Future research should recruit larger and more diverse samples to detect small-tomedium effects. Fifth, several statistical issues require cautious interpretation. Learning accuracy was derived from 10 true/false items and is therefore bounded count data. A binomial generalized linear model would have been more appropriate than treating accuracy as a normally distributed continuous variable; however, the present study relied on ANOVA as an exploratory and comparability-oriented analysis, and no binomial GLM was conducted. In addition, because several dependent variables were examined, inflated Type I error cannot be ruled out; no formal multiplicity correction (e.g., Benjamini-Hochberg FDR) was applied, and interaction effects on secondary outcomes should therefore be interpreted as exploratory. Future research should use binomial or item-level mixed models for bounded accuracy data, report full assumption checks, apply appropriate multiplicity corrections, and provide effect sizes with confidence intervals. Accordingly, nonsignificant findings should be described as absence of statistically significant evidence rather than as evidence of no effect. Sixth, gender-related interpretations remain tentative. Gender was recorded as a binary category based on participant self-report; the source documentation does not specify whether this category reflects self-identified gender or biological sex, and no biological or essentialist interpretation is made. Gender was treated as an observed grouping variable, not as a causal or biological determinant. Baseline spatial ability, technology familiarity, general academic ability, anxiety, interest in woodworking, and prior experience were not objectively measured. Screening for prior woodworking knowledge does not ensure equivalence in these characteristics. The observed differences may therefore reflect unmeasured baseline differences, and they should not be used to prescribe different instructional treatments based solely on gender. Future research should include standardized measures of spatial ability, technology familiarity, and prior interest as covariates and should emphasize learner-controlled or adaptive presentation based on measured needs and preferences rather than gender-based design. Seventh, the qualitative component of this study is descriptive and lacks the methodological rigor expected of standalone qualitative research. The available record does not document participant selection beyond cell counts (three participants per cell, total N = 12; 6 male, 6 female), recording and transcription procedures, coding stages, number of coders, disagreement resolution, language and translation procedures, or criteria for thematic saturation. Interviews lasted 5-10 min and were conducted immediately after questionnaire completion. The interview comments are therefore presented as supplementary illustrations and should not be described as independently corroborating the quantitative findings. Future work should adopt established guidelines for rigorous thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) , employ multiple independent coders with systematic reliability assessment, and provide comprehensive documentation of the analytic process. Eighth, the experimental materials and context limit generalizability. The dynamic condition used a mixed-process approach: base images were AI-generated using Stable Diffusion XL, but motion effects were manually applied using CapCut. This differs from pure AI-generated videos, which may exhibit different motion characteristics, temporal artifacts, or semantic inconsistencies. Exact generation and animation parameters are also incompletely documented, limiting reproducibility. The study focused on a single domain-traditional woodworking structures (mortise-and-tenon joints)-selected for its high visuospatial complexity. The instructional videos were brief (140 s) and delivered on a mobile device. abstract_text: Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

This finding is consistent with research suggesting that generative AI may be associated with learner autonomy and confidence in learning processes ( Chan and Hu, 2023 ; Chiu, 2024 ). Third, the results are consistent with a sequential indirect association linking perceived agentic AI capability, extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and student engagement. This pattern is compatible with the proposed “cognitive relief–motivational enhancement” framework, but it does not validate a causal chain because all constructs were measured at one time point. Future longitudinal or experimental research is needed to examine temporal ordering and causal mechanisms. This study examines associations among perceived Agentic AI capability, extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development education. The findings indicate that higher perceived Agentic AI capability is associated with lower extraneous cognitive load and higher academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The bootstrap analysis identifies statistically significant indirect associations, including a sequential indirect association. The results are consistent with the proposed cognitive relief–motivational enhancement framework. The findings extend discussion of AI-supported complex learning beyond technology acceptance and learning performance, while highlighting the need for further longitudinal, experimental, and multi-source research. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the context-specific sample limits generalizability across disciplines, institutions, and cultural contexts. Second, the cross-sectional design and single-source self-reports constrain causal inference and may introduce common method bias. Future research could employ longitudinal or experimental designs and incorporate learning analytics, behavioral indicators, and independently assessed outcomes. Third, OSE is measured using one item for each of the behavioral, cognitive, and emotional dimensions and should therefore be interpreted as an overall self-reported engagement measure rather than a fully validated higher-order reflective construct. Future studies should use multiple items per dimension and further assess its measurement properties. Fourth, the non-significant multi-group results should be interpreted cautiously, as relatively small subgroup sizes may limit statistical power and do not definitively rule out potential moderating effects of prior programming experience or AI usage frequency. Larger and more diverse samples are needed to examine these potential differences. Finally, although the study involves group-based project work, the available data do not permit cluster-adjusted analysis. Future research should record course-section and project-group membership and account for potential within-group dependence.

abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence has entered animation classrooms faster than research has been able to describe what it does to learning. This study developed a “Learning-Thinking-Applying-Creating” (LTAC) integrated teaching model built on an open-source AIGC toolchain and evaluated it in a twelve-week quasi-experiment with second-year animation students, two intact classes being allocated to an experimental or a control condition. Cognitive load was measured with a three-subscale instrument adapted from Paas and from Leppink and colleagues, and divergent thinking with an abbreviated Torrance-type battery scored for fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration by two trained raters who worked blind to group and occasion (intraclass correlations 0.86 to 0.91). Data were collected at pretest, mid-test, and posttest. Analysis of covariance indicated that the intervention lowered extraneous load and raised germane load while leaving intrinsic load unchanged. Repeated-measures analysis revealed selective gains: originality and elaboration improved more in the experimental group, whereas fluency and flexibility rose in both. Structural equation modelling was consistent with a differentiated mechanism, in which lower extraneous load predicted fluency and flexibility, germane load related to originality and elaboration indirectly through a deep-processing strategy, and intrinsic load showed an inverted-U association with the creative-thinking composite. Because the outcome measure is domain-general, the results speak to divergent thinking rather than to animation ability as such. The study extends cognitive load theory into generative-AI-supported creative education and offers animation programmes a reproducible instructional design that lowers production barriers while protecting deep creative work.

The selective response of the facets asks for a different explanation. Fluency and flexibility trade largely on retrieval speed and category switching, capacities that improve with practice in either condition, so it is unsurprising that they rose in both groups without a group difference 28 . Originality and elaboration depend instead on deeper transformation-combining remote associates, refining a concept until it holds together-and these operations draw on precisely the schema-building resources that germane load names 30 . On this reading the intervention did not make students think more; it changed the quality of thinking that the freed capacity could sustain, which is why the advantage concentrated in the two facets most sensitive to deep processing. The correlations in Fig. 7 sharpen that account. Fluency and flexibility hang together closely, as they should if both index the breadth of an initial search through memory, and their joint insensitivity to condition suggests that the generative toolchain did not simply accelerate idea retrieval. Originality and elaboration form a separate and more moderate pairing, and their weak association with fluency matters for interpretation: had originality risen only because students produced more responses, its correlation with fluency should have been considerably higher than the 0.41 observed. The same two-part structure has emerged from factor analyses of the Torrance battery, where fluency-driven and transformation-driven components separate rather than collapse into a single dimension 31 . Set against the long-run decline in originality and elaboration documented for large samples, the present result reads as a modest counterpoint, since the facets hardest to move historically are the ones this intervention moved 46 . Ulger's finding that creative training can lift divergent-thinking scores without touching problem-solving is a useful caution in the other direction: facet-level gains need not generalise to the wider construct 29 . The inverted-U finding for intrinsic load carries a caution that the earlier sections could only foreshadow. Too little intrinsic challenge leaves creative reasoning underpowered, while too much saturates working memory and crowds out the generative operations creativity needs 34 . The practical lesson is that intrinsic load should be tuned rather than minimised. A teacher designing an AIGC-supported animation task ought to calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range-demanding enough to engage, restrained enough to leave room for exploration-rather than assuming that easier is always better 12 . This tempers a common but simplistic reading of load theory, and it is among the more transferable takeaways here. Set against prior work, these results are largely consonant but not identical. Studies pairing design thinking with germane load in STEAM settings likewise found creativity gains routed through deep engagement, which aligns with the mediation reported above 30 . The divergence lies in specificity: earlier flipped-learning and projectbased interventions reported broad creative-thinking improvement without partitioning which facets responded, so their apparent whole-scale gains may have masked the facet-level selectivity observed here 28 . Measurement grain is the likeliest reason for the discrepancy, since aggregating creativity into a single score can hide exactly the discriminant pattern that makes a mechanism legible 20 . Three implications follow for theory. The first concerns the status of germane load. Cognitive load theory has increasingly treated germane load as a redistribution of resources rather than an independent source of demand 14 , and the mediation estimate reported here gives that reconceptualisation an empirical foothold in a creative domain: germane load acted on originality and elaboration not directly but through a deep-processing strategy, which is what a redistribution account predicts. The second concerns the shape of the intrinsic-load effect. A curvilinear relation is hard to reconcile with the standard prescription to minimise load, and it suggests that the prescription was always domain-bound, holding for schema acquisition but not for tasks whose value lies in exploration. The third concerns creativity theory. Because the four facets responded differently to one instructional manipulation, treating divergent thinking as a single latent ability discards information that a facet-level model retains-an argument the creativity literature has long made on psychometric grounds 31 and that an intervention study can now make on experimental ones. And calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range instead of smoothing it away. reading.overview: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in higher education; however, little is known about what its use means for adult learners’ digital well-being (DWB) and quality of life (QoL). This mixed-methods study, which leaned towards a qualitative design (qualitative dominant), investigated these issues among adult learners at a university in Ghana.
reading.findings: The results showed universal access to smartphones (99%), while 71% had access to a laptop. Adult learners in this cross-sectional survey reported a generally positive appraisal of their DWB. Overall, the DWB mean score (M = 4.58, SD = 0.76) is above the scale midpoint, indicating a favourable orientation towards GenAI use, although some variation exists across the well-being domains. The mental subscale showed modestly positive cognitive and psychosocial gains (M = 4.09, SD = 1.12), with the strongest item endorsements for improved problem-solving (M=4.94, SD=1.49), increased productivity (M=4.42, SD=1.59), greater decisiveness (M = 4.42, SD = 1.48) and feeling more cheerful (M = 4.42, SD = 1.64). The emotional subscale also reflected positive outcomes (M = 4.51, SD = 1.29), driven by items such as increased interest in new things (M = 5.08, SD = 1.46) and clearer thinking (M = 4.60, SD = 1.61). Following reverse coding, the physical DWB subscale recorded the highest mean (M = 5.14, SD = 1.45), with all indicators (sleep, eating, aches, and reduced exercise) scoring above the neutral point (4.93 ≤ M ≤ 5.37). However, item-level frequencies indicate that this pattern was not uniform. While most respondents selected the disagreement options, a minority reported physical strain: 17.0% reported disturbed sleep, 10.9% reported changes in eating habits, 16.5% reported physical discomfort, and 16.5% reported reduced physical exercise. Thus, although the overall trend suggests limited physical strain, less than half of the sample still experienced some bodily effects associated with GenAI use. For QoL, the composite mean (M = 2.06, SD = 0.94) shows that adult learners reported some improvement in daily functioning, safety, control, activity engagement, and time efficiency (Table 3). The item means cluster between 2.25 and 2.58, for instance, control over daily activities (M = 2.58, SD = 0.54) and participation in enjoyable activities (M = 2.54, SD = 0.54). Nonetheless, the QoL findings should be interpreted with caution for two reasons. First, some items had fewer responses (n = 111–135). Second, the non-substantive options (i.e., “Does not apply” and “Do not know”) were excluded from scoring, so the observed mean reflects only substantive responses. For these reasons, the QoL results should be read as modest and suggestive rather than strong, and they should not be generalised to all adult learners without caution. reading.interpretation: The rise of GenAI technologies in educational settings extends beyond instructional implications but also has consequential psychological impacts on the user. As accurately captured by Christodoulou and Zembylas23, technology acceptance is not a clear-cut matter of positive or negative attitudes but involves complicated stories and changes in relationships that affect the views and experiences of users. The present study attempts to address the gap in current literature on the lack of a comprehensive focus and understanding of the consequences of GenAI use on the “human side” of diverse cohorts of adult learners, particularly within the African/Ghanaian Taken together, findings from both the quantitative and qualitative phases paint a similar picture of how adult learners in the study perceive their DWB and QoL when interacting with GenAI. In the two phases of the study, adult learners' engagement with GenAI is characterised by coexisting gains and strain and not just a uniformly positive or negative experience. In the quantitative phase, DWB mean score was slightly above the 7-point Likert scale midpoint, with a meaningful minority of respondents reporting physical strain, and the composite mean of QoL indicated only modest gains in some aspects of GenAI-supported learning. The qualitative phase of the study throws further light on the mixed results in the survey; collaborators reflected on both appreciation for GenAI’s efficiency and anxiety over its encroachment on human creativity and authenticity. For QoL, the composite mean (M = 2.06, SD = 0.94) shows that adult learners reported some improvement in daily functioning, safety, control, activity engagement, and time efficiency (Table 3). The item means cluster between 2.25 and 2.58, for instance, control over daily activities (M = 2.58, SD = 0.54) and participation in enjoyable activities (M = 2.54, SD = 0.54). Nonetheless, the QoL findings should be interpreted with caution for two reasons. First, some items had fewer responses (n = 111–135). Second, the non-substantive options (i.e., “Does not apply” and “Do not know”) were excluded from scoring, so the observed mean reflects only substantive responses. For these reasons, the QoL results should be read as modest and suggestive rather than strong, and they should not be generalised to all adult learners without caution. Most respondents accessed GenAI via smartphones (80.2%) while a few used their laptops (15.1%) and other devices. GenAI usage was mostly for education and research (76.4%), work/business (11.8%) and personal projects (7.1%). Digital self-competence was largely intermediate (56.6%) to advanced (23.6%), and one-third indicated moderate familiarity with GenAI. These results suggest that mobile interfaces are the primary gateway for AI-mediated learning, with most respondents possessing at least baseline proficiency. Further, the frequency of GenAI use showed considerable variability. For instance, 41% rarely use GenAI, nearly one-third use GenAI daily (31.6%), while the remaining (27.4%) report weekly use. Slightly more than half of the respondents spend less than one hour daily using GenAI, and very few are heavy daily users. Respondents reported minimal disruptions/constraints with GenAI usage. For instance, 27.8% reported experiencing power outages and nearly half (49.5%) cited occasionally unstable internet connections that affect and shape their patterns of engagement and the types of tasks they undertake. The most frequently cited facilitators were perceived output quality or improved work quality (83 mentions), and timesaving/efficiency gains (61), followed by improved learning or comprehension (37), personalised support (32), and research support or access to resources (29); accessibility and simplification, and development of AI skills were also noted albeit less frequently. analysis.discussion: The rise of GenAI technologies in educational settings extends beyond instructional implications but also has consequential psychological impacts on the user. As accurately captured by Christodoulou and Zembylas23, technology acceptance is not a clear-cut matter of positive or negative attitudes but involves complicated stories and changes in relationships that affect the views and experiences of users. The present study attempts to address the gap in current literature on the lack of a comprehensive focus and understanding of the consequences of GenAI use on the “human side” of diverse cohorts of adult learners, particularly within the African/Ghanaian Taken together, findings from both the quantitative and qualitative phases paint a similar picture of how adult learners in the study perceive their DWB and QoL when interacting with GenAI. In the two phases of the study, adult learners' engagement with GenAI is characterised by coexisting gains and strain and not just a uniformly positive or negative experience. In the quantitative phase, DWB mean score was slightly above the 7-point Likert scale midpoint, with a meaningful minority of respondents reporting physical strain, and the composite mean of QoL indicated only modest gains in some aspects of GenAI-supported learning. The qualitative phase of the study throws further light on the mixed results in the survey; collaborators reflected on both appreciation for GenAI’s efficiency and anxiety over its encroachment on human creativity and authenticity. Using the unified ecological framework as a lens to understand the reciprocal and dynamic interrelationships between individuals, digital platforms, physical spaces, and macro-level factors, both findings highlight that adult learners’ DWB is a function of these interrelated factors. First, results from the survey and storytelling reveal that adult learners are knowledgeable of digital tools (including GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, etc.) and, on average, possess digital skills and competencies which they use to interact meaningfully across several digital platforms (i.e. Google, learning management systems). Second, interaction on digital platforms occurs at multiple levels and at different physical places (e.g. home, school setting) for some purposeful outcomes. Positive outcomes through GenAI use reflect gains (manifested as strengths) whilst the negative experiences Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:37204 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78289-5 14 and outcomes create digital anxieties (afflictions). Third, GenAI use within the higher education context is constrained or limited by institutional-level factors (macro-level) such as policies on GenAI use, access to digital platforms and type of engagement. Thus, institutional factors mediate and shape adult learners' use of GenAI within this context. As such, adult learners' experiences of the extent to which their level of need and satisfaction is met through GenAI use reveal their state of well-being/wellness. Furthermore, both results highlight that within the higher education context, adult learners’ use of GenAI on a variety of digital platforms to perform academic and non-academic tasks is pervasive. Multiple digital connectivity at different places fosters a continuous cycle of constantly and actively creating and recreating their digital experiences, leading to cognitive and affective gains as well as embodied strains. Through such a process, they develop several coping systems which are mostly culturally embedded to counteract and adjust to the unpleasant physical afflictions. In sum, adult learners' digital well-being occurs through these nested multiple layers of influence (at the individual, meso and macro-levels), and is sustained by the powerful functionalities In addition, the results reveal that adult learners' positive gains with GenAI usage moderately influenced their cognitive, affective, and psychosocial well-being. For example, the qualitative arm of the study showed that adult learners appreciated the powerful functionalities of GenAI through enhanced efficiency in learning, but expressed psychological strain and apprehension. While it is true that GenAI tools like ChatGPT can enhance cognitive tasks, for instance, by making problem-solving activities easier, improving self-efficacy for task resolution and enhancing the quality and originality of solutions83, blind usage does not foster critical thinking and problem-solving, which are essential for academic and lifelong success15. Furthermore, the study found that some adult learners experienced minimal effects on their physical well-being as a result of GenAI usage, necessitating the development of self-adaptive coping mechanisms to alleviate the negative impacts of their digital experiences. Inferring from the unified ecological framework8, which illustrates a linkage between physical and digital domains influencing DWB when interacting with AI, the results imply that while GenAI usage may confer mental and emotional advantages, these are accompanied by modest but consistent reports of adverse bodily effects. Past studies have suggested that GenAI can reduce stress by streamlining tasks or creating a stress-free and emotionally supportive learning environment42,43,84, but excessive use of such technologies can lead to heightened anxiety, burnout, and sleep disturbance85. The survey results further showed that adult learners' experience of unstable internet connectivity and institutional policies inhibit their experiences with GenAI usage and moderately impact their physical well- being. Drawing on the unified ecological framework, this finding highlights the interconnections between physical spaces and macro-social factors which directly or indirectly influence adult learners' well-being. The physical place comprises different built and natural characteristics8. Studies show that the non-human elements in the physical setting impact people’s (students’) well-being in various ways86,87. Within the physical space, in this case, the school (or university environment), which is a digital learning environment, IT infrastructure and reliable internet access are critical to moderating and sustaining interactions at all levels- micro, meso and macro-levels. Institution-wide policies on IT and data usage in teaching and learning mediate peer-to- peer (micro) interactions as well as meso-level interactions (i.e. student–lecturer relationships). abstract_text: ABSTRACT Background As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reshapes the learning process, students will inevitably experience cognitive conflicts when their existing knowledge and beliefs clash with information provided by GenAI. Improper handling of cognitive conflicts may lead to a decline in students' learning efficiency and even hinder the development of critical thinking skills. Objective This study aims to understand how students respond to cognitive conflicts during their interactions with GenAI, with a focus on comparing high‐performing and low‐performing student groups. Methods To identify relationships between cognitive conflict intensity and students' responses, we used a covariate‐dependent Markov chain (a sequential data modelling method) to analyse the response states of 411 students in a simulated academic writing task and observed transitions in student response states across different task performances. Results The results revealed that the intensity of cognitive conflict had a significant impact on students' state transitions. Overall, as the level of conflict increased, students' state changes exhibited a phased pattern, shifting from fluctuation (transitioning to a variety of different states) to inertia or convergence (maintaining the original state or transitioning uniformly to a negative response state). Student response state transitions varied across different task performance levels. Conclusions This study provides a novel methodological perspective for modelling sequential response dynamics in Human‐AI interaction. The findings offer new insights into the cognitive conflict dynamics in GenAI‐assisted learning, providing implications for designing GenAI‐assisted learning environments.

title: Cognitive Predictors of AI-Related Textual Change in Upper-Intermediate L2 Russian Writing: Working Memory, Attention Control, and Critical Thinking

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can alter final second-language (L2) texts, yet cognitive differences may shape which changes emerge. This exploratory study examined 38 upper-intermediate learners of Russian who each produced one composition with AI assistance and one without it. Working memory, attention control, and critical thinking were measured continuously, and 11 textual outcomes were calculated from paired compositions. AI-assisted texts showed higher lemma-based lexical-diversity values, longer words, more connectives per 100 words, and substantially fewer first-person markers, while total word count, sentence measures, and formulaic-expression rate did not differ in the full sample. The higher POS-based content-word density was attenuated after first-person forms were excluded, suggesting a contribution from the change in person marking. Exploratory models suggested negative working-memory associations with lexical-diversity and connective-rate change, and negative attention-control associations with lexical-diversity change. The positive working-memory coefficient for word-count change was sensitive to HC3 estimation and leave-one-out refitting. Critical thinking showed no clear independent association in the primary change-score models, while positive coefficients for MATTR and HD-D appeared in the outcome-conditioned models. Under this supervised, student-mediated procedure, AI assistance was associated with lexical, discourse-marking, and stance differences in completed L2 texts.

title: Cognitive-Professional Resource Configurations for AI-Mediated Teaching: Perceived Teacher-Education Support and Intelligent Professional Action

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: AI-mediated teaching requires teachers to evaluate uncertain information, respond to changing conditions, and integrate AI with pedagogical judgment. This study examined four cognitive-professional resource domains relevant to intelligent professional action: digital literacy, digital resilience, AI-mediated epistemic agency (AMEA), and AI-TPACK. Variable-centered and person-centered analyses drew on a cross-sectional survey of 942 YouShi Plan preservice teachers at one Chinese university. Perceived structured teacher-education support was positively associated with all four resources. Self-reported teaching innovation competence was positively associated with jointly higher digital literacy and digital resilience, with the response surface primarily reflecting their combined level. Four resource profiles mainly differed in overall level and showed graded differences in perceived teaching innovation competence. Higher perceived support was also associated with membership in higher-resource profiles. Together, these findings connect perceived teacher-education support, cognitive-professional resource configurations, and self-reported teaching innovation competence, positioning the latter as a domain-specific perceived capability relevant to intelligent professional action in AI-mediated teaching.

title: Perceived and demonstrated generative AI literacy in engineering problem solving: the role of verification behavior

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used in engineering education, but self-reported literacy may not establish whether students can evaluate its outputs. The distinction between perceived competence and performance on engineering-specific AI scenarios remains insufficiently examined. This study investigated their correspondence and whether reported verification frequency statistically accounted for the association between demonstrated literacy and engineering task performance. Methods A cross-sectional online survey and assessment involved 1,206 mechanical engineering students at three Chinese universities. Measures comprised a 20-item perceived literacy questionnaire, a 12-item scenario test, an eight-item verification frequency scale, and two engineering tasks. Mediation and moderated mediation models controlled gender, year of study, AI use, AI course experience, and university fixed effects. Results Perceived and demonstrated literacy were modestly correlated, r = 0.265, 95% confidence interval [0.212, 0.317]. Demonstrated literacy was associated with verification frequency, b = 0.065, and the adjusted indirect association with engineering performance was 0.124, 95% bootstrap confidence interval [0.096, 0.154]. A small negative interaction suggested a weaker verification-performance association at higher perceived literacy, but its practical importance remains uncertain. A reverse-order model also produced a nonzero indirect association. Discussion The findings support assessing self-perception and scenario performance separately and investigating the quality of verification. Because the assessment was unproctored, the scores do not establish unaided competence; the cross-sectional associations do not establish a causal verification mechanism.
