analysis.methods: A cross-sectional design combined an online questionnaire with a scenario-based generative AI literacy test and two engineering problem-solving tasks. Data were collected from May to June 2026 at three universities in eastern China. University A was a national Double First Class institution, whereas Universities B and C were general undergraduate institutions. Eligible participants were at least 18 years old, were enrolled in a mechanical engineering-related undergraduate programme, and had prior experience using generative AI. Participation was voluntary, and the questionnaire was administered online through Wenjuanxing. The sample included 826 men and 380 women. Participants represented all four undergraduate years, with 284 first-year, 335 second-year, 337 third-year, and 250 fourth-year students. Mechanical engineering accounted for 488 participants, mechanical design, manufacturing and automation for 412, and vehicle engineering for 306. A total of 358 students had completed an AIrelated course, 190 had received other AI training, and 147 had participated in an AI-related project. Most participants used AI on at least 1 day each week. Specifically, 405 reported using it on 1 or 2 days, 449 on 3 or 4 days, and 222 on 5-7 days. The remaining 130 reported no weekly use. A total of 1,378 responses were received. Data quality screening excluded 172 responses that failed the embedded attention check, leaving 1,206 cases for analysis and a valid response rate of 87.5%. University A contributed 468 responses, of which 58 were excluded and 410 retained; the corresponding numbers were 490, 55, and 435 for University B and 420, 59, and 361 for University C (Supplementary Table 1 ). The final analytic dataset contained no missing values or duplicate participant identifiers. Before accessing the survey, participants read an information statement and provided electronic informed consent. The Ethics Committee of Shaanxi Institute of Technology approved the study; the approval did not have a reference number. The relevant departments at the other two universities authorized recruitment and data collection. Study size was determined by the eligible complete responses received during recruitment; the reported power calculation is a design sensitivity analysis rather than a prospective samplesize justification. The Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2026. 1981428/full#supplementary-material
analysis.discussion: Perceived generative AI literacy and performance on engineering-related AI scenarios were associated but only [-0.097, -0.003] modestly. After covariate and university adjustment, students with higher scenario scores reported more frequent verification, and verification frequency statistically accounted for part of the association with engineering performance. A small interaction suggested a weaker verification-performance association at higher perceived literacy. These findings support distinguishing selfperceptions from scenario performance, while leaving the temporal ordering and causal role of verification unresolved. The modest correspondence between perceived and demonstrated literacy addresses an important measurement problem in AI education. Self-report instruments capture how capable students believe they are, whereas scenario-based tests capture whether they can recognize appropriate actions under defined conditions. The two forms of evidence overlap, but they answer different questions. The present correlation of 0.265 is consistent with broader evidence that people have only moderate insight into their abilities and that self-assessments reflect affective and experiential cues as well as knowledge (Ackerman et al., 2002; Sitzmann et al., 2010; Zell and Krizan, 2014) . It also reinforces recent calls to complement AI literacy questionnaires with performance-based measures (Hornberger et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2025; Lintner, 2024) . The findings are more directly relevant to correspondence between self-perception and demonstrated competence than to the Dunning-Kruger effect. The two measures were not expressed on comparable scales, and no task-level confidence judgments were collected. The continuous moderator is not a direct overconfidence measure. Discrepancy-based profiles were removed because correlated score differences and regression to the mean can create apparent miscalibration. A formal calibration test would require matched judgments and performance measures, with analyses that separate measurement error and statistical regression from psychological bias (Burson et al., 2006; Kruger and Dunning, 1999) . Verification frequency was a statistical intermediary in the specified model. This is compatible with the proposal that knowledge of AI limitations relates to checking practices, but the same data also supported the reverse ordering of engineering performance and verification. Moreover, some scenario and task content involves related verification decisions, and shared engineering knowledge may contribute to their association. The data therefore do not establish that literacy causes verification or that verification improves subsequent performance. Observational mediation here organizes conditional associations rather than identifies a behavioral mechanism. This interpretation aligns with research on appropriate reliance and automation bias. Automated advice often improves performance overall, yet it can introduce errors that users fail to detect when monitoring is weak (Goddard et al., 2012; Skitka et al., 1999) . Trust supports efficient interaction only when it is calibrated to system capability and task demands (Hoff and Bashir, 2015; Lee and See, 2004) . Verification is therefore not an expression of blanket skepticism. It is a means of matching reliance to the evidential demands of a task. Engineering education is well suited to make this principle concrete because many outputs can be checked through calculation, source inspection, dimensional reasoning, simulation, or constraint testing. At every examined level of perceived literacy, reported verification frequency was positively associated with engineering performance. Its estimated slope was somewhat smaller at higher perceived literacy, conditional on demonstrated literacy. Explanations involving confirmatory checking or reduced persistence are hypotheses for future research, not observed processes. The frequency measure cannot distinguish diagnostic checks from superficial or dependent checks, so it cannot establish why the slopes differed. The small interaction should not be treated as a dominant determinant of engineering performance. Its direction persisted when X × W and X × M terms were added, but the significant X × M term showed that the simple Model 14 specification did not exhaust the possible conditional relationships. The bootstrap index interval remained close to zero, and design sensitivity was insufficient for reliable detection of an effect this small. Replication and direct observation of verification quality are needed before drawing strong practical conclusions. These results do not justify discouraging student confidence. Perceived generative AI literacy and engineering-scenario performance should be assessed separately. Demonstrated literacy was associated with reported verification frequency and engineering performance, with a positive adjusted indirect association in the specified cross-sectional model. The small moderation finding is preliminary, and neither the mediation analysis nor the unproctored assessment establishes a causal mechanism or unaided competence. The findings motivate future evaluation of observable verification quality and feedback that helps students relate self-perceptions to demonstrated performance. ensure accuracy, including review by the authors wherever possible. analysis.limitations: The cross-sectional design establishes conditional associations rather than temporal or causal effects. The reverse-order indirect association was also nonzero, and covariate adjustment cannot exclude unmeasured confounding. Longitudinal studies could examine changes across a course (Ovi et al., 2025) , while experiments could manipulate verification instructions or calibration feedback and assess later performance. All assessments were online and unproctored. Participants were instructed to work independently without generative AI or external assistance, but compliance was not verified. Concurrent AI use could affect both scenario and engineering scores; these are therefore performances under the administered conditions rather than definitive tests of unaided competence. Perceived literacy and verification were both self-reported. The single-factor diagnostics did not describe the covariance as well as the specified multifactor model, but this does not rule out common-method variance. Frequency does not establish quality, and several perceived items also describe checking behavior. The low cross-construct HTMT supports empirical separation in this dataset, not absence of conceptual overlap. Future studies could record source retrieval, independent recalculation, contradiction detection, and revisions to distinguish reported checking from effective verification. The 12-item test had acceptable internal consistency and positive item discrimination, but it sampled a narrow set of engineering-related AI decisions. Item statistics do not establish comprehensive literacy, external validity, or stability over time. The adapted perceived questionnaire differs substantially from GenAI-LLs; the content crosswalk documents its engineeringspecific coverage, although the original source-item revision history is unavailable. Its domain reliabilities were modest, and high interdomain HTMT values limit separate subscale interpretation. CFA used a continuous-item ML approximation; ordinal estimation and threshold-invariance tests remain necessary sensitivity checks. The moderation model examined perceived literacy after controlling demonstrated literacy. This specification captures relative differences in self-perception among students with comparable demonstrated scores, but it is not a direct test of congruence. Future studies can place perceived and demonstrated measures on comparable scales and use polynomial regression with response surface analysis to examine whether performance is highest when both are high and aligned (Shanock et al., 2010) . Taskspecific confidence judgments may offer an even more precise test because the unit of judgment would correspond directly to the unit of performance. The sample was drawn from three Chinese universities and mechanical engineering-related programmes. University fixed effects address intercept differences within these institutions, but three schools provide limited information about broader institutional variability or residual dependence. Exclusion was also associated with AI use and course experience, so retained respondents may not represent all respondents equally. Cultural expectations, curriculum structure, domain expertise, and tool access may shape the relationships; replication across settings is needed (Giannakos et al., 2025) . Future longitudinal studies could track AI use, verification behavior, and engineering performance over time to clarify their temporal relationships (Li et al., 2025) . Neuroimaging methods could also help investigate how AI use relates to brain health and the neural processes involved in verification (Li et al., 2026) .

abstract_text: This study investigates the factors associated with university students’ intention to use Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in Ghana, with particular attention to the role of psychological barriers in shaping technology use intention. This study extends the UTAUT model by incorporating the concept of digital learning anxiety in understanding the psychological dimension of students using generative AI. The study employed a quantitative approach using a cross-sectional survey design, with data analyzed through covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). The sample consisted of 350 university students in Ghana. Structural equation modeling and a bias-corrected percentile bootstrapping method were conducted in AMOS (v 23) to estimate the path coefficients. The results showed that performance expectancy and effort expectancy were positively associated with students’ intention to use GenAI. Additionally, a significant but small indirect association was found between effort expectancy and behavioral intention through digital learning anxiety. However, the findings indicate the insignificant influence of social influence. This study contributes to the literature by providing context-specific evidence from Ghanaian higher education on the role of Digital Learning Anxiety in students’ intention to use GenAI. However, because the study used cross-sectional data, this indirect relationship should be interpreted as an association rather than evidence of a causal mechanism. The findings suggest that students’ intention to use GenAI is associated with both their perceptions of the technology and their psychological responses to its use. These findings provide context-specific evidence on GenAI acceptance among the students surveyed.

analysis.methods: The study employed a quantitative approach using a cross-sectional survey design, with data analyzed through covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). According to Creswell and Creswell (2018) , a cross-sectional survey examines the relationship between constructs within a population at a precise time. Data were collected at a single point in time to examine the relationships among the study variables. The study targeted undergraduate students from the College of Humanities at the public university in Ghana, encompassing departments such as English, Linguistics, and Communication Studies, with a total population of 3,200. These students were selected because their academic coursework is conducted substantially in English and involves language-intensive academic activities. A total of 350 undergraduate students participated in the study. The sample size of 350 was considered adequate for the specified CB-SEM model, given the model’s complexity and the number of observed indicators. SEM sample-size adequacy depends on factors such as model complexity, factor loadings, and estimation conditions rather than on a single universal sample-size rule ( Wolf et al., 2013 ). With this approach, respondents who were available and willing to respond to the questionnaire were finally selected for the study ( Sterner et al., 2024 ). The questionnaire was administered in paper format during scheduled lecture sessions to maximize participation. A cover letter accompanied the questionnaire, detailing the objectives of the study, the criteria for qualification (university students using digital tools), and an assurance of anonymity and confidentiality. The data collection began on November 10, 2025, and ended on December 2, 2025. After 3 weeks of the data collection process, 350 questionnaires were appropriately filled out and used for the analysis. From Table 1 , it was clear that Level 300 students dominated the study, constituting 41.1%, followed by Level 400 students with a percentage of 32.6%, and Level 200 students, who constituted 26.3%. Regarding gender, males constituted 54.3%, while females constituted 45.7%. A structured questionnaire was utilized to collect the data. Although the measurement items were adapted from prior studies, we piloted the questionnaire to determine the necessity of clarifying any ambiguous statements, particularly regarding technical AI terminology. The study was pilot-tested on a sample of 30 students, of whom 10 students were randomly selected from different lecture groups. With their comments and suggestions, the questionnaire was amended and subsequently used for the main data collection. The questionnaire had three sections. Part A consisted of the basic demographics: gender, age, and university level. Part B contained items measuring the UTAUT constructs of Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, and Social Influence. Items measuring these constructs were adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003) and contextualized to GenAI-supported learning. The third part, Part C, contained items measuring Digital Learning Anxiety (DLA) and Behavioral Intention (BI). The DLA items were adapted from the identified literature on technology- and AI-related anxiety and contextualized to Generative AI-supported learning, while the BI items were adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003) . All items were measured on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree). The measurement items and their corresponding sources are presented in Appendix A . Content validity was first established through expert review. The suitability of the draft instrument was assessed by three senior researchers and two lecturers in the Department of English and Linguistics. This assessment was done to check whether the items of measurement sounded ambiguous, were appropriate for the research objectives with regard to Generative AI, and whether the statements were clear to university students. From their suggestions, minor adjustments in wording were made in the items measuring Digital Learning Anxiety to make them even clearer. Following the assessment of content validity, statistical analysis through SPSS (v.23) was used to check the internal consistency of the constructs. Although Cronbach's alpha is widely reported, McDonald's Omega was adopted as the principal reliability coefficient because it provides a more robust estimate of internal consistency for latent variable models. As shown in Table 2 , the reliability analysis was conducted for the five core constructs: performance expectancy (PE), effort expectancy (EE), social influence (SI), digital learning anxiety (DLA), and behavioral intention (BI). It can be observed that all constructs demonstrated high internal consistency, with values above the commonly recommended threshold of 0.70 ( Hair et al., 2012 ). Effort Expectancy (EE) obtained the highest reliability ( ω = .969), followed by Digital Learning Anxiety ( ω = .966), Behavioral Intention ( ω = .957), and Performance Expectancy ( ω = .964). The lowest value, for Social Influence (SI), was still satisfactory at ω = .884. These results indicate satisfactory internal consistency among the items measuring the five constructs. To minimize common method bias, procedural and statistical actions were taken ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Participants were assured of their anonymity and that their answers would be treated on a confidential basis to avoid social desirability bias. In addition, the questionnaire items were separated into different sections to reduce response pattern tendencies. The single questionnaire was divided into several sections, each consisting of the corresponding items. The first unrotated factor accounted for 43.24% of the total variance. However, because Harman's single-factor test provides only a limited diagnostic of common method bias, this result was not treated as conclusive evidence that common method bias was absent ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Although procedural remedies and Harman's single-factor assessment were used to assess the possibility of common method bias, Harman's test alone cannot conclusively establish the absence of such bias. Therefore, the results should not be interpreted as demonstrating that common method bias has been completely eliminated. Exploratory Factor Analysis was conducted using the SPSS statistical package version 23. EFA was conducted to examine the underlying factor structure of the measurement items and to assess whether the observed variables loaded onto their intended latent constructs. analysis.discussion: This study examined the associations of traditional UTAUT constructs and Digital Learning Anxiety with university students’ intention to use Generative AI. The findings showed that Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy were positively associated with Behavioral Intention, whereas Digital Learning Anxiety was negatively associated with Behavioral Intention. Social Influence was not significantly associated with Behavioral Intention. These findings provide context-specific evidence that both cognitive evaluations and affective responses are relevant to understanding students’ intention to use GenAI. Among the predictors examined, Performance Expectancy had the largest positive standardized association with Behavioral Intention. This finding indicates that students primarily evaluate Generative AI based on its perceived ability to improve their academic performance. This finding is consistent with the original UTAUT model, which identifies performance expectancy as the strongest determinant of technology adoption ( Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). The present study extends this evidence to Generative AI within a Ghanaian higher-education context, suggesting that students primarily consider the perceived educational value of GenAI when forming their intention to use it. This reinforces the argument that students evaluate AI according to its educational value and contribution to learning outcomes. Regarding language learning, Matthews (2024) argued that interaction becomes more fluid for students who view AI as a cognitive partner that assists with outlines or syntax. Furthermore, the significant positive association of Effort Expectancy suggests that the nature of the interaction is defined by its accessibility. The natural language processing (NLP) abilities of large language models allow for a plug-and-play experience that is far simpler than traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS), which often require technical training ( Karahan and Bilgili, 2025 ). Furthermore, the significant positive association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention suggests that perceived ease of interaction is relevant to students’ intention to use GenAI. The natural-language interface of many GenAI systems may make interaction more accessible than technologies requiring greater technical familiarity. However, the present study did not directly compare GenAI with other educational technologies. Contrary to the original UTAUT model, Social Influence was not significantly associated with Behavioral Intention. This finding suggests that Social Influence did not explain additional variation in students’ intention to use GenAI after the other predictors in the model were considered. The finding differs from the traditional UTAUT proposition that social influence contributes to technology acceptance ( Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). However, the present study did not examine the specific social circumstances surrounding students’ GenAI use. Therefore, the reason for the non-significant relationship cannot be established from the present data. Future research could examine how lecturer expectations, peer influence, institutional norms, and students’ patterns of GenAI use may help explain the role of Social Influence in GenAI acceptance. A key finding of this study was the significant negative association between Digital Learning Anxiety and students’ intention to use Generative AI (H5). Effort Expectancy was also negatively associated with Digital Learning Anxiety (H4), indicating that students who perceived GenAI as easier to use tended to report lower levels of anxiety. These findings are consistent with Karal and Özdemir (2025) and Kristandl (2025) , who identified AI-related anxiety as relevant to students’ engagement with Generative AI. However, the cross-sectional nature of the present data does not establish the direction or causal nature of these relationships. The mediation analysis showed that lower Effort Expectancy was associated with higher Digital Learning Anxiety, while higher Digital Learning Anxiety was associated with lower Behavioral Intention. The indirect association was statistically significant but small; however, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering or causality among these variables. The findings contribute to research on GenAI acceptance by showing that affective responses may be considered alongside traditional UTAUT constructs. Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy were positively associated with Behavioral Intention, whereas Digital Learning Anxiety was negatively associated with Behavioral Intention. Social Influence, however, did not explain additional variation in Behavioral Intention within the specified structural model. These findings suggest that models of GenAI acceptance may benefit from considering students’ affective responses alongside their evaluations of usefulness and ease of use. The significant indirect association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention through Digital Learning Anxiety also provides evidence for examining affective processes alongside UTAUT predictors. However, this indirect association was small, accounting for approximately 11% of the total association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention. Most of the association was therefore direct. Moreover, because the variables were measured at the same point in time, the indirect association should not be interpreted as evidence that Effort Expectancy causes changes in Digital Learning Anxiety or that anxiety subsequently causes changes in Behavioral Intention. The findings suggest some practical considerations that may be examined further in the design of GenAI-supported learning environments. Given the positive association between Performance Expectancy and Behavioral Intention, universities may consider helping students understand the potential academic uses and limitations of GenAI. Similarly, the associations involving Effort Expectancy and Digital Learning Anxiety suggest that accessible guidance and opportunities to become familiar with GenAI may be worth investigating as possible ways of supporting students’ engagement with these technologies. Universities may also consider providing low-stakes opportunities in which students can explore appropriate uses of GenAI and receive guidance on academic integrity and responsible use. However, the present cross-sectional findings do not demonstrate that such interventions will increase GenAI adoption or reduce anxiety. These suggestions should therefore be treated as design hypotheses that require evaluation through experimental, longitudinal, or intervention-based research. This study
analysis.limitations: Despite its contributions, this study has several limitations. First, the cross-sectional design does not permit the establishment of long-term causal relationships. Because Effort Expectancy, Digital Learning Anxiety, and Behavioral Intention were measured at the same point in time, the indirect relationship identified in the model does not establish temporal or causal mediation. Reverse relationships and unmeasured factors that may influence these constructs cannot be ruled out. Accordingly, the observed indirect association may also reflect alternative directional relationships or common causes that were not included in the model. Additionally, because all measures were collected using self-reported responses, the findings may be influenced by respondents’ subjective perceptions. Although statistical procedures were employed to assess the validity and reliability of the measurement model, future studies may benefit from combining survey data with behavioral or observational measures of AI usage. The use of convenience sampling also limits the representativeness of the sample. Because participants were recruited during scheduled lecture sessions, students who were absent during data collection were less likely to be represented. The findings should therefore not be generalized to all university students in Ghana without caution. The structural model did not include potential control variables such as gender, university level, prior GenAI experience, device access, or English proficiency. Some of these factors may be associated with students’ perceptions of GenAI, Digital Learning Anxiety, and Behavioral Intention. Consequently, the observed relationships may partly reflect unmeasured confounding, and future studies should examine the robustness of these associations after accounting for relevant demographic, technological, and language-related characteristics. Although the study was conducted among university students in an English-medium academic setting and the questionnaire included items contextualized to language-related academic activities, English proficiency and L2-specific psychological constructs were not directly measured. The findings should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that the observed relationships are specifically attributable to students’ English proficiency or L2-related anxiety. Again, the rapidly evolving nature of generative AI limits the temporal stability of the findings. By targeting humanities students in one academic setting, it becomes difficult to establish the effectiveness in other disciplines, such as STEM. Moreover, the convenience sampling approach may have introduced selection bias because participation depended on students’ availability and willingness to respond. Finally, the quantitative design did not permit an in-depth exploration of students’ lived experiences when interacting with Generative AI. Future qualitative studies could provide richer insights into these experiences. Future studies could extend the framework by examining additional factors such as Academic Integrity Awareness and investigating whether the observed relationships differ across academic disciplines. Longitudinal research could examine how students’ AI-related anxiety and acceptance change as their experience with GenAI develops over time. Qualitative research may also provide deeper insight into the social and institutional factors associated with students’ decisions to use GenAI. Finally, empirical studies examining the effects of GenAI-supported learning on students’ actual academic performance and AI-use behaviour would provide a more balanced understanding of its educational implications. abstract_text: Background Although artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into music education, limited research has examined how students’ classroom engagement, flow experience, and emotional intelligence develop together over time. This study investigated the longitudinal relationships among these three psychological constructs in AI-assisted music classrooms, with particular attention to their developmental trajectories and the indirect association involving changes in flow experience. Methods A five-wave longitudinal survey was conducted among 850 undergraduate music students from four Chinese universities, with 718 participants retained at the final measurement. AI-assisted music classroom engagement, flow experience, and self-perceived emotional intelligence in musical learning contexts were assessed at each wave. Longitudinal measurement invariance was examined, and parallel-process latent growth modeling was employed to investigate developmental trajectories and associations among growth factors. Indirect effects were evaluated using 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results Classroom engagement (slope = 0.044), flow experience (slope = 0.051), and emotional intelligence (slope = 0.046) exhibited significant positive growth over time (all p &lt; 0.001), with significant individual differences in growth rates. The growth rate of classroom engagement was positively associated with that of flow experience ( r = 0.39), while the growth rate of flow experience was positively associated with that of emotional intelligence ( r = 0.40). Furthermore, a significant indirect association between engagement growth and emotional intelligence growth was observed through flow growth (indirect effect = 0.120, 95% bootstrap CI [0.064, 0.205]). This association remained significant in additional robustness analyses. Conclusion The findings reveal interconnected developmental trajectories of classroom engagement, flow experience, and self-perceived emotional intelligence in AI-assisted music learning contexts. Growth in flow experience emerged as a significant statistical link between changes in classroom engagement and emotional intelligence. These findings extend research on the longitudinal associations among engagement, flow, and emotional functioning in technology-supported music education, while highlighting the need for further research to establish the temporal and causal mechanisms underlying these relationships.

As students become more familiar with task formats and classroom expectations, their ways of participating may also stabilize. Flow experience showed a similar developmental pattern. Sustained learning gives students opportunities to continually adjust the match between their abilities and task demands and to form more stable attention investment and activity absorption. The growth in musical emotional intelligence reflects that emotional abilities themselves have room for development. Music learning continuously involves perceiving emotional information in music and regulating one’s own emotional states, and these experiences accumulate through repeated practice. Musical emotional intelligence is therefore not merely a stable characteristic students have already formed before entering the classroom. Some students improved relatively quickly during the study, while others changed more modestly. The parallel-process growth model builds on such individual differences in development to further examine whether different processes of change are interrelated. This study therefore asks whether a student’s speed of change in one psychological process is related to their speed of change in another psychological process. The positive relationship between growth in classroom engagement and growth in flow experience supported H1. In the three-process model, the classroom engagement slope was significantly positively correlated with the flow slope. In the growth mediation model, the path between engagement growth and flow growth also remained significant. Compared with the relationship whereby students with higher engagement at a given time point also have higher flow, this study reveals a connection between two psychological processes in terms of their rates of change. Students whose classroom engagement grew faster also tended to show faster growth in flow experience. Classroom engagement and flow represent different aspects of learning, and their linked growth suggests that sustained participation may provide more opportunities for concentration and task absorption. A higher level of engagement does not necessarily produce flow, but sustained increases in engagement can increase students’ opportunities to engage with tasks, process feedback, and adjust their performance. When students can invest more stably in the current task, the conditions needed to maintain attention and form activity absorption also increase. The relationship between classroom engagement and flow is therefore evident not only in level differences but also in its clear developmental properties. The significant relationship between growth in flow experience and growth in musical emotional intelligence supported H2. In the three-process model, the two slopes were significantly positively correlated, and in the growth mediation model, the path between flow growth and musical emotional intelligence growth was likewise significant. One important feature that distinguishes music learning from general knowledge learning is that the learning process itself continuously involves emotional information. When performing, listening, or composing, students not only need to complete tasks but also need to perceive musical expression and continually adjust their own emotional states. The sustained attention and deep absorption of flow allow learners to maintain processing of such information for extended periods. As deep immersive experience strengthens over the course of learning, processing experiences related to musical emotions may also accumulate in parallel. The key point here is not that flow itself equals musical emotional intelligence, but that the developmental processes of the two are systematically connected. Repeated experiences of flow during music learning may provide opportunities for students to recognize and regulate their emotions during practice and performance. abstract_text: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can provide preservice teachers with a complete lesson plan before they have articulated the reasoning the plan is intended to develop, creating conditions for automation bias and cognitive offloading. This multiple-case study examined how five preservice mathematics teachers in China negotiated epistemic authority while planning using GenAI. Methods Cases were selected from 42 preservice teachers through preliminary quantitative screening. Screen-recording-derived event logs, concurrent verbalizations, video-stimulated recall interviews, and written reflections were integrated into an evidence matrix comprising 34 decision episodes. Authority was interpreted as retained, shared, or ceded based on the relationship among the source of a proposal, the participant’s action, the warrant invoked, and whether that warrant was enacted in the lesson plan. Results Authority was retained in 16 episodes, shared in 12, and ceded in 6, with variation across cases. Visible actions did not map onto authority positions in a fixed way, and professional warrants were sometimes not enacted. Two vulnerabilities emerged. A closed verification loop, observed in four episodes across two cases, occurred when participants recognized uncertainty about AI output yet asked the same AI to validate it. An insight–action gap, illustrated by three episodes in a single case, occurred when recognized pedagogica problems were not translated into planned teacher responses. Discussion The findings support the proposition that the educative value of AI-assisted planning depends less on how much novices edit AI output than on whether tasks require independent verification and warranted, enacted decisions.

reading.interpretation: The first contribution of this study concerns how GenAI changes the starting conditions of learning to plan. A complete AI plan did not simply supply ideas. It shifted planning from constructing an instructional trajectory to authorizing a ready-made one. T1’s first action was not an absence of participation—she prompted, copied, and formatted—but the mathematical or pedagogical criterion for accepting the plan remained unarticulated. Later reconstruction restored part of the reasoning work that planning is meant to develop. T3’s case followed the opposite order. His self-authored framework initially kept this reasoning work with him, but it did not prevent him from later adopting an AI-generated activity without a visible warrant. From a psychological perspective, T1’s initial acceptance is consistent with research on automation bias, in which people rely on automated recommendations instead of evaluating the available information themselves ( Goddard et al., 2012 ; Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010 ). Her reflection that she was “not very sure that it was a good design” but still accepted it suggests that the apparent coherence of the AI output supplanted her own evaluation. As automation bias was not measured as a psychological construct in this study, this is an interpretation informed by that research rather than evidence of the effect itself. However, this reliance was not fixed. Once she noticed a specific gap in the plan, she moved from accepting the output to revising it. This finding adds to existing research on preservice teachers and GenAI. First, complete AI-generated plans shifted plans by changing the starting task from constructing a lesson to deciding whether to accept one. Second, the most frequent visible actions did not correspond to a single authority position, and an articulated professional warrant was not always enacted in the plan. Third, when participants were uncertain, authority tended to shift toward the AI, unless they could draw on professional resources, such as knowledge of student thinking or practicum experience. T1 began by asking Doubao for a Grade 8 lesson on the properties of parallelograms. The screen recording shows that she scrolled through the entire response once, then selected it all and pasted it into Word. In her written reflection, she explained: “I thought there was no major problem with the overall framework, but I was not very sure that it was a good design, so I accepted it”. The AI plan became the default trajectory before she had articulated a mathematical or pedagogical criterion. This episode was coded as ceding authority. T1’s later decisions, however, showed a different pattern. After reviewing the plan she pasted, she noticed that it did not address how students might respond during the activities or how the teacher should respond in turn. She entered a follow-up prompt: “You overlooked anticipated student responses and response strategies in your design”. Drawing on the content that Doubao then generated, she added anticipated student responses and response strategies to the activities in her Word document. This decision was coded as shared: T1 identified the gap and selected what to include, but the AI supplied most of the substantive content. However, for the proof of the second property, T1 did not rely on the AI’s content. The AI’s plan presented complete teacher demonstrations of both proofs. T1 reorganized this sequence so that the teacher would model the first proof, after which students would attempt the second proof themselves by drawing on the first. She typed a new teacher–student activity directly into the Word document: “The teacher asks students to discuss in groups how to prove the property, and invites a student to write the proof on the board”. For this activity, she did not adopt the anticipated responses that Doubao had generated. Instead, she wrote her own: “Students have gained experience from the previous proof and know that the property can be proved by showing that triangles are congruent.” In the stimulated-recall interview, she explained that after the teacher’s model, students should be able to “draw inferences from one case to another.” This interview account was consistent with the anticipated response she had outlined during planning. The reconstruction was coded as retained. The shift, therefore, was not from using AI to not using it. Rather, it was a shift from accepting an entire plan because it appeared coherent to redesigning part of it based on how students might reason. T3 began from the opposite position. Before prompting DeepSeek, he divided the lesson into four modules: objectives, key and difficult points, materials, and lesson content. His reflection explained: “If I have my own framework first, I can keep adjusting it”. He then asked the AI to fill these modules one at a time. For example, he first requested objectives for a lesson on SAS triangle congruence, then asked the AI to shorten and summarize them, and only after settling the objectives and key points did he ask for a sequence of lesson activities based on them. This teacher-authored structure determined what the AI was asked to generate and in what order, and it was coded as retained. Within this structure, most of T3’s subsequent decisions involved working with AI-generated content rather than replacing it. He asked the AI to anticipate students’ possible answers and simulate the classroom interaction for the introduction. For the “standard proof writing” segment, he asked the AI what students should pay particular attention to when writing proofs. Then he used its answer to add notes on format, the correspondence of conditions, and the completeness of conditions. In some places, however, he contributed content of his own. For the AI-generated variation exercises, he used a mathematical drawing tool to create figures that matched each problem’s conditions. The framework did not guarantee continued control. When he reached the “hands-on exploration” segment late in the session, the screen recording shows he hesitated for a long time before engaging with the AI-generated activity. In his recall interview, he explained that time was running short and that he did not know how to design the activity himself. No independent mathematical or pedagogical warrant for the activity appeared in any source, and the decision was therefore coded as ceded under the first criterion. His reflection suggested an awareness of this risk: accepting the AI’s wording, he wrote, could lead him to “gradually enter its rhythm”. T3’s case thus shows that a teacher-authored framework can support authority over the overall structure of a lesson without preventing local shifts back toward the AI. These cases address RQ1 in two ways. First, T1’s case shows that a complete AI-generated plan can change a novice’s starting task from constructing a lesson to deciding whether to accept one. Second, neither case settled into a stable position of authority. T1 later reclaimed authority by redesigning part of the plan, whereas T3, who began with his own framework, later adopted AI-generated content without a visible warrant. Authority thus shifted in both directions over the course of a single planning session. Across all five cases, this movement exhibited a temporal pattern: two of the six ceded episodes were the first episode of a case (T1, T5), in which a complete AI plan was adopted, and the remaining four occurred later in the planning session. analysis.discussion: The first contribution of this study concerns how GenAI changes the starting conditions of learning to plan. A complete AI plan did not simply supply ideas. It shifted planning from constructing an instructional trajectory to authorizing a ready-made one. T1’s first action was not an absence of participation—she prompted, copied, and formatted—but the mathematical or pedagogical criterion for accepting the plan remained unarticulated. Later reconstruction restored part of the reasoning work that planning is meant to develop. T3’s case followed the opposite order. His self-authored framework initially kept this reasoning work with him, but it did not prevent him from later adopting an AI-generated activity without a visible warrant. From a psychological perspective, T1’s initial acceptance is consistent with research on automation bias, in which people rely on automated recommendations instead of evaluating the available information themselves ( Goddard et al., 2012 ; Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010 ). Her reflection that she was “not very sure that it was a good design” but still accepted it suggests that the apparent coherence of the AI output supplanted her own evaluation. As automation bias was not measured as a psychological construct in this study, this is an interpretation informed by that research rather than evidence of the effect itself. However, this reliance was not fixed. Once she noticed a specific gap in the plan, she moved from accepting the output to revising it. This finding adds to existing research on preservice teachers and GenAI. Previous studies have mainly examined preservice teachers’ AI-related knowledge (AI-TPACK), their perceptions of the benefits of GenAI, and their integration of it into lesson planning ( Aldemir et al., 2025 ; Hsu et al., 2024 ; Kılıçkaya and Kic-Drgas, 2025 ). These aspects remain important, but they do not show which instructional decisions preservice teachers actually make for themselves when AI is involved. Nor does visible human participation guarantee the kind of hybrid intelligence envisioned in human-AI collaboration ( Cukurova, 2025 ). The present cases show that participation in the process alone is not enough to meet this condition. These cases point to a more demanding standard: preservice teachers should be able to identify, warrant, and assume responsibility for consequential instructional decisions. The finding also contributes to practice-based teacher education. Approximations are valuable when they preserve the core work novices need to learn ( Grossman et al., 2009 ). Simulation-based environments similarly create protected opportunities to rehearse decisions and examine their consequences ( Dieker et al., 2014 ; Ke and Xu, 2020 ). We propose that AI-assisted planning is more likely to remain an approximation of practice when the task requires preservice teachers to decompose the problem, anticipate students, compare alternatives, and justify transformations. A task that simply asks for a complete lesson plan may allow the AI to do much of this work. A task that asks preservice teachers to examine an AI plan and revise it against explicit professional criteria is more likely to help them retain this work. The second contribution is a decision-level account of professional judgment in lesson planning. The findings show that judgment could not be inferred from the amount of prompting or editing because the same visible action carried different meanings across episodes. Prompting the AI could keep authority with the participant or leave the AI as the substantive source. Retaining an AI proposal could follow deliberate comparison or unexamined trust. Recognizing a missing response could demonstrate pedagogical awareness while leaving AI’s plan unchanged. As warrant and enactment are part of how authority was defined, the substantive finding is that neither the type nor the amount of visible activity tracked these criteria. This finding brings research on epistemic agency into direct contact with professional judgment and professional noticing. Epistemic agency has emphasized responsibility for knowledge advancement and the negotiation of what counts as legitimate knowledge ( Damsa et al., 2010 ; Scardamalia, 2002 ; Stroupe, 2014 ). In lesson planning, the knowledge object is prospective practice. Responsibility is therefore visible when a teacher’s mathematical, curricular, pedagogical, or feasibility judgment changes what students would encounter. This interpretation is consistent with accounts of teacher judgment and noticing in which teachers attend to consequential information, interpret it through professional knowledge, and connect it to action ( Shulman, 1987 ; van Es and Sherin, 2008 ; Jacobs et al., 2010 ). The source-action-warrant-enactment sequence offers a way to observe that responsibility without treating AI contribution as inherently displacing or teacher editing as inherently agentic. The decision-level analysis also qualifies participant typologies. Song et al. (2025) identified useful patterns and levels in teachers’ GenAI integration, but the present cases show that professional authority can vary across different objects within the same planning session. T1 both ceded and retained authority; T4 both enacted a student-oriented sequencing decision and left other pedagogical insights outside the plan. Typologies may summarize broad orientations, but they should not be assumed to describe every professional decision. In these cases, ecological agency offered a more plausible account of this variation than a stable user trait ( Priestley et al., 2015 ). In the present cases, knowledge of student thinking, practicum experience, mathematical structure, and judgment about lesson capacity enabled authority to remain with the preservice teacher. Uncertainty about content or curriculum, limited teaching experience, and the fluent completeness of AI output made independent evaluation more difficult. Authority therefore had to be re-established for each consequential decision rather than secured once for the whole task. The third contribution is methodological: claims about professional judgment require evidence of how decisions developed. In this study, the screen recordings established what participants did and in what order, while the interviews and reflections supplied, extended, or complicated their reasons. Together, these sources revealed two vulnerabilities that would have been difficult to identify from final plans alone. The two differ in empirical breadth. abstract_text: Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into university learning, raising questions about dependency-oriented reliance and self-regulation. Drawing on a self-regulated learning perspective, this study examined associations among GenAI dependency, effort regulation, and multidimensional perceived learning outcomes, including the statistical indirect association involving effort regulation. Methods Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 982 students at three higher education institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling were conducted, with indirect associations tested using 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for GenAI use frequency. Results The measurement model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.043, SRMR = 0.041). GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = −0.087) and was negatively associated with effort regulation ( β = −0.257). Effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.497). The residual direct association was nonsignificant ( β = 0.041), whereas the indirect association was negative and significant ( β = −0.128). After adjustment for GenAI use frequency, the indirect association remained significant, but the small total association was no longer significant. Conclusion The findings highlight effort regulation as a relevant learner-controlled process in the association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. They also distinguish dependency-oriented reliance from frequency of GenAI use. The cross-sectional design and potential classroom clustering warrant cautious interpretation.

Previous research has associated GenAI dependency with procrastination, cognitive failures, poorer task performance, and weaker critical thinking ( Goh et al., 2025 ), while greater AI dependence has also been associated with lower critical thinking among university students ( Tian and Zhang, 2025 ). AI over-reliance has likewise been linked to less favorable learning performance ( Gao et al., 2026 ). However, these outcomes are not equivalent to perceived learning. The present study assessed students’ perceived cognitive, behavioral, and affective learning gains rather than objectively demonstrated achievement. Because perceived learning and independently assessed performance may diverge ( Deslauriers et al., 2019 ), the findings cannot establish whether GenAI dependency is similarly associated with objective learning outcomes. The present data cannot fully disentangle these subjective and objective dimensions, and the nonsignificant residual direct association should not be interpreted as evidence that GenAI dependency is educationally inconsequential. GenAI dependency was negatively associated with effort regulation, consistent with emerging evidence connecting AI dependency with self-regulatory functioning. Liu and Liu (2026) reported a negative association between metacognitive self-regulation and GenAI dependency, and Liu (2026) similarly identified a negative association between broader self-regulated learning and AI dependence among frequent AIGC users. More directly, Maizel et al. (2026) identified stronger effort regulation as being associated with lower AI dependency. In the present study, effort regulation was in turn positively associated with perceived learning outcomes, consistent with the role of persistence and resource management in academic functioning ( Pintrich, 2000 ; Waldeyer et al., 2022 ). These associations are particularly relevant in GenAI-supported learning because external assistance is readily available when academic work becomes difficult. Under such conditions, students’ capacity to sustain their own effort remains an important learner-controlled component of the learning process. The significant negative indirect association further indicates that GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes were statistically connected through effort regulation within the specified model. This association should be interpreted in light of the measures’ reference frames: GenAI dependency was specific to reliance on generative AI, whereas effort regulation reflected a broader academic self-regulatory tendency and perceived learning outcomes referred to recent coursework rather than a specific GenAI-supported task. The comparison of unadjusted and frequency-adjusted score-based models provided a more differentiated assessment of robustness. The negative association between GenAI dependency and effort regulation, the positive association between effort regulation and perceived learning outcomes, and the negative indirect association remained similar after adjustment for GenAI use frequency. However, the small negative total association was no longer statistically significant in the adjusted model, indicating that the evidence for this overall relationship was less robust. The change in the total coefficient was small and should not be interpreted as demonstrating that use frequency substantially explained the association. These results suggest that dependency-oriented reliance and frequency of GenAI use should be distinguished, but they do not establish their independent causal contributions to learning. Because the data were cross-sectional, the indirect association represents a statistical feature of the specified model rather than evidence of a causal mechanism. Reverse, reciprocal, and alternative directional relationships remain plausible. Moreover, the score-based sensitivity estimates should not be directly compared with the coefficients from the primary latent-variable SEM because the two approaches differ in their measurement specifications. The findings contribute to self-regulated learning research by identifying effort regulation as a specific resource-management process associated with dependency-oriented GenAI use and perceived learning outcomes. The negative indirect association suggests that learner-controlled persistence is relevant when examining students’ reliance on readily available AI assistance. However, GenAI dependency explained only 6.6% of the variance in effort regulation, indicating that other motivational, instructional, and contextual factors remain important. The distinction between dependency and frequency of use further suggests that frequent GenAI engagement should not automatically be interpreted as problematic reliance. Because perceived learning outcomes reflected students’ broader evaluations of recent coursework, these findings extend understanding of subjective learning experiences without establishing effects on task-specific or objectively assessed performance. analysis.methods: Before the formal study, we conducted a pilot study with two experts in educational technology. The pilot aimed to validate the clarity of the study scenario, the realism of the agent’s behavior, and the usability of the design. Participants in the pilot interacted with the agent and provided open-ended feedback on the interaction flow, personality expression, and perceived peer-likeness. Data from the pilot study were not included in the analysis. We adopted an exploratory qualitative approach to examine how the theory-informed AI peer design was experienced and interpreted in interaction [8]. The initial design was grounded in theories of peer learning and social interaction, and the study aimed to understand how these theoretical principles translated into the agent’s interactional behaviors and how they were perceived during use. Rather than testing learning outcomes, we focused on identifying interactional patterns, tensions, and characteristics that could inform the development of a framework for designing AI agents as We conducted the qualitative study between December 2025 and January 2026 with seven researchers in User Experience, Learning Sciences, Educational Technology, and Computer Science, with experience ranging from 3 to over 20 years. Participants were asked to critically engage with the AI agent as a peer and examine how the proposed design dimensions manifested during interaction. In particular, we explored how participants interpreted the agent’s social role, perceived its position of authority, and identified moments of collaboration, role shifts, or interactional breakdown. The study was approved by the university ethics board, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. Each session lasted approximately 30 minutes and was conducted through an online meeting platform. After consent, participants were asked to take the perspective of a student learning quadratic functions. Participants then interacted with the AI agent for approximately 20 minutes to collaboratively solve quadratic equations (Figure 2). They received the same information about quadratic functions that had been provided during the agent’s development and were encouraged to treat the agent as a classmate and reason collaboratively, rather than expecting direct instruction or final answers. No specific conversational structure was imposed so as to preserve the natural development of the interaction. The interview focused on how they interpreted the agent’s social role and authority, how the interaction reflected the proposed design dimensions, and where they observed moments of collaboration, role shifts, All sessions were audio-recorded with participants’ permission and transcribed. The interview transcripts were de- identified before analysis. We conducted an iterative thematic analysis [31]. analysis.results: 5.1 RQ1: Perception of an AI peer agent 5.1.1 Reduced Pressure and Increased Safety. A dominant theme across the interviews was that participants associated a stronger sense of safety with interacting with the AI compared to a real peer, when considering the experience from a learner’s perspective. This allowed them to focus on the math problem without worrying about being judged. P1 explained that when compared to regular class setting, seeing other students finish faster made them feel “anxious and ashamed," while with the AI there was no comparison. P3 shared that because the agent was “not a real human being," they felt “less embarrassed" and “more comfortable making mistakes"; P5 also emphasized that safety came from the lack of human judgment: “I know he won’t think I’m fool...He doesn’t have any human emotions, he’s just AI." P6 further explained that safety increased when the AI felt like an equal. They suggested that if the agent was presented as ”your classmate...same level as you," then “it feels safer", as “with your friend or someone equal to you, you can make mistakes without a problem." This shows that safety was created both by the AI’s non-human nature and by the feeling 8 Yiran Lin, Ye Deng, Ziqi Pan, Yongan Yu, and Alexandra I. Cristea of equality. For these participants, experiencing the AI as a peer meant being able to make mistakes without fear of 5.1.2 Peer Through Imperfection.Participants described the AI’s peer-likeness through its willingness to acknowledge its own imperfections, which are caused by the inherent imperfections of LLM. P3 felt the agent was peer-like because it was “not very clever" and made “stupid and simple mistakes." When P3 gave a wrong answer and the agent accepted it, they said it felt “like a real human peer." P7 expressed a similar view; the agent felt like a peer, as it “did not show the solution directly," but instead “made some assumptions and asked for my idea." They also noted that the agent “made mistakes sometimes" and tried wrong approaches before asking for participants’ opinion, which made the interaction However, not all participants welcomed this behavior. P5 disliked an AI that was “as stupid as I am," and believed a peer should be “smarter than me" to provide helpful ideas. This shows that while mistakes helped some participants see the AI as human-like, others felt that too many mistakes reduced its usefulness. This indicates a distinction between peer-likeness and peer-usefulness, which were not always aligned in participants’ experiences. 5.1.3 The Impact of Personality and Motivation Embeddings.Personality and motivation had different effects on participants. P1 felt the agent’s personality was “steady" and that it “really wants me to learn," which made the interaction feel meaningful. However, P7 did not experience the personality as stable. They said it was “more a surface level" and changed according to the user’s input. They added that they mainly saw the AI “as a tool, not ... with personality... like friends." This shows that for some participants, the personality design was not strong enough. Personality also caused problems when the tone felt inappropriate. P1 became anxious when the agent said it was “feeling a bit unconcerned," which sounded dismissive. Others described the agent as “strict" (P4) or a “know-it-all" (P2). When the agent sounded confident or directive, participants were more likely to see it as a teacher rather than a peer. This shows that personality can help create consistency, but it can also create distance, if the tone is too authoritative. 5.1.4 Collaboration versus Instruction.Participants described collaboration as situations where the AI guided their thinking without taking control. P6 felt like “working together as a team" because the agent “has the information but . . . gives you hints and lets you think and be part of the solution." This feeling changed when the AI moved too quickly. P7 felt “a little annoyed" when they were still thinking and the agent “just gave me the right number." For them, showing the answer too early broke the sense of collaboration. Similarly, P4 felt the agent was “examining me, not helping me," and P2 said it was “very fixed on a direction of travel." In these moments, the AI was no longer seen as a peer, but as a tutor giving instructions. analysis.discussion: This study responds to the growing attention in AIED that looks beyond designing AI systems merely as instructional tools. We examined how learners experience an AI agent in the social–cognitive role of a peer, laying the groundwork for future research on AI systems that emulate human-like social and cognitive behaviors in learning environments. Our findings show that in peer-oriented designs, correctness alone is insufficient; the enactment of authority, uncertainty, and shared responsibility is central. We contribute a human-centered set of design and evaluation dimensions for AI peer agents that emphasize interaction quality, emotional safety, and shared control. This perspective clarifies AI peers not as simplified tutors or information providers, but as partners that support collaborative reasoning and sustained engagement.

title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
preview: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) an…
abstract_text: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. Implications for practice and/or policy Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI syste

verified_article_review.provenance: Full-article synthesis of verified publisher HTML; original paraphrases
verified_article_review.methods: A preregistered randomized classroom experiment assigned 144 Danish high-school students to standard ChatGPT, an AI chatbot that guided self-regulated learning (SRLbot), or the same approach with emotional support (Emotional SRLbot), with 48 participants in each condition. One learning session lasted about 25 minutes. Tests and surveys were administered before and after, and 85 students completed a four-week follow-up. Interaction traces were coded to examine self-regulatory behaviors.
verified_article_review.results: All three groups improved on immediate conceptual-knowledge and learning-transfer tests; however, condition-by-time comparisons were not statistically significant for either outcome (p = .980 and p = .953). At the four-week follow-up, knowledge and transfer change likewise did not differ significantly between groups. Both SRL-based chatbot groups showed larger improvements in enjoyment and reductions in boredom than the general-purpose ChatGPT group. Emotional SRLbot also showed higher task-level performance and reflection indicators in the interaction traces. Hopelessness fell across all groups without a differential treatment effect, and self-efficacy and chatbot trust did not show clear between-group benefits.
verified_article_review.discussion: The authors interpret the findings as preliminary support for combining AI prompts about planning, monitoring and reflection with encouragement sensitive to students' emotional states. An intervention that makes learning feel better and increases momentary self-regulatory behavior is not yet evidence of lasting independent learning gains. Theoretical expectations about emotional regulation pathways were not themselves fully tested as causal mediators.
verified_article_review.limitations: The intervention lasted only one 25-minute session. The pretest and follow-up knowledge measures had internal consistency below .60, making the learning estimates less reliable. title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Cognitive Scaffolding, Substitution, and the Risk of Deskilling
preview:
Abstract

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. Evidence from recent empirical studies suggests a dual pattern: structured forms of AI assistance can sustain users’ cognitive activity and enhance engagement and performance, whereas more substitutive forms of use are associated with reduced autonomous reasoning and poorer subsequent independent performance. This article argues that these findings can be understood by considering how cognitive work is distributed between users and AI systems and how this distribution may evolve over time. In particular, I examine a six-step sequence in which successful complementary assistance can increase trust and delegation; greater delegation can remain complementary or become increasingly substitutive; and increasingly substitutive interactions can reduce the autonomous exercise of critical thinking and potentially hinder the development or maintenance of critical-thinking capacities over time. The available evidence provides substantial support for the first five steps considered individually and substantial, though less direct, support for the sixth. The article concludes by discussing educational, design, and social implications, arguing that preserving cognitive agency requires fostering complementary rather than progressively substitutive forms of interaction.

title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
preview: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining appro…
abstract_text: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.

First, school-based mental health education should incorporate stress management as a core component of the curriculum and establish routine stress screening mechanisms to identify adolescents under high stress and provide timely psychological support.
