analysis.discussion: Findings of the study showed different patterns of change across the five dimensions of English writing anxiety following the blended intervention. The two classes showed different patterns of change in somatic anxiety and avoidance scores following the blended intervention, with the intervention group showing greater reductions in these scores than the control group. In contrast, no significant between-group differences in change over time were observed for test anxiety, self-doubt, or time anxiety. Students in the blended AI-supported writing condition showed greater reductions in somatic anxiety and avoidance behavior than students in the comparison condition. Participants reported fewer physical symptoms and were less likely to delay or avoid writing. These findings should, however, be interpreted in light of the class-level assignment of instructional conditions. Because one intact class received the blended AI-supported writing condition and one intact class received the comparison condition, class membership was completely confounded with instructional condition. The observed differences therefore indicate that the two participating classes followed different patterns of change over the study period, rather than independently demonstrating an intervention effect. In addition, the two instructional conditions differed in several respects, including writing practice, feedback opportunities, tutorials, and process monitoring. The greater reductions observed in somatic anxiety and avoidance in the blended AI-supported writing condition should therefore not be attributed independently to Doubao or to the instructional condition as a whole. From the perspective of Self-Determination Theory (SDT; Ryan and Deci, 2017 ), one possible interpretation of these improvements is that the blended AI-supported writing condition may have provided learning opportunities that supported students’ needs for autonomy and competence. The interview findings indicated that some students perceived the chatbot as a private and non-judgmental space in which they could express ideas, experiment with language, and revise their writing with less concern about negative evaluation. Such experiences may be relevant to students’ perceptions of control during writing and may provide one possible interpretive context for the different patterns of change observed in somatic anxiety and avoidance behavior. In addition, the immediate feedback and scaffolding provided by Doubao may have supported students’ perceived competence by making some writing tasks more manageable. Consistent with this interpretation, Allagui (2024) suggested that when writing tasks are perceived as less threatening and more manageable, learners may experience lower levels of writing-related stress and engage more actively in writing activities. However, these SDT-based explanations are interpretive rather than empirically tested mechanisms in the present study, as autonomy, competence, and relatedness were not directly measured. Moreover, reductions in somatic anxiety scores should not be interpreted as direct evidence of reduced physiological stress responses. The findings are consistent with prior research showing the beneficial role of AI-based writing tools in mitigating writing anxiety. For example, a meta-analysis found that automated writing evaluation significantly mitigates writing anxiety (including writing and computer anxiety), increases motivation, and improves L2 writing performance ( Huang et al., 2024 ). Similarly, portfolio-based writing instruction has been shown to mitigate EFL learners’ writing anxiety ( Fathi et al., 2020 ), and AI-generated corrective feedback has been found to reduce writing anxiety more effectively than teacher feedback ( Wang, 2024 ). These findings provide broader empirical support for the potential of supportive technological and instructional environments to alleviate writing-related anxiety, although the mechanisms underlying the present findings were not directly tested. Despite the reductions in somatic anxiety and avoidance behavior observed following the Doubao intervention, no statistically significant changes were detected in test anxiety, self-doubt, or time anxiety. This pattern suggests that the effects of AI chatbot-assisted writing instruction may have been more evident for anxiety dimensions that were directly addressed through low-risk practice, immediate feedback, and on-demand writing support. From the perspective of Self-Determination Theory ( Ryan and Deci, 2017 ), Doubao may have supported students’ autonomy by allowing them to seek assistance at their own pace and may have strengthened aspects of perceived competence through immediate feedback and opportunities for repeated practice. However, the intervention primarily focused on writing-related support and did not explicitly target test-taking strategies, time-management skills, or broader interpersonal and instructional support. Therefore, the absence of significant changes in test anxiety, self-doubt, and time anxiety may partly reflect a mismatch between the specific content of the intervention and these dimensions of anxiety, rather than indicating that they are inherently more stable or resistant to change. Other explanations should also be considered, including the sensitivity of the measurement instruments, the statistical power available to detect smaller effects, and the relatively limited duration of the intervention. Future studies could combine AI-assisted writing support with explicit test-taking practice, time-management training, teacher guidance, and longer-term interventions to examine whether broader changes in writing anxiety can be achieved. More specifically, the three dimensions may involve demands that were not fully addressed by the intervention. For test anxiety, time constraints, evaluative demands, and the consequences associated with formal writing assessments may introduce pressures that are less salient during routine writing practice. Although Doubao provides repeated practice, immediate feedback, and opportunities for revision, these forms of support may not fully reproduce the demands of formal testing. This possibility is broadly consistent with research linking test-related worry within cognitive test anxiety to academic performance ( Cassady et al., 2024 ). However, because Cassady et al. examined general cognitive test anxiety rather than English writing test anxiety specifically, their findings provide contextual rather than direct evidence for interpreting the present result. Self-doubt may also require sustained opportunities for successful performance to develop stronger writing

abstract_text: Introduction Adolescents increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots for schoolwork, yet evidence on whether this use supports or undermines learning is mixed. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading and self-regulated learning, we examined whether GenAI use for schoolwork is related to scientific literacy directly and through two components of self-regulated learning, academic help-seeking and metacognitive strategy use, and whether the purpose of use matters. Methods We analyzed the Program for International Student Assessment 2025 (PISA 2025) data from 12,191 15-year-old students in 374 schools in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China. Weighted two-level mediation models compared students within the same school, used all ten plausible values, and evaluated indirect effects with Monte Carlo confidence intervals. Results were checked against a design-based model with school fixed effects and balanced repeated replication weights. Results Students who used GenAI more often than their schoolmates reported more help-seeking ( β = 0.17) and more metacognitive strategy use ( β = 0.30). Help-seeking was positively associated with scientific literacy, yielding a positive indirect effect ( β = 0.013, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]); the indirect effect through metacognitive strategies was smaller ( β = 0.007) and was fully accounted for by science self-efficacy. The direct association between GenAI use and scientific literacy was negative ( β = −0.048, about 4 PISA points), and the positive indirect effects offset about 40% of it, leaving a small negative total association ( β = −0.028). Purpose mattered: among users, using GenAI “to help me learn” was associated with higher scientific literacy (+5.8 points per response category), whereas using it to summarize texts, research new topics, or draft assignments was associated with lower scores (−6.6 points). The results did not differ by gender or socioeconomic status and were identical under the design-based model. Discussion GenAI use for schoolwork is associated with scientific literacy through opposing pathways: a positive one through academic help-seeking and a negative direct one, and the direction of the association differs by purpose of use. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations may partly reflect which students use GenAI rather than the effects of its use.

More frequent GenAI use for schoolwork is positively associated with (a) metacognitive strategy use and (b) academic help-seeking. H3 (SRL and scientific literacy) . Controlling for GenAI use, (a) metacognitive strategy use and (b) academic help-seeking are positively associated with scientific literacy. H4 (indirect associations and opposing pathways) . Do the direct and indirect associations differ by gender and by economic, social, and cultural status (ESCS)? PISA assesses the reading, mathematics, and science literacy of 15-year-old students and collects background information through questionnaires. Science was the major domain in 2025. Schools are sampled with probability proportional to size, and researchers then randomly select a fixed number of eligible students within each school ( OECD, 2026c ). We used the OECD-reported sample B-S-J-Z (China), which covers Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang ( OECD, 2026b ). It comprised 12,385 students in 374 schools, representing about 1.43 million 15-year-olds. Participation was high: 96.8% of originally sampled schools took part before replacement and 100% after replacement; 98.4% of sampled students were assessed (weighted), and the overall exclusion rate was 2.4% ( OECD, 2026c ). Weighted, 47.9% of students were female; the mean age was 15.76 years ( SD = 0.29), and most students were in Grade 9 (43.0%) or Grade 10 (56.1%). The data were collected by national centers under the coordination of the OECD in accordance with national ethical and legal requirements, including informed consent procedures. This study is a secondary analysis of anonymized public-use files, for which no additional ethical approval was required. No study variable had more than 0.5% missing values (the largest was ESCS, 0.47%), and 194 students (1.6% unweighted, 1.7% weighted) lacked data on at least one variable. We used one analytic sample for all main analyses, consisting of the 12,191 students (98.4%) in 374 schools with complete data on every variable in the main, purpose, and self-efficacy models (listwise deletion). Schafer (1999) suggested that missing rates of 5% or less are unlikely to matter, and at these low rates the choice of missing-data method has little influence on the estimates ( Graham, 2009 ); a single complete-case sample also keeps all models directly comparable. The excluded students were not a random subset, however: they scored lower in science than the analytic sample (by 59 points, SE = 10; weighted, BRR standard errors) and reported less metacognitive strategy use and help-seeking. We therefore checked the main results against multiple imputation of the missing values for all 12,385 students (Section 3.4.4). Sample sizes differ only in robustness checks that, by design, add variables or restrict the sample. Questionnaire constructs were measured with PISA 2025 scale indices ( OECD, 2026a ). The OECD scaled the items with the generalized partial credit model and reported weighted likelihood estimates, standardized to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 across OECD countries ( OECD, 2026c ). Higher values indicate more of each construct. We report Cronbach’s α computed from the raw items in our sample and McDonald’s ω from the ordinal measurement model described in Section 3.4.1. The α values are within 0.01 of the OECD values reported for this sample ( OECD, 2026c ). Scientific literacy was represented by ten plausible values, randomly drawn from each student’s posterior proficiency distribution and accounting for measurement error in the test ( von Davier et al., 2009 ). In this sample, the weighted mean was 598.1 and the standard deviation 87.2. The intraclass correlation (ICC) was 0.47: nearly half of the variance lay between schools. Students indicated how often they used “Artificial Intelligence chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT) for your school work” to summarize a text they had to read, to conduct preliminary research on a new topic, to draft texts for writing assignments, and to help them learn (items ST438Q01–Q04; 1 = never or almost never , 2 = about once or twice a year , 3 = about once or twice a month , 4 = about once or twice a week , 5 = every day or almost every day ). Overall frequency of use was measured with the OECD index AIUSESCH, which summarizes the four items (α = 0.88, ω = 0.89). The four items correlated between 0.59 and 0.74, and a confirmatory model with separate factors for learning-oriented and other uses was not identified (latent correlation above 1.0), so we analyzed purposes at the item level rather than as latent factors (Section 3.4.3). Academic help-seeking was measured with four statements: “When I do not fully understand something, I ask my classmates,” “I ask my teachers for help when I need it,” “When I have trouble learning, I ask for help,” and “I only ask for help after trying hard to find the solution on my own” (ST433; four-point agreement scale; all four items were reverse-scored by the OECD so that higher values indicate more help-seeking; α = 0.80, ω = 0.79). The items describe a general tendency to seek help from classmates, teachers, and others when learning is difficult; they do not refer to help from chatbots or to a particular school subject. This is the construct our hypotheses concern: H2b and H4b ask whether students who use GenAI more often also turn to people for help more often, which requires a measure of help-seeking from people rather than from chatbots. The database labels the index SELFREG (“self-regulation”), and the OECD’s PISA 2025 report describes it as self-regulated help-seeking ( OECD, 2026b ). analysis.discussion: Using the first international assessment to ask adolescents about their use of AI chatbots for schoolwork, this study found that GenAI use was associated with scientific literacy through two opposing pathways. Students who used GenAI more often than their schoolmates also sought more help from teachers and classmates and used more metacognitive strategies, both of which were associated with higher scientific literacy. At the same time, GenAI use was directly and negatively associated with scientific literacy. The positive indirect effects offset part of this direct association, leaving a small negative total association within schools. The purpose of use was also associated with scientific literacy: using GenAI to help one learn was associated with higher scientific literacy, and using it to summarize or research was associated with lower scientific literacy. These patterns were observed for an alternative help-seeking score, with multiple imputation of missing data, and with mathematics and reading as outcomes. Because the data are cross-sectional, we interpret all of these findings as associations. The bivariate correlation between GenAI use and scientific literacy was zero, suggesting that GenAI use makes little difference. The mediation models show why this impression is misleading. Within schools, positive indirect effects through help-seeking and metacognitive strategies offset about 40% of a negative direct association, and the remaining total association was negative. GenAI use was also more common among students from advantaged families ( r = 0.17), who tend to score higher. A direct test confirmed that this contributes to the zero bivariate correlation: in a single-level regression, the association of GenAI use with scientific literacy was close to zero ( β = 0.004, 95% CI [−0.028, 0.036]) but became negative once ESCS was controlled ( β = −0.052, 95% CI [−0.080, −0.024]; about −4.5 points; Supplementary Table S6 ). This pattern of competitive mediation ( Zhao et al., 2010 ) offers one explanation for why studies of GenAI and learning disagree: depending on which pathway dominates in a sample or setting, the overall association can be positive, negative, or null. The negative direct association is consistent with the offloading account ( Risko and Gilbert, 2016 ; Chi and Wylie, 2014 ). PISA measures what students can do independently, without digital assistance. Students who routinely let a chatbot summarize readings or draft answers have fewer opportunities to practice the reasoning such a test requires, a pattern also observed when experiments withdraw AI support ( Bastani et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2025 ). The exploratory curvilinear analysis suggests that this association is concentrated among the heaviest users, who make up a small share of students. Reverse causation offers an alternative explanation for the negative direct association that deserves equal weight. Students who struggle with science may use chatbots more often to keep up with assignments, so lower achievement leads to heavier use rather than the reverse. Several features of the results fit this account as well as the offloading account: the association was concentrated among the heaviest users, and it was strongest for summarizing texts, the purpose most useful to a student who finds the reading difficult. If prior achievement were available, controlling for it would absorb this selection. Under the reverse-causation account, the direct association would shrink toward zero; under the offloading account, it would largely remain. Because PISA provides no measure of prior achievement, the present data cannot distinguish the two, and the negative direct association should be read as a description of who uses GenAI heavily as much as of what heavy use does. The indirect association through help-seeking was the most consistent result of the study. It was significant in every model for each of the four purposes, using a three-item help-seeking score that omitted the item on trying first, after multiple imputation of missing data, and after we controlled for perseverance and family support. The help-seeking measure refers to asking classmates and teachers, not chatbots, so the finding is that students who use GenAI more for schoolwork also report turning to people for help more often. This pattern is consistent with the view of help-seeking as an adaptive self-regulatory strategy ( Newman, 2002 ; Karabenick and Newman, 2006 ) and with the OECD’s descriptive finding that, among users, more frequent AI use is associated with more help-seeking ( OECD, 2026b ). However, the finding does not show that GenAI use leaves human support intact, let alone that it promotes it. The association between GenAI use and help-seeking was roughly halved when perseverance and family support were controlled (from β = 0.169 to 0.090), which suggests that shared dispositions or shared social resources account for part of it (see Lyu et al., 2026 , on social support and the adoption of AI tools). The reverse-order model fit the data equally well, so students who seek help more may also turn to chatbots more. Furthermore, because the measure does not refer to particular learning episodes, students may seek help from people and from chatbots for different problems. The indirect association shows that the part of GenAI use that co-occurs with help-seeking is associated with higher scientific literacy. Whether chatbot use prompts students to bring new questions to teachers and classmates cannot be determined from these data and deserves direct study, for example, with measures that ask students which sources of help they use for which problems. GenAI use was more strongly related to metacognitive strategy use ( β = 0.30) than to help-seeking ( β = 0.17). However, metacognitive strategies were only weakly related to scientific literacy, and this relation was fully accounted for by science self-efficacy. Students who reported more planning, monitoring, and adjusting felt more capable in science, and self-efficacy was in turn associated with higher scientific literacy. This fits social cognitive theory, in which successful self-regulation provides the mastery experiences that build self-efficacy ( Bandura, 1997 ; Usher and Pajares, 2008 ). The weak direct relation may also reflect the limits of questionnaire reports of strategy use, which say little about how well strategies are carried out ( Veenman, 2011 ). abstract_text: Background AI feedback holds promise for supporting student learning, but unstructured use can lead students to passively accept AI-generated answers, weakening their independent reasoning. This study examined whether structured AI feedback affects undergraduate students' critical thinking, learning performance, and engagement in a data science analytics course. Methods An exploratory two-class quasi-experimental study was conducted in a three-month undergraduate data science course ( N = 167). One class received four-phase structured AI feedback, while the comparison class received conventional instructor feedback. Propensity score matching was used to improve comparability on observed baseline characteristics. Critical thinking was assessed using an adapted 40-item assessment covering five dimensions. Results Students receiving structured AI feedback demonstrated higher post-test critical thinking scores than matched controls, with a baseline-adjusted difference of 5.64 points (95% CI [3.62, 7.65], p &lt; 0.001). A significant between-group difference in pre-to-post changes was also observed. Dimension-level analyses revealed significant differences in Evaluation of Arguments, Interpretation, Recognition of Assumptions, and Inference, while Deduction showed no significant difference. Higher learning performance, cognitive engagement, and behavioral engagement were also observed in the structured AI feedback group, whereas emotional engagement did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusion The findings provide exploratory evidence of differences in critical thinking and learning outcomes between the structured AI feedback and conventional instructor feedback classes. They highlight the potential relevance of feedback designs that encourage students to actively evaluate, question, and revise AI-supported analytical work, while underscoring the need for further studies that can isolate intervention-specific effects.

analysis.methods: The study adopted an exploratory two-class quasi-experimental design in a 3-month data science analytics course at a higher education institution in Guangdong, China. Two naturally formed class sections were included, with one assigned to structured AI feedback and the other receiving conventional instructor feedback. Both sections were taught by the same instructor using identical instructional materials, learning objectives, and assessment criteria. To maintain comparability between the two conditions, both groups completed identical course activities, assignments, and assessments during the intervention period. For each of the three data analysis tasks, students independently planned their analysis, selected variables, and completed an initial draft before submitting it through the course learning management system. Feedback began after this initial submission and before revision and final submission. Students in the structured AI feedback condition then entered the four-phase feedback cycle described in Section 3.2 and were required to complete it within 48 h of the initial submission deadline. In the first phase, Elicitation, students explained the analytical approach and variable choices already presented in their submitted draft. The subsequent phases involved examining the evidence supporting their conclusions, considering alternative explanations, and consolidating revisions to their work. Students in the conventional instructor feedback condition received written comments within 48 h of the initial submission deadline. Instructor feedback addressed analytical procedures, interpretation of results, and areas requiring improvement. Students in both groups were allowed to revise their work after receiving feedback and were required to submit the final version within seven days of the initial submission deadline. Task grading took place after the final submission deadline using the same assessment criteria and rubric for both conditions. The task scores included in the analysis were based on the final revised submissions. Further details of scoring and the calculation of final course grades are provided in Section 3.5. Students in both groups were instructed to complete their initial drafts independently. Students in the structured AI feedback condition used the system during the subsequent feedback stage, whereas students in the conventional instructor feedback condition were not provided with access to it. At the start of the semester, 167 students were enrolled across the two sections, with 88 in the treatment group and 79 in the control group before matching. All participants were undergraduates with no prior exposure to the structured AI feedback system used in this study. At the beginning of the semester, all participants completed a baseline assessment, which included demographic information (gender and year of study), academic background (cumulative GPA), and a pre-course assessment of critical thinking. In addition, prior experience with AI-based tools was collected. These variables were used as covariates in the propensity score estimation procedure to reduce potential pre-existing differences between groups. Before outcome analysis, PSM was conducted using baseline covariates to improve comparability on observed student-level characteristics. At the end of the semester, all participants completed post-intervention assessments. These measures were used to compare outcomes between the two classes. Because each feedback condition was implemented in only one class, these comparisons could not separate the association with feedback condition from other class-level influences. The overall structured AI feedback process is illustrated in Figure 1 . The four-phase feedback cycle began after students independently completed and submitted an initial draft, and before they submitted their final revised work. In Phase 1 (Elicitation), the AI prompts students to articulate their reasoning before receiving any feedback, asking them to explain the rationale behind their analytical choices and the assumptions underlying their interpretations. This phase activates metacognitive awareness and establishes a baseline for personalized feedback. In Phase 2 (Inquiry), the AI poses targeted follow-up questions that lead students to test the validity of their assumptions, consider alternative analytical approaches, and appraise the strength of the evidence supporting their conclusions. This phase is anchored in the upper levels of Bloom's taxonomy, analyzing, evaluating, and creating, ensuring that feedback moves past surface-level error correction toward deeper cognitive engagement. In Phase 3 (Reframing), the AI introduces alternative perspectives or counterexamples relevant to the student' s analysis, prompting them to reconcile conflicting interpretations and revise their reasoning accordingly. In Phase 4 (Consolidation), students prepared a revised analysis or reflective summary explaining how they had addressed the issues raised during the feedback cycle. This activity marked the completion of the four-phase cycle within the 48-h feedback period. Students could continue revising their work afterward and submitted the final version for grading within seven days of the initial submission deadline. This approach follows evidence-based feedback design principles: formative feedback should build from what students already know toward skills within reach, fostering advanced cognition through elaborated feedback instead of simple verification of correctness ( Lee and Moore, 2024 ). Structured AI intervention process design diagram. Across these phases, the framework is intended to preserve students' responsibility for analytical decisions. Elicitation makes their initial choices and assumptions available for examination. Inquiry directs attention to whether the evidence supports those choices and whether suggested alternatives are relevant to the task. Reframing creates an opportunity to compare competing interpretations and decide whether revision is warranted. Consolidation brings the reasoning together in a final analysis or reflective account. For Tasks 1, 2, and 3, the number of students completing the full cycle was 88, 86, and 80, respectively. Across the three tasks, students completed a total of 254 cycles, averaging 2.89 cycles per student (SD = 0.38; range = 1–3). A total of 80 students completed all three cycles, representing 90.9% of the AI group. The number of AI feedback messages for Tasks 1, 2, and 3 were 452, 444, and 420, respectively. analysis.discussion: The present study examined the relationship between structured AI feedback and critical thinking in an undergraduate data science course. Within the matched sample, students receiving structured AI feedback demonstrated higher post-test critical thinking scores and greater pre-to-post improvement than those receiving conventional instructor feedback. The findings suggest that the pedagogical organization of AI-supported learning may be relevant to how students develop and apply critical thinking skills in analytically demanding tasks. This pattern is consistent with the meta-analysis by Deng et al. (2025) , which synthesized experimental studies and found that ChatGPT-supported learning was generally associated with higher academic performance and higher-order thinking outcomes. However, the substantial heterogeneity reported in that review suggests that the educational benefits of GenAI may vary according to instructional design, learning context, and assessment approach. The present findings extend this discussion to data science education, where students are expected not only to produce technically correct analyses but also to examine assumptions, evaluate evidence, and justify their analytical decisions. The findings also complement those of Fan et al. (2025) , who observed that ChatGPT support improved students' essay revision performance without corresponding significant differences in knowledge gain or transfer. In the present study, differences were observed in both task performance and an independently scored critical thinking assessment, suggesting that the relationship between AI feedback and learning may be broader than immediate task completion. Nevertheless, the extent to which particular feedback activities contributed to these differences remains an important question for future investigation. The dimension-level findings provide a more differentiated understanding of critical thinking in structured AI-supported learning. Higher post-test scores were observed for Evaluation of Arguments, Interpretation, Recognition of Assumptions, and Inference, whereas the difference for Deduction was not statistically significant. The largest adjusted point estimate was observed for Evaluation of Arguments, although the present analyses did not establish that this difference was statistically greater than those observed for the other dimensions. One possible explanation for the pattern in argument evaluation is the close conceptual relationship between this dimension and the activities emphasized in the Inquiry and Reframing phases, which resonates with Lee et al. (2025) , who found that critical thinking during GenAI-supported work often involved verifying information, integrating AI-generated responses, and maintaining responsibility for task outcomes. This is also conceptually consistent with Hou et al. (2025) , who reported positive associations between undergraduate students' critical thinking and reflective, cautious, and collaborative patterns of GenAI reliance. These phases encourage students to examine the strength of evidence, consider counterexamples, and reconsider their initial analytical claims. Evaluation of Arguments may therefore be particularly relevant to the kinds of reasoning opportunities provided by the structured feedback framework. The observed differences in Recognition of Assumptions and Inference may reflect related opportunities for reflective reasoning. During Elicitation, students are asked to explain their analytical choices and identify the assumptions underlying their interpretations. Subsequent questioning may encourage them to reconsider whether particular conclusions are warranted by the available data. These processes correspond conceptually to the identification of unstated assumptions and the formation of evidence-based inferences, although the present study did not directly examine whether individual feedback phases were associated with changes in specific critical thinking dimensions. In contrast, Deduction did not show a statistically significant difference. A possible explanation is that formal deductive reasoning involves determining whether a conclusion necessarily follows from specified premises, whereas the feedback framework primarily emphasizes open-ended analysis, interpretation, and evaluation. The distinction may be relevant because reflective inquiry and formal logical reasoning, although related, are not identical cognitive activities. The learning performance findings showed that students receiving structured AI feedback obtained higher scores across all three data analysis assignments and the final course grade. This pattern suggests that structured feedback may be associated with students' ability to complete analytical tasks and communicate their findings within the course. The differences across the three tasks were not progressively increasing, with the largest adjusted difference observed for Task 2. This suggests that the relationship between structured feedback and assessed performance may vary with the characteristics of individual assignments rather than follow a simple cumulative pattern. Task-specific demands, opportunities for revision, and the alignment between feedback activities and assessment criteria may all be relevant to understanding these differences. The engagement findings showed higher cognitive and behavioral engagement in the structured AI feedback group, whereas emotional engagement did not differ significantly between the two conditions. This pattern suggests that the relationship between structured feedback and engagement may be more evident in how students think about and participate in learning activities than in their reported emotional experience of the course. The higher cognitive and behavioral engagement observed in the present study may therefore reflect the alignment between the feedback framework and the activities it explicitly requires. Future research could examine whether integrating socio-emotional support, peer discussion, or greater opportunities for learner choice is associated with different emotional engagement outcomes. The present study contributes to research on AI-supported learning by extending the conceptualization of AI feedback beyond automated response generation and task correction. The four-phase framework positions students as active participants in evaluating, questioning, and revising analytical information. This perspective emphasizes the role of human judgment within AI-supported learning. A second contribution concerns the multidimensional assessment of critical thinking. analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the study involved only two naturally formed class sections, with one class assigned to each feedback condition; consequently, intervention condition was completely confounded with class membership. Although propensity score matching improved comparability on observed student characteristics, it could not separate the intervention from other class-level influences or fully account for unobserved confounding factors, such as study habits, time commitment, or intrinsic motivation, which may have partially explained the performance differences. The results should therefore be interpreted as exploratory associations rather than definitive intervention-specific causal effects. Second, the study compared two feedback arrangements: a four-phase AI-supported dialogue and written instructor comments. These arrangements differed in feedback provider and mode of interaction and may also have differed in feedback exposure and time on task. Although both groups had opportunities to revise their work, the study could not isolate the contribution of feedback structure from that of the provider, interactivity, or feedback exposure. An unstructured-AI comparison condition was not included for ethical reasons, reflecting concerns about possible overreliance and reduced independent reasoning. Its absence further limited the ability to distinguish the contribution of the four-phase structure from other features of AI feedback. Finally, the task scores were based on submissions completed after feedback and revision and therefore reflected performance following the full instructional process. Third, engagement was measured only after the intervention, preventing conclusions about changes in engagement over time. Moreover, the study did not directly measure the proposed metacognitive, reflective, or self-regulatory mechanisms, leaving the underlying process explanations unexamined. Fourth, the study was conducted in a single course at a single institution, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other disciplines, institutional environments, and student groups. Fifth, the intervention involved only three feedback cycles across three tasks, and it remains unclear whether the observed improvements in critical thinking would persist beyond the end of the semester or transfer to novel analytical tasks outside the curriculum. Future research should employ multiple classes per condition and incorporate process-level measures to examine how structured feedback activities relate to students' critical thinking development. Studies should also investigate the long-term sustainability and transferability of structured AI feedback effects across tasks, disciplines, and broader educational contexts.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to obtain feedback in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing, but its educational significance depends on how learners interpret and regulate that feedback. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and self-regulated learning theory, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined an AI-supported motivated self-regulated learning framework using a cross-sectional survey of 486 university EFL students and follow-up interviews with 20 students. Structural equation modeling identified a positive direct association between reported AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement, together with a positive indirect statistical association through learning autonomy and self-regulated learning. The AI feedback use–autonomy association was stronger at higher modeled levels of AI literacy. Interview accounts described feedback-related control, critical evaluation, and awareness of AI limitations, alongside contrasting experiences of rapid polishing and careful evaluation despite limited familiarity with AI. Integration of the two strands highlighted variation in how learners evaluated and incorporated feedback. These self-report findings do not establish temporal ordering or causal effects. They identify learner agency, strategic regulation, and critical evaluation as relevant considerations for future investigations of AI-supported writing.

reading.interpretation: AI feedback use was positively associated with deep cognitive engagement, alongside indirect statistical associations involving autonomy and self-regulated learning. The interview accounts contextualized these patterns through descriptions of feedback access, selective uptake, and reliance. These findings identify related learner perceptions without showing that any one process produces another. The combined evidence identifies variation in reported AI-supported revision rather than a uniform benefit or harm. Reflective uptake and rapid polishing appeared in different accounts ( Barrot, 2023 ; Teng, 2024 ). This is compatible with feedback scholarship emphasizing learners’ interpretation and use of advice ( Carless and Boud, 2018 ; Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick, 2006 ). The study did not measure learning gains or demonstrate that reflective use improved writing. The positive direct association between AI use and engagement does not imply that frequent use is sufficient for reflective revision. S05’s emphasis on polishing illustrates a different immediate purpose from the evaluative practices described by S03 and S15. Such variation helps explain why use frequency alone provides an incomplete account of the reported learning experience. A second contribution concerns the role of learning autonomy. Consistent with SDT, students who reported greater use of AI-generated feedback also reported greater control over the writing process ( Ryan and Deci, 2000 ). However, the kind of autonomy observed here is not equivalent to working independently from teachers or peers. analysis.methods: This study employed a cross-sectional explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. This design was selected because the research questions required both quantitative testing of theoretically specified associations and qualitative elaboration of how learners interpret and enact AI-supported feedback in practice ( Creswell and Plano Clark, 2018 ; Fetters et al., 2013 ). In the first phase, survey data were collected to examine the relationships among generative AI feedback use, learning autonomy, self-regulated learning, deep cognitive engagement, and AI literacy. Structural equation modeling was used to test the proposed model. In the second phase, semi-structured interviews were conducted with a subset of survey participants to elaborate, contextualize, and qualify the quantitative findings. The qualitative phase was not intended to establish temporal causality, but to examine how learners described the conditions under which AI feedback use was experienced as supportive, superficial, or difficult to evaluate. Connection between phases occurred through purposive selection from survey respondents and the use of preliminary quantitative findings to develop interview prompts. Variation in reported AI feedback use, engagement, and AI literacy guided selection alongside participant characteristics. The interviews examined how learners described feedback access, autonomous decisions, evaluation, and reliance. Model-consistent and divergent cases refer to interpretive patterns in linked questionnaire profiles and interview accounts, not statistically classified groups or cases selected using model residuals. The explanatory sequential design was appropriate for two reasons. First, the proposed framework included multiple latent constructs and indirect associations that required quantitative modeling. Second, because the educational significance of AI feedback is likely to depend on how learners interpret and regulate their interactions with AI-generated suggestions, qualitative follow-up was needed to illuminate how these processes were perceived from students’ perspectives. The quantitative phase was cross-sectional. The structural model therefore examined theoretically informed associations rather than causal relationships ( Brady et al., 2023 ; Robinson, 2026 ). Ethical review and informed consent procedures are reported in the Ethics Statement. The study was conducted in EFL academic writing courses at three public universities in China. The courses required multiple writing assignments and permitted digital writing tools, including generative AI systems, during drafting and revision. Survey data were collected from mid-November to early December 2024, when students had accumulated experience with AI-supported writing. Follow-up interviews were conducted in January 2025 after preliminary quantitative analysis. Platform-specific use was not systematically recorded in the questionnaire. Some interviewees spontaneously mentioned ChatGPT, ERNIE Bot (Wenxin Yiyan), Kimi, or Tongyi Qianwen, but these mentions do not provide a platform-use distribution. The findings therefore concern reported generative AI feedback use across unspecified tools and versions rather than a particular platform. Course instructors distributed the online questionnaire to students in the target courses. Of 512 responses, 26 were excluded through screening for incomplete responses, implausibly short completion, or patterned answering; 486 cases were retained. All 24 item responses were complete in the retained sample, so item-level imputation was not used. The sample represented a range of disciplinary backgrounds, including humanities, social sciences, business, science, and engineering. The demographic profile of the sample is presented in Table 2 . Demographic characteristics of survey participants ( N = 486). Percentages may not total 100 exactly because of rounding. Twenty survey respondents were selected using purposive maximum-variation sampling. Questionnaire construct means informed variation in AI feedback use, engagement, and AI literacy, alongside discipline, year of study, and gender. No fixed AI-literacy cutoffs, median split, or residual-based rule was applied. Selection sought contrasting combinations of reported use and engagement and different literacy profiles; the sample was not intended to represent their population frequencies. Preliminary results informed questions about autonomous decisions, monitoring, evaluation, and reliance. Interviews were conducted primarily in Chinese in January 2025, lasted 35–55 min, were audio-recorded with permission, and were transcribed. Anonymized identifiers S01–S20 link quotations to cases. The questionnaire comprised 24 items measuring AI feedback use (four items), learning autonomy (five items), self-regulated learning (six items), deep cognitive engagement (five items), and AI literacy (four items). Items were rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Construct scores were the means of their corresponding items; there were no reverse-scored items. Item order was randomized and construct labels were not shown. There were no missing item responses in the retained sample of 486 students. The measures capture self-reported perceptions and practices, not directly observed AI use, revision behavior, or demonstrated AI competence. Supplementary Table S1 provides the complete Chinese and English items with their standardized factor loadings. HH drafted 28 English items: AI feedback use 5, autonomy 6, self-regulated learning 7, engagement 6, and AI literacy 4. Team discussion reduced the pool to 26; expert review in September 2024 reduced it to 25; the October 2024 pilot reduced it to 24. No items were added. Two associate professors with expertise in applied linguistics and educational psychology reviewed content coverage, wording, and conceptual differentiation, including autonomy and engagement. Deletions addressed redundancy and conceptual overlap; wording changes addressed clarity. In the pilot, 48 students from a comparable academic writing course completed the questionnaire. Internal consistency exceeded 0.80 for each construct; item–total relationships and open-ended clarity feedback were also examined. Two items were reworded to avoid absolute frequency language, and one engagement item overlapping with self-regulated learning was removed. No numerical item–total deletion threshold or formal content-validity index is claimed. No EFA, item response theory analysis, cognitive interviews, or independent validation sample was used. Main-sample CFA therefore provides initial within-sample evidence, not independent confirmation of the final

Four themes elaborated and qualified the survey associations. The excerpts show how participants described control, evaluation, and reliance during revision; they are not observations of actual revision behavior. Anonymized identifiers are attached to each quotation. Section 4.6 presents the integrated joint display. Immediate feedback access was described as control over revision timing. S07 explained, “When I get stuck in writing, I can ask the AI immediately. It makes me feel that I can manage my writing by myself,” adding that not having to wait for a teacher’s reply helped maintain control over progress. S12 stated, “AI lets me get feedback whenever I need it, without waiting for the teacher; I feel more in control,” and described deciding which paragraph to revise. These accounts locate perceived autonomy in initiating support and directing attention to a chosen part of the text. They contextualize the AI feedback use–autonomy association without showing that convenient access improved writing or independent learning. Critical evaluation centered on alignment with intended meaning. S03 explained, “I usually read the AI suggestions carefully and decide whether they fit my meaning before using them,” and described modifying or rejecting fluent suggestions that changed the intended message. S15 similarly stated, “I compare the AI’s suggestions with my original ideas; sometimes I make changes, and sometimes I do not use them,” explaining that clearer expression was the deciding consideration. These accounts show how selective uptake could involve comparison and judgment rather than automatic acceptance. They elaborate the regulation–engagement association, although the study did not independently assess the quality of the resulting revisions. Participants differed in the authority assigned to AI output. S09, whose AI-literacy mean was 4.25, stated, “No matter how fluent the AI sounds, it can still be wrong, so I only use it as a reference,” and described judging both accuracy and fit with the text. These two cases connect questionnaire scores with contrasting accounts of reliance. They offer one interpretation of the interaction but do not independently establish moderation or define fixed higher- and lower-literacy groups. analysis.discussion: AI feedback use was positively associated with deep cognitive engagement, alongside indirect statistical associations involving autonomy and self-regulated learning. The interview accounts contextualized these patterns through descriptions of feedback access, selective uptake, and reliance. These findings identify related learner perceptions without showing that any one process produces another. The combined evidence identifies variation in reported AI-supported revision rather than a uniform benefit or harm. Reflective uptake and rapid polishing appeared in different accounts ( Barrot, 2023 ; Teng, 2024 ). This is compatible with feedback scholarship emphasizing learners’ interpretation and use of advice ( Carless and Boud, 2018 ; Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick, 2006 ). The study did not measure learning gains or demonstrate that reflective use improved writing. The positive direct association between AI use and engagement does not imply that frequent use is sufficient for reflective revision. S05’s emphasis on polishing illustrates a different immediate purpose from the evaluative practices described by S03 and S15. Such variation helps explain why use frequency alone provides an incomplete account of the reported learning experience. A second contribution concerns the role of learning autonomy. Consistent with SDT, students who reported greater use of AI-generated feedback also reported greater control over the writing process ( Ryan and Deci, 2000 ). However, the kind of autonomy observed here is not equivalent to working independently from teachers or peers. It is better understood as feedback-related agency: the perceived ability to decide when feedback is sought, how it is used, and which suggestions are accepted, modified, or rejected. Immediate, repeatable feedback may be experienced as greater control over timing and access, as illustrated by S07 and S12. However, this perceived control should not be equated with improved learning or freedom from dependence. The present findings do not establish autonomy as either necessary or sufficient for deep engagement; they identify a positive association with reported regulatory practices. Self-regulated learning was positively associated with deep cognitive engagement ( β = 0.47). This relationship highlights the relevance of reported regulatory practices to perceived cognitive investment in revision. The largest listed main-path coefficient was the autonomy–self-regulated learning association ( β = 0.52); differences between coefficients were not formally tested. This finding contributes to emerging research on generative AI by challenging tool-centered explanations. Much recent work has treated AI itself as the main explanatory factor, emphasizing perceived usefulness, adoption, or performance gains ( Lee et al., 2024 ; Lim et al., 2023 ). The present findings suggest that such explanations are incomplete. In writing contexts, learners still need to decide whether AI suggestions are accurate, whether they align with communicative goals, and how they should be integrated into revision. Students who regulate these processes actively appear more likely to report deep engagement with writing. The indirect statistical associations are consistent with the specified AI-MSRL framework but do not establish the temporal ordering of its constructs. Autonomy, regulation, and engagement may also influence how learners seek AI feedback. The theoretical contribution is therefore a model of related motivational and regulatory perceptions that can inform future longitudinal investigation, rather than a demonstrated mechanism of AI-supported learning. The reported interaction suggests that the AI feedback use–autonomy association differs with perceived AI literacy. It is provisional because the complete interaction parameterization and coefficient scaling are not documented. It does not establish that literacy creates motivational benefits or that a training intervention would alter the association. AI literacy was operationalized as self-reported critical understanding and use. S09’s recognition that fluent output can be wrong contrasts with S18’s description of direct uptake, offering an interpretation of differing reliance practices. These cases should not be generalized to all students at similar scores. The four-item measure does not assess the full range of technical, ethical, or performance-based AI competence. Future research could examine these dimensions and their relationships with autonomy, regulation, and engagement. The findings suggest that access and evaluative use warrant separate attention. Whether wider AI access reduces inequalities in learning opportunities was not examined and cannot be inferred from this study. The findings connect with psychological research on human–AI reliance and trust calibration ( Lee and See, 2004 ; Parasuraman and Riley, 1997 ). Interviewees described differing judgments about the reliability and relevance of AI suggestions. These accounts concern perceived reliance rather than measured trust calibration, but suggest questions for studies that compare users’ judgments with the actual accuracy of AI feedback. AI-supported writing can thus be considered an activity in which learners negotiate external advice in relation to their communicative goals and standards. AI literacy and self-regulation may be relevant resources for this negotiation. Direct evidence of appropriate reliance would require assessment of the suggestions encountered and the decisions made about them ( Hoff and Bashir, 2015 ; Lee and See, 2004 ). The study contributes an integrated theoretical account of reported feedback use, autonomy, regulation, engagement, and critical AI understanding. Its contribution lies in connecting these perceptions with contrasting accounts of feedback uptake, not in establishing an explanatory mechanism. The qualitative phase adds attention to timing, intended meaning, time pressure, and inherited feedback standards; the quantitative phase describes their theoretically relevant correlates. The study did not experimentally test instructional interventions. Nevertheless, future studies could examine activities in which students compare AI-generated feedback with teacher or peer feedback, justify acceptance or rejection, and identify inaccuracies or rhetorical mismatches. These are hypotheses for intervention research rather than practices validated by the present evidence ( Martella et al., 2024 ; Robinson, 2026 ). Instruction addressing AI limitations and critical evaluation is another direction for investigation. This proposal aligns with feedback-literacy and AI-literacy research emphasizing interpr

plain_reading.detail: Researchers surveyed 486 university students learning English and interviewed 20. The interviews explored who decided which feedback to keep and how students judged its usefulness.
plain_reading.limit: The study relies on what students remembered and reported. It cannot show whether their writing improved because of the way they used feedback.

title: Information overload, cognitive fatigue, and postgraduates’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence for English academic writing: the role of lower-order cognitive offloading

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

analysis.methods: This study used a three-wave survey with two-week intervals among postgraduates (master’s and doctoral students) at Chinese universities. A professional market research firm recruited participants and administered the three waves between June and September 2026. Recruitment used quotas for degree level and discipline group, the latter separating the humanities, social sciences, and arts from science, engineering, agriculture, and medicine. Eligible participants were at least 18 years old and had used generative AI for English academic writing in the past 4 weeks. They were also working on an English academic writing task. All 475 analyzed participants met these criteria in their Time 1 responses. The study received ethical approval from the Ethics Committee of the School of Journalism and Communication, Chongqing University, before data collection. Participants read information on voluntary participation, confidentiality, and withdrawal and gave electronic informed consent. A total of 625 postgraduates completed the Time 1 survey and passed the eligibility and quality checks. Of these, 88.2% completed Time 2 and 76.0% completed Time 3, and 475 completed all three waves. The firm’s quality checks comprised eligibility screening, checks for duplicate participant identifiers, attention checks, and review of unusually short completion times. These checks removed 29, 17, and 14 responses at Times 1, 2, and 3, respectively. The firm linked each participant’s responses across waves through participant identifiers. Incomplete records were removed during data cleaning, so the data set contained only participants who completed all three waves. Among the 475 completers, no item responses were missing, so the analyses used complete data without imputation. The questionnaires were administered in Chinese. Time 1 (Week 1) measured perceived information overload, lower-order cognitive offloading, cognitive fatigue, behavioral intention, and background characteristics ( Table 1 ). Time 2 (Week 3) measured cognitive fatigue, and Time 3 (Week 5) measured behavioral intention. Participants answered with reference to their current English academic writing, including directly related literature preparation and research-information processing. The questionnaire defined generative AI as tools that produce text, explanations, summaries, or other content in response to user requests. The analytic sample comprised 475 postgraduates who completed all three waves ( Table 2 ). Master’s students made up 68.4% of the sample and doctoral students 31.6%. Mean age was 25.55 years ( SD = 3.05), and 52.4% of participants were female. Social sciences (30.1%) and engineering (21.7%) were the largest disciplines. Journal manuscripts (40.8%) and theses or dissertations (26.7%) were the most common writing tasks. ChatGPT (36.6%) and DeepSeek (31.6%) were the most common main AI tools. Participants had used AI for academic writing for a mean of 12.94 months ( SD = 8.69) and on a mean of 13.59 of the past 28 days ( SD = 4.98). N = 475. Values are n (%) unless marked M (SD). The other writing task was a conference poster. All items used 5-point response scales and are listed in Table 3 with their standardized loadings. Adaptation changed only the referent of each item and its reference period, for example from AI-related information to writing-related information provided by AI. Supplementary Table S1 lists the source wording, the adapted English wording, and the Chinese wording of every item. Two bilingual researchers translated the adapted items into Chinese, and an independent bilingual researcher back-translated them into English. Discrepancies were resolved by comparing the back-translation with the source wording and the construct definitions. Reference periods for each measure are given in Table 1 . Scale scores were item means, with higher scores indicating higher levels of each construct. Loadings at Time 1 come from the four-factor model, and loadings at Time 2 (cognitive fatigue) and Time 3 (behavioral intention) from the longitudinal configural model. All loadings were significant, p < 0.001. (R) = reverse-scored. Items were administered in Chinese. Supplementary Table S1 gives the source, adapted English, and Chinese wording of each item. Perceived information overload was measured at Time 1 with five items ( Qiu et al., 2025 ). The items referred to writing-related information provided by AI, such as feeling overwhelmed by its amount. IO4 asks about the time and effort needed to understand this information, which describes the processing demand of the information. A sensitivity model scored the scale without IO4 (Section 4.8). Responses ranged from 1 (never) to 5 (very often). In this study, α = 0.85 and ω = 0.86. Cognitive fatigue was measured at Time 1 and Time 2 with the four mental fatigue items of the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI; Smets et al., 1995 ). The MFI separates mental fatigue from general fatigue, physical fatigue, reduced motivation, and reduced activity ( Smets et al., 1995 ). Its mental fatigue items concern keeping one’s thoughts on a task, concentrating, the effort needed to concentrate, and wandering thoughts ( Table 3 ). The label cognitive fatigue refers to this attentional dimension of fatigue. An MFI-based measure with the same label has been used in research on students’ AI dependence ( Tian and Zhang, 2025 ). The items referred to concentration during AI use and the processing of AI output for English academic writing. Responses ranged from 1 (not at all true) to 5 (completely true), and CF1 and CF2 were reverse-scored. At Time 1 and Time 2, α = 0.85 and 0.87, and ω = 0.85 and 0.87. Lower-order cognitive offloading was measured at Time 1 with the five-item lower-order subscale of the AI-based cognitive offloading scale ( Jiang and Chen, 2026 ). The items asked how often participants used AI for tasks such as summarizing the key arguments of papers and generating search queries. The subscale thus records the frequency of delegating lower-order tasks, and the higher-order subscale was not administered. LO5 concerns data cleaning and preprocessing, which supports writing based on empirical data, and a sensitivity model scored the subscale without LO5 (Section 4.8). In its development study, the subscale was derived with exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses and showed adequate reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity ( Jiang and Chen, 2026 ). Responses ranged from 1 (never) to 5 (always). In this study, α = 0.87 and ω = 0.87. Behavioral intention was measured at Time 1 and Time 3 with three items ( Garcia, 2025 ). The items referred to using AI

analysis.discussion: This study asked whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also asked whether lower-order cognitive offloading conditions the first stage of this pathway. Chinese master’s and doctoral students reported overload and offloading at Time 1, cognitive fatigue at Time 2, and behavioral intention at Time 3. The answers address three open questions: AI output demands in intention research, fatigue as a mechanism over time, and offloading as a boundary condition. Higher perceived information overload at Time 1 accompanied weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, with Time 1 intention held constant, which supports H1. The association therefore concerns how intention changed over 4 weeks among writers with the same baseline intention. This result is consistent with the role of expected effort in intention to use ChatGPT ( Dong, 2024 ; Foroughi et al., 2024 ; Strzelecki and ElArabawy, 2024 ). It also parallels students who chose not to use AI tools when reviewing their suggestions took too much time (Cummings et al., 2024, as cited in Zhang et al., 2026 ). It extends them by locating the effort in AI output, a demand that ease-of-use measures tend to merge with others ( Huang et al., 2026 ). Demands located outside AI show mixed associations with AI use ( Abbas et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ). Processing AI output accompanied weaker plans, so the source of a demand appears to matter for its association with AI use. A plausible reason is that processing AI output makes the effort of AI use itself salient. Anticipated effort counts as a cost when people weigh whether to engage in a task (Eccles and Wigfield, 1995, as cited in Grund et al., 2024 ). Perceived information overload at Time 1 was associated with higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later, which supports H2. Cognitive fatigue at Time 2 was associated with weaker intention 2 weeks later, which supports H3. Cognitive fatigue carried part of the association between overload and intention, which supports H4. This sequence is consistent with stressor-strain-outcome pathways on social media, where overload relates to exhaustion and exhaustion to discontinuance intention ( Pang and Ruan, 2023 ) or lower educational attainment ( Pang et al., 2024 ). It also parallels message fatigue linking overload with behavioral intention ( Sun and Lee, 2023 ) and cognitive fatigue linking AI dependence with weaker critical thinking ( Tian and Zhang, 2025 ). The present design separates the stressor, the strain, and the outcome in time. It found the pathway across waves, without the concurrent association that single-wave designs would capture. Overload may relate to later fatigue because writers keep processing AI output in the following weeks, which draws on limited capacity. Fatigued writers may then anticipate the effort of another round of AI interaction, and mental effort feels inherently aversive ( David et al., 2024 ). Overload was unrelated to fatigue and intention measured at the same time, a pattern that departs from the concurrent associations that stressor-strain accounts usually imply. Strain that builds with continued exposure to AI output would fit this lagged pattern, which repeated overload measures could examine. Intention would then shift only after such strain had built, which fits its lagged association with overload. Baseline intention was not significantly associated with later fatigue, so the data gave no sign of a reverse path from intention to fatigue. Baseline fatigue was also not significantly associated with later intention once Time 2 fatigue was held constant. The latent model, which allowed for measurement error, showed the same indirect pathway. Since all associations were estimated net of baseline fatigue and intention, they describe how writers’ fatigue and intention moved relative to their own earlier levels. The association between perceived information overload and later cognitive fatigue was weaker among postgraduates who offloaded lower-order tasks more often, which supports H5. Among the most frequent offloaders, the association was not statistically significant, and its interval included both zero and moderate positive values. This result therefore shows a weaker association at high offloading, and it does not show that offloading removes the link between overload and fatigue. The indirect association with intention through fatigue was weaker in the same way, which supports H6. These patterns are consistent with cognitive offloading as a means of overcoming capacity limits ( Risko and Gilbert, 2016 ) and as a value-based choice about which cognitive work to delegate ( Gilbert, 2024 ; Jiang and Chen, 2026 ). They also parallel doctoral writers who offload language polishing to focus on research ( Li and Lin, 2025 ) and learners whose load eases when AI corrects grammar ( Cen and Shakibaei, 2026 ). A plausible reason is that writers who hand summarizing and searching to AI keep more capacity for judging the AI output that perceived overload concerns. The result adds a possible short-term benefit to concerns that offloading to AI weakens critical thinking ( Gerlich, 2025 ) and independent performance ( Darvishi et al., 2024 ). Offloading benefits depend on the offloaded demand being unnecessary for the learning goal ( Risko and Gilbert, 2016 ), and the measured offloading concerned foundational tasks such as summarizing and searching. The moderation and the conditional indirect association held when AI-use days entered the models and when a competing interaction with AI-use days was added. They also held when overload, offloading, and fatigue were scored without IO4, LO5, and CF1, respectively. The moderation therefore does not reduce to how many days writers used AI, which correlated weakly with offloading and not significantly with fatigue. Offloading correlated positively with overload, which fits the possibility that frequent offloaders receive more AI output, a quantity the present measures did not capture. These checks concern covariates, a competing moderator, item content, and the moderated paths, and Section 5.7 discusses other sources of confounding. In an exploratory model, offloading also conditioned the direct association, which was less negative among frequent offloaders. Perceived AI value accompanies offloading ( Jiang and Chen, 2026 ), so frequent offloaders may value AI highly enough to keep their plans for AI use under overload. Since no hypothesis concerned this path, the pattern needs confirmation in an independent sample before it informs theory. Offloading did not significantly condition t
