analysis.discussion: Read across all five themes, this review's central interpretation is that the crisis of critical thinking is better modeled as a scaffolding and validity failure than as a motivation or character failure on the part of students. Theme 1 shows why the cognitive demand on students has genuinely increased; Theme 2, sharpened by the Vygotskian contrast with fading scaffolds, shows why generative AI may be an unusually poor fit for that demand despite feeling like exactly the right tool in the moment of use; Theme 3 shows why fluent output and automated detection both mislead; and Theme 4 shows that the most promising responses act either on how AI support is designed or on what assessment can observe. But a concept is not a policy, and Theme 5 shows that translating this diagnosis into curricular and assessment change runs into real institutional frictionworkload, equity, and the seductive but unreliable shortcut of AI-detection software. The most important apparent contradiction is that GenAI improves performance in some studies while appearing to harm learning or critical thinking in others. The synthesis suggests that these findings are compatible once performance during AI use is distinguished from independent performance afterwards. Studies that measure output while AI is available tend to find gains (Bastani et al., 2025; Darvishi et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025) , whereas studies that measure independent performance, reasoning quality, or transfer find no gain or a loss (Bastani et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025; Stadler et al., 2024) . Offloading theory and desirable-difficulties research predict exactly this dissociation (Bjork and Bjork, 2011; Grinschgl et al., 2021) . A second apparent contradiction, between claims of a criticalthinking crisis and meta-analytic evidence that critical thinking improves during college (Huber and Kuncel, 2016) , is better read as a question about what current assessments certify than as evidence that students' capacities have collapsed. A pattern worth naming explicitly is how often the same underlying mechanism recurs across themes framed as separate problems. The illusion of competence and the AI-detector bias are, in a sense, mirror images of the same confusion between fluency and validity: in one direction, a fluent AI output is mistaken for a reliable one; in the other, a non-native speaker's less statistically "predictable" prose is mistaken for AI output. Both errors share a root causetreating a statistical property of text as a proxy for a property it does not reliably track. This suggests that AI and information literacy, as a dimension of critical thinking, needs to include explicit instruction in why fluency is not evidence. Several features of the evidence base may explain variation in findings. Measurement differs: self-reported effort (Gerlich, 2025; Lee et al., 2025) and neural connectivity (Kosmyna et al., 2025) are not measures of critical thinking, and only a few studies measure delayed or transfer outcomes. Populations differ: knowledge workers, university students, and secondary-school students bring different prior knowledge, which theory suggests should change how much they can scrutinise AI output. Tool design differs: unguided chatbots and guardrailed tutors are not the same intervention (Bastani et al., 2025) . Context differs: samples come from the United States, Europe, Australia, China, Turkey, and Bangladesh, with different assessment cultures and AI policies, but few studies compare contexts directly. Finally, most studies capture single sessions or a single term, whereas the concern about critical thinking is cumulative. The synthesis extends existing perspectives in five ways. For cognitive offloading theory, it suggests a distinction between offloading that reduces extraneous load and offloading that removes the germane processing through which learning occurs, with GenAI unusually able to do the latter. For scaffolding theory, it proposes that fading be used as an explicit design criterion for AI tools, not only for human tutors. For criticalthinking theory, it specifies four dimensions suited to an AIsaturated environment and links each to a mechanism it counteracts. For information literacy, it extends lateral reading from evaluating web sources to auditing AI output. For selfregulated learning, it identifies calibration of trust in AI, not only of self-knowledge, as a regulatory target. Several questions remain open: whether the short-term effects observed in experiments accumulate into lasting differences in critical thinking; how critical thinking should be measured when AI is legitimately part of the task; whether AI tools can be designed to fade in practice and whether students will use such tools when unrestricted alternatives are freely available; and how the costs of process-visible assessment can be met equitably. This review set out to examine how information abundance, algorithmic curation, and GenAI use may influence critical thinking in higher education, and what universities should therefore teach and assess. Across five themes, the synthesis suggests that the central cognitive task for students has shifted from retrieving information to evaluating it; that unguided GenAI use is associated with reduced cognitive engagement and, in several experiments, with performance gains that do not translate into independent learning; that fluent AI output is readily mistaken for validated knowledge, while automated detection is too unreliable and biased to serve as a remedy; that critical thinking and lateral reading are teachable and that guided AI use and process-visible assessment are promising responses; and that workload, equity, and policy constraints shape which institutions can adopt them. The evidence establishes some of these claims more firmly than others. It establishes that language models hallucinate, that AI detectors are unreliable and biased, and that critical thinking and lateral reading can be taught. It suggests, with growing but still short-term support, that unguided AI use reduces cognitive effort and can dissociate performance from learning, and that tool design moderates this. It remains uncertain whether these effects accumulate into lasting declines in critical thinking, how critical thinking should be measured when AI is part of the task, and whether process-visible assessment improves outcomes in practice. Theoretically, the synthesis refines several perspectives at once. It distinguishes offloading that reduces extraneous load from offloading that removes the germane processing through which learning occurs; it proposes fading as a design criterion for AI tools, extending scaffolding theory; it specifies four dimensions of critical thinking matched to the mechanisms they counteract; it extends information literacy from evaluating sources to auditing AI output; and it identifies calibrated trust in AI as a target for self-regulated learning. No structured search of Scopus or Web of Science with PRISMA-style screening was conducted, so the search cannot be fully reproduced, and relevant studies may have been missed. Coding was conducted by a single reviewer, so inter-coder agreement could not be assessed, although the source-by-theme matrix and evidence-strength judgements are reported to make the interpretation auditable. No formal riskof-bias instrument was applied. Several of the most directly relevant empirical sources (Kosmyna et al., 2025; Roy and Jony, 2026) are very recent, and at least one (Kosmyna et al., 2025) has drawn published methodological criticism regarding sample size and analytic transparency that this review has not independently adjudicated; its findings are reported here as suggestive rather than settled. The strongest experimental evidence on delayed effects comes from a secondary-school sample (Bastani et al., 2025) . The proposed connections between classical cognitive science and contemporary GenAI-specific findings are this review's own interpretive synthesis rather than a claim directly tested by any single included study. Finally, only English-language sources were included, and although the corpus includes studies from Asia and the Middle East as well as Western contexts, most sources come from Western highereducation systems, limiting confidence in how far the findings generalize elsewhere. A further limitation concerns the scaffolding-fade component of the framework: while the underlying scaffolding literature (Vygotsky, 1978; Wood, Bruner, and Ross, 1976) is well established, its application to generative AI specifically is this review's own extension, and empirical work directly testing whether AI tools can be redesigned to fade in the way human scaffolding does remains largely absent from the current literature. The Fade-Visibility Matrix is likewise unvalidated; Section 6.4 sets out propositions for testing it, and a systematic review with a registered protocol is a natural next step.

analysis.discussion: This study estimated differentiated associations between five critical thinking dispositions, two GenAI interaction pathways, and perceived support-dependence discrepancy. The findings are consistent with several propositions derived from distributed cognition and depth-of-processing perspectives, while the cross-sectional and self-report design limits causal and mechanistic interpretation. This study examined the associations among five dimensions of critical thinking disposition, cognitive offloading, cognitive enhancement, and perceived support-dependence discrepancy in GenAI-assisted academic learning. Inquisitiveness was positively associated with both interaction pathways, whereas open-mindedness and systematicity showed small positive associations with cognitive enhancement. Analyticity and truth-seeking were not significantly associated with either cognitive offloading or cognitive enhancement. Both interaction pathways were positively associated with perceived supportdependence discrepancy, although the association was stronger for cognitive offloading. The findings contribute to research on learner-AI interaction by distinguishing cognitively substitutive and cognitively constructive forms of GenAI engagement while recognizing that they may coexist. The significant indirect associations further indicate that critical thinking dispositions may be linked to perceived supported-versusunsupported competence through different patterns of human-AI interaction. However, the study assessed perceived support-dependence discrepancy as a monitoring-related self-report rather than as a direct measure of metacognitive monitoring, cognitive ownership, or objective calibration. The present findings should therefore be interpreted as associations with a perceived support-dependent competence gap rather than as evidence of any single established psychological mechanism. Academic stress did not significantly moderate the association between cognitive offloading and perceived support-dependence discrepancy in the present observed-score analysis. This result indicates only that the hypothesized moderation was not detected in the current sample and does not establish invariance across tasks, institutions, or stress conditions. Given the cross-sectional design, single-item outcome measure, common data source, and heterogeneous task contexts, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of conditional statistical associations. Longitudinal, behavioral, and experimental studies incorporating AI-assisted performance, unaided performance, confidence judgments, and validated support-dependence measures are needed to test the direction and mechanisms of these relationships.
analysis.limitations: First, academic stress and perceived support-dependence discrepancy were measured with single items. Reliability sensitivity analyses showed that the focal latent-path conclusions were stable across several assumed reliability values, but this does not substitute for direct evidence of reliability, construct coverage, or measurement validity. The PSD item captures learners' perceived awareness of a gap between AI-supported and unaided competence; it does not directly measure the accuracy of ongoing judgments about understanding or independent reproducibility, nor does it establish illusory self-assessment, overconfidence, or objectively verified calibration bias. Future studies should develop and validate separate multi-item measures of perceived support-dependence discrepancy and metacognitive monitoring and combine them with repeated confidence judgments, AIassisted performance scores, delayed unaided performance scores, and objective calibration indices. Second, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal or causal ordering. Structural paths and indirect associations should be interpreted as conditional covariance patterns under the specified model. Longitudinal panels, cross-lagged designs, randomized interventions, and delayed transfer tests are needed to evaluate directionality. Third, convergent and discriminant validity were not uniformly strong. Three AVE values were below 0.50, and several critical-thinking dimensions showed high HTMT values and semantically overlapping items. Future measurement studies should revise overlapping items, confirm the factor structure in an independent sample, assess convergent and incremental validity against established AI-literacy and GenAI-use measures, and test measurement invariance across institutions and disciplines. Fourth, all focal variables came from the same questionnaire. Procedural controls and the common-method-factor analysis reduced but did not eliminate common-method concerns. Future studies should combine self-reports with prompt logs, source-check records, think-aloud protocols, instructor ratings, and objective transfer tasks to determine whether reported interaction patterns correspond to observable behavior. Fifth, participants answered with reference to usual academic tasks rather than a standardized task, so task type, complexity, discipline, and permitted assistance may be confounded. Future research should use standardized tasks and systematically vary or record task complexity, disciplinary context, and the permitted level of GenAI assistance to test whether the observed associations are task-contingent. Sixth, although the stratified purposive sampling strategy provided variation across regions and institution types, the sample was not probability-based. Future multicenter studies should adopt probability-based or clearly enumerated sampling frames, document institutionspecific recruitment and exclusions, and test the model across a broader range of regions and institutions. The findings should therefore be generalized beyond the participating universities with caution.

analysis.discussion: This study investigated the psychological mechanisms underlying undergraduate students' overreliance on GAI feedback by integrating perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and metacognitive monitoring into a unified research model. Based on survey data from university students, this study examined how learning-related cognitive demands influence students' use of GAI and how cognitive offloading contributes to the formation of GAI feedback dependence. The findings provide a cognitive perspective for understanding students' interaction with generative artificial intelligence in learning environments. The results demonstrate that perceived cognitive load plays an important role in shaping students' GAI-related behaviors. When students experience higher cognitive demands during learning, they are more likely to adopt cognitive offloading strategies by using GAI as external cognitive support. Cognitive offloading further contributes to overreliance on GAI feedback, indicating that students' dependence on AI feedback is not only related to technological factors but also reflects their cognitive responses to learning pressure. In addition, perceived cognitive load directly influences overreliance on GAI feedback, suggesting that cognitive demands can affect students' reliance on AI-generated information through both direct and indirect pathways. Furthermore, this study reveals the role of metacognitive monitoring in shaping the relationship between cognitive demands and GAI feedback dependence. The comparison between groups with different levels of metacognitive monitoring shows that students follow different pathways when developing reliance on GAI feedback. Students with lower metacognitive monitoring show a stronger direct association between perceived cognitive load and GAI feedback overreliance, whereas students with higher metacognitive monitoring show a stronger role of cognitive offloading in explaining GAI feedback dependence. These findings suggest that metacognitive monitoring influences not only students' learning regulation but also how they manage their cognitive relationship with intelligent tools. Overall, this study extends the understanding of GAIsupported learning by demonstrating that overreliance on AI feedback emerges from the interaction between cognitive demands, external cognitive support, and self-regulatory processes. The findings highlight that effective GAI use requires more than access to intelligent tools; it also depends on students' ability to regulate cognitive resources and evaluate AI-generated information appropriately. This study provides theoretical and practical insights into how university students can develop a more balanced and productive relationship with generative artificial intelligence in learning contexts.
analysis.limitations: Although this study reveals the relationships among perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, metacognitive monitoring, and overreliance on GAI feedback, several aspects require further investigation. First, the cross-sectional design of this study limits the ability to establish causal relationships among the variables. Although the structural equation model supports the hypothesized associations and mediation pathways, the findings should be interpreted as relationships among variables rather than causal effects. Students' interactions with GAI may involve dynamic processes in which cognitive load, cognitive offloading strategies, metacognitive monitoring, and feedback reliance influence each other over time. Future studies could adopt longitudinal designs, experimental methods, or experience sampling approaches to further examine the developmental and causal mechanisms underlying students' interactions with GAI. Second, this study used a single-item measure to classify students' metacognitive monitoring levels. Although this approach provides a concise indicator of students' perceived metacognitive monitoring and facilitates comparisons between groups, it may not fully capture the complexity and multidimensional characteristics of metacognitive monitoring. Metacognitive monitoring involves various processes, including monitoring understanding, evaluating learning progress, and regulating cognitive strategies, which may not be sufficiently represented by a single item. Future research could employ validated multi-item scales or combine selfreported measures with behavioral indicators to obtain a more comprehensive assessment of students' metacognitive monitoring abilities. Third, the comparisons between the low-and high-metacognitive-monitoring groups in this study were based on differences in path coefficient patterns rather than formal statistical tests of betweengroup differences. Therefore, these results should be interpreted as variations in structural relationships across metacognitive monitoring levels rather than confirmed differences between groups. Future research could apply formal multi-group analysis approaches to further examine whether the strength of relationships among variables significantly differs across different levels of metacognitive monitoring. Fourth, the present study mainly relied on self-reported questionnaires to measure students' GAI use experiences, cognitive perceptions, and behavioral tendencies. Although self-reported measures are useful for capturing students' subjective experiences, they may also be influenced by recall bias, social desirability, and individual interpretation differences, which may introduce potential common method bias. Future research could integrate multiple data sources, such as GAI interaction logs, learning behavior records, task performance data, and experimental measures, to provide a more objective understanding of students' cognitive regulation processes during GAI use. Finally, the participants in this study were recruited from a single university, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Students from different universities, academic disciplines, and educational contexts may differ in their access to AI technologies, learning environments, and patterns of GAI engagement. Therefore, future studies should include samples from multiple institutions and diverse educational backgrounds to further validate the proposed model and examine its applicability across different learning contexts.

reading.interpretation: The present study developed and validated the AI Cognitive Offloading Scale for College Students (AI-COS) by examining how different cognitive functions are delegated to generative AI in learning contexts. The contribution should be understood as an alternative and context-specific operationalization rather than as the first measurement of AI cognitive offloading. Recent work has already provided complementary approaches. Jiang and Chen (2026) developed the AIBCO Scale for highereducation students in China, distinguishing lower-order from higher-order cognitive offloading according to the level of cognitive demand. Zhu et al. (2026) distinguished dependent from autonomous cognitive offloading according to whether users substitute their own thinking or use AI as a scaffold while retaining cognitive agency. In contrast, the AI-COS organizes offloading by the primary cognitive function delegated to AI-memory, assistive task-related processing, and thinking-and was developed specifically for Chinese college students' learning activities. These distinctions make the AI-COS conceptually complementary to existing measures: the AIBCO framework emphasizes cognitivedemand level, the dependent/autonomous framework emphasizes the manner of delegation, and the AI-COS emphasizes the function being delegated. This function-based perspective may be useful when researchers need to distinguish information storage and retrieval from AI participation in academic task execution and from delegation of judgment or decision support. From a theoretical standpoint, the findings suggest that the influence of generative AI on college students' learning is no longer confined to information provision or efficiency enhancement. Rather, AI systems can be implicated in task execution, cognitive process
reading.limitations: Although the present study provides relatively comprehensive evidence for the development and validation of the scale, several limitations should be acknowledged. analysis.methods: Participants were recruited from several universities through university student groups and class groups using a convenience sampling approach. The questionnaire was administered online. Following commonly used procedures (Curran, 2016; Xu and Li, 2021) , 11 participants with incomplete responses were excluded, resulting in a final valid sample of 665 college students. Among them, 312 were male (46.9%) and 353 were female (53.1%). In terms of academic year, 183 were first-year students (27.5%), 159 were second-year students (23.9%), 172 were third-year students (25.9%), and 151 were fourth-year students (22.7%). The sample size was considered adequate for item analysis and exploratory factor analysis given the initial 26-item pool and the observed sample size. The resulting participant-to-item ratio was approximately 25.6:1, providing a substantial empirical basis for estimating the factor structure. For Study 1, the questionnaire was distributed online through student groups and class groups associated with several universities using a convenience sampling approach. Before participation, students were informed of the study purpose, the voluntary nature of participation, confidentiality of responses, and the scientific use of the data. The AI Cognitive Offloading Scale for College Students (AI-COS) was developed through sequential stages. First, the construct definition and provisional dimensional structure were established through literature review and theoretical analysis of cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, transactive memory, and AI-assisted learning. No formal open-ended or semi-structured interviews were conducted, and no separate pilot study was conducted before the main survey. Second, an initial pool of 26 items was generated and refined for clarity, conciseness, conceptual relevance, and appropriateness to college learning contexts. Third, a panel of five experts (all holding Ph.D. degrees in Psychology or Educational Technology, with average professional academic experience exceeding 5 years) independently evaluated all 26 items using a 3-point relevance scale (1 = inappropriate, 2 = appropriate after revision, 3 = appropriate). Their judgments focused on conceptual relevance, representativeness of AI cognitive offloading, wording clarity, and suitability for college learning contexts. The item wording and conceptual fit were revised in response to this evaluation, and the 26-item preliminary questionnaire was retained for empirical evaluation. Fourth, the preliminary questionnaire was evaluated empirically in the Study 1 sample through item discrimination, item-total correlations, and reliability analysis before EFA. Thus, preliminary questionnaire evaluation in the present study refers to expert content evaluation followed by empirical item analysis rather than to a separate pilot sample. A 5point Likert response format ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree" was used. Finally, SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 8.3 were used for item analysis and EFA. For Study 2, the questionnaire was distributed online through student groups and class groups associated with several universities, using the same convenience-sampling procedure as in Study 1. The Study 2 participants were newly recruited and did not overlap with the Study 1 sample. Before completing the questionnaire, participants were informed that participation was voluntary, responses would remain confidential, and the data would be used only for scientific research. After data collection, Mplus 8.3 was used to conduct confirmatory factor analysis, whereas SPSS 26.0 was used to examine reliability and validity indices.
analysis.discussion: The present study developed and validated the AI Cognitive Offloading Scale for College Students (AI-COS) by examining how different cognitive functions are delegated to generative AI in learning contexts. The contribution should be understood as an alternative and context-specific operationalization rather than as the first measurement of AI cognitive offloading. Recent work has already provided complementary approaches. Jiang and Chen (2026) developed the AIBCO Scale for highereducation students in China, distinguishing lower-order from higher-order cognitive offloading according to the level of cognitive demand. Zhu et al. (2026) distinguished dependent from autonomous cognitive offloading according to whether users substitute their own thinking or use AI as a scaffold while retaining cognitive agency. In contrast, the AI-COS organizes offloading by the primary cognitive function delegated to AI-memory, assistive task-related processing, and thinking-and was developed specifically for Chinese college students' learning activities. These distinctions make the AI-COS conceptually complementary to existing measures: the AIBCO framework emphasizes cognitivedemand level, the dependent/autonomous framework emphasizes the manner of delegation, and the AI-COS emphasizes the function being delegated. This function-based perspective may be useful when researchers need to distinguish information storage and retrieval from AI participation in academic task execution and from delegation of judgment or decision support. From a theoretical standpoint, the findings suggest that the influence of generative AI on college students' learning is no longer confined to information provision or efficiency enhancement. Rather, AI systems can be implicated in task execution, cognitive processing, and intellectual regulation, functioning as components of an extended cognitive system. The extended mind theory argues that external tools are not merely ancillary to cognition, but may become constitutive elements of the cognitive system itself (Clark and Chalmers, 1998) . Likewise, cognitive offloading research indicates that external resources can reduce internal cognitive load, while the consequences of offloading may depend on the nature and regulation of the delegated activity (Risko and Gilbert, 2016; Turner, 2022) . Within this framework, the present study conceptualized three functionally distinct forms of AI cognitive offloading-memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading. These dimensions describe different cognitive functions that may be delegated to AI; the present cross-sectional factor structure does not establish that students move from one form to another over time. One of the important findings is that AI cognitive offloading among college students can be differentiated into three interrelated dimensions: memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading. Importantly, this three-dimensional structure represents one empirically supported operationalization of the construct rather than a claim that these are the only possible dimensions. The exploratory factor analysis yielded a clear factor pattern, and the confirmatory factor analysis supported a higherorder structure. The resulting dimensions are also conceptually distinguishable from recent alternatives. Jiang and Chen (2026) separated AI-based cognitive offloading into lower-order and higher-order forms, while Zhu et al. (2026) distinguished dependent and autonomous offloading according to the degree to which users retain cognitive agency. The AI-COS instead differentiates the functions delegated to AI within college learning: memory-related storage and retrieval, task-related assistance and execution, and higher-order thinking-related judgment and decision support. The three approaches therefore address related but non-identical questions about AI-mediated cognition. TABLE Fit indices and testing for measurement invariance across groups. Within this framework, memory offloading primarily reflects students' tendency to delegate basic cognitive operations-such as memorization, retrieval, storage, and organization-to AI systems, thereby transferring part of the cognitive burden to external technological resources. This dimension is closely aligned with the classic notion of cognitive offloading, namely the use of external media to reduce internal cognitive costs. Assistive offloading, in contrast, involves AI-supported completion and organization of learning tasks, including content generation, textual organization, expression refinement, and the handling of complex academic assignments. Thinking offloading involves the delegation of judgment support, analytic integration, logical inference, and decision assistance. These dimensions therefore differ in the type of cognitive function being delegated, but the present factor analysis does not demonstrate that they form a developmental continuum, that one dimension necessarily precedes another, or that greater endorsement of one dimension causes movement toward another. Their co-occurrence under a higher-order factor indicates shared variance in AI cognitive offloading, not temporal progression. The confirmatory factor analysis further supported the proposed multidimensional structure. The second-order model provided the best fit among the three competing specifications, and the three first-order dimensions showed strong loadings on the higher-order AI cognitive offloading factor. This pattern supports a hierarchical representation in which memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading are distinguishable functions that share substantial common variance. The model therefore provides a statistical basis for reporting both dimension-specific scores and an overall AI cognitive offloading score. Importantly, the higher-order representation should not be interpreted as evidence that the three dimensions form a temporal sequence or a developmental hierarchy. The criterion-related validity findings are particularly informative because they reveal differentiated association patterns across dimensions. The total AI cognitive offloading score and all three dimensions showed significant positive associations with AI dependence, indicating that greater reported AI cognitive offloading was associated with greater AI dependence across the three function-based forms. Similarly, the total score and all three dimensions were negatively associated with metacognitive monitoring. In relation to need for cognition, the total score and assistive offloading were negatively associated with need for cognition, whereas the memory and thinking offloading dimensions were not significantly related to this criterion. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence that cognitive offloading is inherently beneficial or detrimental. Instead, they suggest that the psychological meaning of offloading may depend on which cognitive function is delegated, the extent of delegation, and the degree to which learners continue to monitor and regulate the process. From a functional perspective, cognitive offloading may enhance cognition when external resources reduce unnecessary cognitive demands, support information organization and retrieval, or free internal resources for monitoring, integration, and other higher-order activities (Risko and Gilbert, 2016; Dunn and Risko, 2016) . analysis.limitations: Although the present study provides relatively comprehensive evidence for the development and validation of the scale, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, although the sample included a relatively large number of college students, it was still drawn primarily from undergraduate students in a specific contextual setting. Future studies should therefore further examine the external validity of the scale across different regions, types of institutions, and graduate student populations. Second, the present study employed a cross-sectional design, which does not allow for the examination of dynamic changes in AI cognitive offloading during the learning process, nor does it permit causal inference regarding its antecedents or consequences. Third, although the current scale distinguishes among memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading, the rapid evolution of generative AI may continue to reshape how students use such systems. Future research should therefore revise and refine the items in light of new model capabilities, task contexts, and educational norms. Fourth, the initial item-development stage was based on literature review, theoretical analysis, and expert content evaluation rather than formal qualitative interviews. Therefore, the present study does not provide interview-derived qualitative evidence for item generation. Future scale-development studies could incorporate systematic open-ended interviews or focus groups, together with detailed coding procedures, to further examine students' lived experiences of AI cognitive offloading and whether additional dimensions or context-specific behaviors should be represented. Combining qualitative exploration with quantitative validation has been illustrated in other domains, such as the development of a multidimensional career-success scale for Chinese employees (Zhou et al., 2013) , and offers a methodological example for future scale refinement. Fifth, future research may also combine interviews, learning logs, or behavioral data to examine whether different forms of AI cognitive offloading correspond to different actual learning outcomes, thereby gradually extending this construct from a self-report measure toward a multi-method assessment framework. Future assessments could also distinguish metacognitive knowledge, monitoring, and control and incorporate taskbased measures alongside self-report, drawing on measurement approaches reviewed in educational settings (Rivers et al., 2020) . Sixth, although three dimensions were retained, their coverage of AI cognitive offloading should be examined further across tasks, populations, and contexts. Unexplained item variance may reflect specific variance and measurement error as well as other influences. Existing research suggests that AI cognitive offloading may also vary according to the cognitive-demand level of the delegated task and the manner in which users engage with AI. For example, Jiang and Chen (2026) distinguished lower-order and higher-order AI cognitive offloading and showed that AI evaluation capability may condition associations with these forms, whereas Zhu et al. (2026) distinguished dependent from autonomous offloading according to whether users retain cognitive agency. Future research should therefore examine whether cognitive-demand level, delegation style, AI evaluation capability, task characteristics, and learner characteristics account for additional variance or function as antecedents and boundary conditions of AI cognitive offloading. Longitudinal, experimental, behavioral, and cross-context validation studies may help determine whether these dimensions represent additional components of the construct or complementary dimensions that operate alongside the function-based structure identified in the present study. Existing reviews also suggest that this field remains in a phase of rapid expansion but uneven evidence development, underscoring the need for structured measurement tools such as the present scale to address the current gap at the level of cognitive processes (Schei et al., 2024; McDonald et al., 2025) . A review of early public claims about ChatGPT highlights the need to distinguish expectations about educational transformation from empirical evidence (Jensen et al., 2025) . A review of empirical studies further identified heterogeneous approaches and limited shared theoretical grounding in research on generative AI chatbots in higher education (McGrath et al., 2025) .

This offloading deprived metacognitive monitoring of its raw material and weakened the perceived necessity of self-checking, thereby producing a chain from cognitive offloading through reduced metacognitive engagement to metacognitive disengagement. The finding that cognitive offloading only partially mediated the relationship suggests that other mechanisms may also be at work, such as changes in self-efficacy or perceived task responsibility. These possibilities remain open for future investigation. 5 Experiment 3: the causal effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality Experiment 2 provided evidence that cognitive offloading mediates the relationship between AI assistance and metacognitive disengagement. However, because cognitive offloading was measured rather than manipulated, the causal direction remained uncertain. Experiment 3 addressed this limitation by manipulating the degree of cognitive delegation to AI-the core behavioral expression of cognitive offloading in human-AI collaboration-and examining its causal effect on knowledge innovation quality, with metacognitive disengagement as a mediator. Experiment 3 provided causal evidence for the effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality through metacognitive disengagement. First, manipulating cognitive offloading produced the expected difference in metacognitive disengagement: participants in the high-delagation condition showed significantly stronger metacognitive disengagement than those in the low-delagation condition. Because cognitive offloading was experimentally manipulated rather than merely measured, these results strengthen the inference that workflow features involving greater delegation to AI lead to stronger metacognitive disengagement. Second, cognitive offloading significantly impaired knowledge innovation quality across all three dimensions. Interestingly, the between-group difference was somewhat smaller for developability than for novelty and usefulness. One interpretation is that AI-generated solutions often appear structurally complete and operationally plausible in the short term, but lack the depth and sustainability that come from genuine iterative reflection. This pattern is consistent with the illusion of competence described by Fan et al. (2025) , in which the fluent output of AI masks underlying deficiencies in quality (Tsakalerou et al., 2026) . Third, metacognitive disengagement partially mediated the effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality. This finding indicates that cognitive offloading damages innovation quality primarily, though not exclusively, by weakening metacognitive planning, monitoring, and reflection. The residual direct effect also suggests that other mechanisms may operate alongside metacognitive disengagement. At the same time, the two workflow conditions inevitably differed in other features such as the detail of AI responses, the amount of independent effort requested, and the allocation of responsibility for core content. The findings should therefore be interpreted as reflecting the combined influence of a high-delegation workflow, within which cognitive offloading is the central feature. Future research could hold these features constant while varying only the degree of cognitive delegation to isolate the unique contribution of cognitive offloading. Consistent with Amabile's (1983) componential theory of creativity, the results imply that when metacognitive skills are no longer exercised in human-AI collaborative tasks, the formal completeness of AI-generated output may conceal a loss of deeper creative quality. Experiment 4 extended the findings of Experiments 1 through 3 by identifying two boundary conditions of the indirect effect from cognitive offloading through metacognitive disengagement to knowledge innovation quality. First, task complexity strengthened the negative indirect effect. Under high task complexity, the indirect effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality through metacognitive disengagement was significantly stronger than under low task complexity. This pattern is consistent with the proposition that complex innovation tasks require more extensive metacognitive processing (Campbell, 1988) . When tasks are complex, AI outputs typically serve only as a starting point, and individuals must critically evaluate, integrate, and deeply process AI-generated content. Under such conditions, metacognitive disengagement leads to particularly severe losses in innovation quality. Second, AI literacy buffered the negative indirect effect. Individuals with higher AI literacy maintained relatively higher knowledge innovation quality even under high cognitive offloading, whereas those with lower AI literacy showed stronger negative effects. This finding suggests that the value of AI literacy lies not simply in better technical operation of AI but in the ability to maintain critical distance from AI outputs and to preserve metacognitive vigilance during human-AI collaboration (Long and Magerko, 2020) . Third, the supplementary analyses clarified that neither task complexity nor AI literacy moderated the first-stage path from cognitive offloading to metacognitive disengagement. Instead, both moderators operated at the stage at which metacognitive disengagement translated into innovation quality. This distinction indicates that metacognitive disengagement may arise fairly generally under AI-assisted conditions, but its consequences depend on task characteristics and individual capabilities. For individuals with high AI literacy or for simple tasks, even if metacognitive disengagement occurs, its actual damage to innovation quality is relatively limited; for complex tasks or low-AIliteracy individuals, the same level of metacognitive disengagement leads to more substantial quality loss. analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, a critical limitation concerns the temporal scope of the present measure. This research focuses on task-level metacognitive disengagement, and the nine-item scale captures the immediate, task-specific reduction in planning, monitoring, and reflection within a single AI-assisted task rather than a habitual, cumulative decline. The experiments therefore demonstrate immediate reductions in metacognitive engagement but cannot determine whether such reductions persist or accumulate over time. Future research should employ longitudinal or repeatedexposure designs to examine this developmental trajectory. Second, the experiments relied on online samples and short, simulated tasks. This design supports causal inference but limits ecological validity, as real innovation work is longer in duration, more socially embedded, and subject to different accountability structures. The findings may therefore not generalize to high-stakes, long-cycle projects, and effect sizes may differ. Future research could use field experiments or experience sampling methods to examine metacognitive disengagement in actual knowledge work settings (Dell' Acqua et al., 2026) . Third, the cognitive offloading manipulation in Experiments 3 and 4 was compound in nature. The high-and low-delegation conditions differed not only in the degree of cognitive delegation but also in AI response detail, independent effort requested, and responsibility allocation. The findings therefore reflect the combined influence of a highdelegation workflow, with cognitive offloading as its central feature. Future research could hold these features constant while varying only the degree of delegation to isolate the unique effect of cognitive offloading. Fourth, knowledge innovation quality was assessed through expert ratings. Although interrater reliability was acceptable, expert judgment remains partly subjective. Future studies could incorporate more objective indicators, such as the originality of proposals, downstream implementation outcomes, or peer evaluations. Fifth, cognitive offloading served only as a partial mediator. The present model focuses on cognitive offloading and metacognitive disengagement because they represent the most proximal mechanisms linking AI assistance to innovation quality. However, the residual direct effect indicates that other mechanisms are also involved. Future research could examine additional mediators such as trust in AI (Jiang et al., 2025) , perceived responsibility (Yousefi et al., 2026) , and creative psychological ownership (Ma et al., 2026) , and test multiple-mediator models for a more complete account. Sixth, although we conducted Harman's single-factor tests in Experiments 2, 3, and 4, this approach is a relatively weak test of common method variance. Because all measures were self-reported, the mediation effects observed in Experiment 2 may be partly inflated by common method variance. Future research could employ CFAbased common latent factor models, multi-source ratings, or objective behavioral measures, such as platform analytics data, to further validate the proposed relationships. Finally, the present study did not directly test interventions to reduce metacognitive disengagement. The buffering effect of AI literacy was measured as an individual difference rather than experimentally manipulated. Future research should design and evaluate interventions such as metacognitive prompting, structured human-AI workflow separation, or targeted AI literacy training. Given recent work on hybrid human-AI regulation (Molenaar, 2022) and the augmentation potential of AI (Jia et al., 2024) , such interventions may help organizations capture the efficiency benefits of AI while preserving the cognitive engagement that sustains innovation quality.

Particular attention was given to modal constructions such as should , must , may , and encourage , as well as passive constructions associated with diffuse or indirect responsibility attribution. It suggests that what constitutes misconduct depends on institutional interpretation and cannot be treated as settled. The term ‘responsible use’ shows how this instability extends across jurisdictions. [ OECD (2026 ), p. 37] notes that the most common immediate national response to generative AI has been the introduction of system-level guidance. analysis.discussion: This study examined how international AI policy discourse constructs academic integrity in higher education and what these constructions suggest about a changing cheating habitus. Analysis of four UNESCO and OECD publications shows that academic integrity is constructed through ethical language whose operational conditions remain underdefined. Generative AI changes the relationship between submitted work and the intellectual activity it is expected to represent. Terms such as responsibility, transparency, trust, authenticity, and responsible use provide normative coherence without establishing consistent rules for practice. The resulting interpretive burden falls on institutions and educational actors working between pressures for AI integration and inherited assumptions about authorship. In theoretical terms, the study proposes that these discursive conditions may affect the dispositions through which students approach academic participation. The changing cheating habitus describes a possible recalibration of the frames through which legitimate participation is recognised under conditions of governance uncertainty. The analysis also proposes that this process may vary according to the academic capital recognised within particular institutional fields. It generates a related hypothesis that enforcement mechanisms may operate as capital filters if the visibility of AI assistance varies with students’ capacity to evaluate and revise AI-generated material. These propositions extend the discourse analysis but are not empirical findings about student behaviour or enforcement outcomes. What the paper's title names, cheating or being cheated, is not treated here as an either/or question. The analysis proposes that these conditions may occur concurrently. Students who are sanctioned for AI-assisted participation may simultaneously be cheating in the conventional sense and being cheated by governance frameworks that normalise the same technologies through which their participation is adjudicated. This concurrent conditionality acquires an additional dimension when integrity frameworks reflect particular epistemic traditions and provide limited recognition of other knowledge practices and understandings of authorship. Read alongside decolonial scholarship, the findings raise a further question: who bears the burden of governance ambiguity, and whose ways of knowing may be classified as violations when particular academic conventions are treated as universal ( Eaton, 2024 ; Langeveldt and Pietersen, 2024 )? The analysis is confined to four publications issued or commissioned by two intergovernmental organisations, and its design is conceptual. These publications differ in genre and institutional authority and cannot be treated as expressions of a unified policy position. The changing cheating habitus is theorised from policy discourse, not from an empirical study of student dispositions. The analysis identifies conditions that may enable dispositional change but cannot establish what particular students experience. Longitudinal and institutionally situated research is needed to examine how any such change develops across disciplinary fields, institutional contexts, and different distributions of capital. The contextual studies considered in the Discussion identify mechanisms through which institutional resources and local cultures may shape policy enactment, but they do not establish that these mechanisms operate in the same way in the UAE or the Gulf. The proposed relationship among field position, capital recognition, and the changing cheating habitus therefore requires examination within particular institutions. Future research should investigate how students and educators interpret AI rules under different institutional conditions and how these interpretations affect judgments of legitimate academic participation. The student in the opening vignette, whose polished essay was submitted in an unusually short amount of time and was subsequently identified as potentially reliant on AI, remains at the centre of the problem addressed here. The analysis cannot determine whether this hypothetical student committed misconduct. Such judgments depend on whether institutional and assessment-level rules clearly define the permitted extent of AI assistance. When these rules remain unclear in practice, detection may indicate reliance on AI but cannot determine how that reliance should be classified. Academic integrity is therefore being redefined under conditions that higher education institutions have yet to address fully. Hypotheses were tested using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) across the five weekly measurement occasions. LMMs account for the nested structure of repeated observations within students, accommodate unbalanced panel data and missing observations under the missing-at-random assumption, and allow the simultaneous estimation of fixed and random effects (Bates et al., 2015; Muth et al., 2016) . Consequently, they are particularly suitable for longitudinal educational data and have been previously applied in studying cognitive load over time. Separate models were estimated for ECL and GCL. Fixed effects included time (simulation round), group membership (intention-to-treat or usage-based groups), ICL, SRL, and their respective interactions with group membership, corresponding to the proposed hypotheses. In the usage-based models, regular users (group 3) were used as the reference group because the hypotheses proposed that sustained engagement with conversational AIassisted feedback would produce the strongest effects. Likewise, the first simulation round served as the temporal reference category. Accordingly, parameter estimates for group effects represent differences relative to regular users, whereas time effects and time interactions represent changes relative to the first simulation round. No additional baseline covariates were included because preliminary analyses indicated baseline equivalence between both the intention-to-treat groups and the usage-based groups. Variance inflation factor (VIF) diagnostics were examined to assess potential multicollinearity among predictors. All VIF values were below 1.36, indicating low levels of multicollinearity and suggesting no concerns regarding predictor overlap (Shrestha, 2020) . J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f control variable. Model fit was evaluated using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), with lower values indicating improved model fit (Burnham & Anderson, 2004) . Marginal and conditional coefficients of determination were additionally reported to quantify the variance explained by the fixed effects alone and by the complete model including random effects, respectively (Nakagawa & Schielzeth, 2013) . Statistical significance was evaluated using a significance level of α = .05. Random intercepts for students were included in all models to account for repeated measurements and between-student differences in cognitive load. Additional random slopes for ICL and, in GCL models including ECL as a covariate, for ECL were considered to account for individual differences in cognitive processing. Random effects were retained only when they significantly improved model fit according to likelihood-ratio tests (LRTs) (West et al., 2022) . Because treatment assignment occurred at the group level, group-level random intercepts were additionally included when supported by model comparisons based on LRTs. LRTs supported the inclusion of random slopes for ICL in all main models and for ECL in the GCL main models, whereas group-level random intercepts did not improve model fit and were therefore omitted from the final models. Final models were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML), which provides less biased estimates of variance components, particularly in smaller samples (West et al., 2022) . Because all hypotheses were specified a priori and derived from established theoretical frameworks, no formal correction for multiple hypothesis testing was applied. The analyses were therefore treated as confirmatory rather than exploratory, and effect estimates, 95% confidence intervals, and exact p values are reported to facilitate interpretation. analysis.discussion: The findings of this study suggest that the cognitive effects of conversational AIassisted feedback depend not merely on access to the technology, but also on learners' actual engagement, the stage of the intervention, and individual learning characteristics. By examining these processes longitudinally within an authentic business simulation embedded in higher education, the present study provides ecologically valid insights into how cognitive load evolves during extended AI-supported learning. More broadly, the distinction between access and engagement, while relevant to educational technologies more generally (Kraft, 2020) , appears to be particularly important in the context of conversational AI. Unlike static instructional materials or conventional feedback, conversational AI provides adaptive support J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f that is co-constructed through learners' prompts and subsequent interactions (e.g., Ba et al., 2025) . Consequently, its educational value depends not only on the availability of the technology but also on how learners engage with it, consistent with the ICAP framework, which proposes that meaningful learning emerges through active and interactive engagement (Chi & Wylie, 2014) . The present findings therefore suggest that the educational effects of conversational AI should be understood not merely as a function of access, but of learners' sustained and meaningful interaction with the system over time. This overarching perspective provides the context for the hypothesis-specific findings discussed below. Hypothesis 1. The findings from the main analyses indicate that neither mere access to nor regular engagement with conversational AI-assisted feedback uniformly reduced ECL compared with students who only received static in-game feedback. Likewise, the exploratory within-student analysis showed no significant reduction in ECL during simulation rounds in which students interacted with the conversational AI-assisted feedback. Consequently, neither H1A nor H1U was supported. Moreover, the exploratory estimates indicated a descriptive increase of ECL during weeks in which students used the conversational AI-assisted feedback. Although this effect did not reach statistical significance, it may indicate a practically meaningful trend. One possible explanation is that conversational AI-assisted feedback represents an additional instructional component that learners must coordinate alongside the business simulation. Although intended to scaffold decision making, interacting with the chatbot may initially require additional attentional and self-regulatory resources, thereby offsetting potential reductions in ECL. This interpretation aligns with CLT, which suggests that additional instructional elements can impose unnecessary processing when they require learners to divide attention or coordinate multiple information sources, following the split attention principle (Sweller, 2020) . This possible J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f explanation also aligns with the increasing recognition that the cognitive demands imposed by instructional design features should be considered in relation to their potential benefits for learning (Skulmowski & Xu, 2022) . At the same time, the present study only distinguished between weeks in which students used the chatbot and weeks in which they did not, without considering the frequency, duration, or depth of these interactions. Consequently, meaningful differences in engagement may have remained undetected. Hypothesis 2. The findings from the main analyses indicate that merely providing access to conversational AI-assisted feedback did not increase GCL, providing no support for H2A. However, the usage-based analyses revealed that students who regularly engaged with the conversational AI-assisted feedback reported significantly higher GCL than both students in the control condition and students who had access to the chatbot but did not use it. Complementing these findings, the exploratory within-student analysis further demonstrated that students reported significantly higher GCL during simulation weeks in which they actively interacted with the conversational AI-assisted feedback compared with weeks in which they did not use the chatbot. Together, these findings suggest that improvements in GCL are associated with learners' actual engagement with conversational AI-assisted feedback rather than its mere availability, providing partial support for H2U and aligning with notions of the ICAP framework (Chi & Wylie, 2014) . As effects were stronger and only significant in the usage-based model, our findings suggest that mere accessibility alone may not automatically imply added value of conversational AI-assisted feedback, confirming prior suggestions of educational technology effects (Kraft, 2020) . They further indicate that fixed engagement classifications (no engagement/ irregular engagement/ regular engagement) may not fully capture the dynamic relationship between AI-assisted feedback and GCL, as they cannot distinguish between weeks in which students actively engaged with the chatbot and weeks in which they did not despite belonging to the same engagement group. The present study examined how conversational AI-assisted feedback is associated with cognitive load during an extended business simulation game by integrating intention-totreat, usage-based, and exploratory within-student analyses. By combining a longitudinal field-study design with repeated measures of cognitive load in an authentic business simulation, this study contributes ecologically valid evidence on how conversational AIassisted feedback shapes cognitive processing over time. Overall, the findings demonstrate that the cognitive effects of conversational AI-assisted feedback depend less on its mere availability than on learners' actual engagement with the technology, the progression of the J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f learning intervention, and individual learning process characteristics. While regular engagement with conversational AI-assisted feedback did not consistently reduce ECL, its effects depended on simulation progression and learners' intrinsic cognitive load. Furthermore, sustained engagement was associated with higher GCL. Beyond demonstrating the potential of conversational AI as an instructional support tool, this study contributes to CLT and AI-supported learning research by highlighting the importance of conceptualizing engagement as a dynamic process rather than a static treatment characteristic. Methodologically, the findings illustrate the value of combining betweenperson and within-person perspectives to capture the evolving nature of learner-AI interaction during authentic educational interventions. As conversational AI becomes increasingly integrated into education, understanding not only whether learners have access to AI-supported feedback but also how, when, and under which conditions they engage with it will be essential for designing instructional support that effectively promotes productive cognitive processing and learning. analysis.limitations: Despite its theoretical and practical contributions, the present study has several limitations, primarily stemming from its longitudinal field-study design. While this design provides high ecological validity and captures authentic learning processes (e.g., De Witte et al., 2025), it necessarily limits the strength of causal conclusions. Moreover, building on technology acceptance research (Venkatesh, 2022) , future studies should examine learners' perceptions of conversational AI-assisted feedback to identify which factors promote sustained engagement and ultimately shape cognitive load. Second, although chatbot engagement was assessed repeatedly throughout the intervention, the analyses focused on whether learners interacted with the chatbot rather than on how they interacted with it. Consequently, differences in the frequency, duration, quality, or instructional value of learner-AI interactions could not be examined. The exploratory within-student analyses suggest that temporally aggregated engagement measures may not fully capture the dynamic nature of conversational AI use during learning. Future research should therefore investigate more fine-grained engagement characteristics, including prompting strategies, feedback retrieval, conversational depth, and the subsequent integration of AI-generated feedback into learners' decision-making and collaborative processes. Third, because the business simulation was completed in teams, conversational AIassisted feedback may have been shared among group members. Consequently, students who rarely or never interacted directly with the chatbot may nevertheless have indirectly benefited from teammates who did, potentially attenuating group differences. Although potential within-group dependencies were examined, future research should explicitly investigate how AI-assisted feedback is shared and collectively processed within collaborative learning settings by combining chatbot log data with communication or collaboration measures. Such research would extend the present individual-level perspective to a collaborative cognitive load perspective (Kirschner et al., 2018) .

reading.interpretation: Based on cross-sectional data from 1,760 terminology workers, this study used structural equation modeling (SEM) and latent profile analysis (LPA) to examine the multidimensional structural relationship among prompt strategy preference, AI interaction self-efficacy, and subjective cognitive load in the context of generative large language model assistance. The data analysis results supported most of the theoretical hypotheses of this study and suggested that the role of traditional professional experience in mitigating cognitive load may be weakened when exploring experience boundaries. The results of this study provide quantitative empirical evidence for understanding the cognitive coping mechanisms of knowledge workers in the era of generative artificial intelligence. The path coefficients of the structural equation model indicate that structured and deep prompt strategy preferences are significantly and negatively associated with the subjective cognitive load level of workers. In actual terminology extraction and concept alignment tasks, the core challenge faced by practitioners is usually semantic ambiguity control in specific contexts. When users prefer to introduce explicit rules such as Chain-of-Thought or Few-shot in prompts, while requiring upfront working memory resources for instruction design, this strategic tendency ultimately exhibits a strong inverse association with the overall task-related cognitive load. This phenomenon reveals a mechanism of cognitive resource allocation during the interaction process: well-structured upfront instruction design acts to constrain the generation space of large language models (LLMs), thereby substantially lowering the reported burden of subsequent evaluation and error-checking phases caused by algorithmic hallucinations

The target population was defined as professionals with practical experience in terminology extraction and professional translation, or with academic backgrounds in linguistics and computational linguistics. To ensure the alignment of the data with the research context, the inclusion criteria for the survey were restricted to: subjects must have actually used large language models, such as ChatGPT, Claude, etc., within the past 3 months to complete domain-specific terminology alignment, definition delineation, or related text validation tasks. Data were distributed through an online survey platform and targeted professional language service networks (e.g., translation forums, terminology practitioner communities, and university alumni groups), during which a total of 1,920 initial questionnaires were retrieved. To reduce invalid responses and insufficient attention that self-administered questionnaires might bring, this study set up multiple data screening procedures during the implementation process. First, the system background automatically excluded samples with abnormal response durations (e.g., completion time of less than 120 s). Second, the researchers screened out straight-lining response patterns that showed a single fixed value on continuous Likert scales (defined as providing identical answers to 10 or more consecutive items). Finally, forced attention check questions (e.g., “Please select ‘Strongly Disagree' for this item to confirm your attention”) were embedded in the questionnaire, and those who failed to answer as required were excluded from the final analysis. After the above strict cleaning procedures, this study excluded 160 invalid questionnaires and finally obtained 1,760 valid samples, with a valid response rate of 91.67%. To ensure methodological transparency, the complete statistical syntax (including SPSS, AMOS paths, and Mplus code for LPA) has been comprehensive documented in Supplementary Material S2 . The demographic characteristics of the valid sample show a distinct pattern of knowledge-intensive industries. Female subjects accounted for 55.63%, and male subjects accounted for 41.76%. In terms of educational background, those with a master's degree or higher accounted for 95.23%. Regarding work experience, the novice group with less than 3 years of experience comprised 837 people (47.56%), the intermediate group with 3 to 5 years comprised 490 people (27.84%), and the expert group with 5 or more years comprised 433 people (24.60%). This distribution provides a relatively balanced sample base for the subsequent multi-group structural equation modeling test, as detailed in Table 1 . Demographic characteristics of the participants. All measurement tools used to evaluate latent variables were based on standardized questionnaires in the existing literature and were contextually revised to fit generative AI interaction scenarios. A 7-point Likert scale was uniformly adopted, with a value of 1 representing “strongly disagree” or “extremely low” and a value of 7 representing “strongly agree” or “extremely high”. The full items of all scales and demographic questions have been attached to the supplementary materials (see Supplementary Material S1 ). This study developed the PESP-T scale based on the operational principles in algorithmic prompt optimization foundation corpus research by ( Brown et al. 2020 ) and ( Wei et al. 2022 ). Prior to the formal large-scale survey, the scale underwent a rigorous development procedure. The initial item pool was evaluated by a panel of three computational linguistics experts to ensure content validity. Subsequently, a pilot study ( N = 120) was conducted. Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) on the pilot data confirmed that all seven strategy items loaded strongly onto a single dominant factor (explaining 65.4% of the total variance). Consequently, these seven strategies were identified as reflective indicators measuring an underlying unidimensional construct of strategy preference: persona setting (P1), few-shot guidance (P2), chain of thought (P3), corpus-driven (P4), iterative feedback (P5), constraint instructions (P6), and structured instructions (P7). For example, for dimension P3, the item is phrased as: “I will ask the model to show its reasoning steps before giving an answer”; dimension P6 is defined as: “I will clearly list prohibited items or boundary conditions to follow specific domain standards.” Subjective cognitive load was measured using the Raw NASA-TLX scale revised by ( Hart 2006 ). The scale comprises six single-item dimensions designed to capture different aspects of the operator's subjective experience: mental demand (N1), temporal demand (N2), effort (N3), frustration level (N4), physical demand (N5), and self-reported performance (N6). In this study, the task descriptions within the items were systematically contextualized to reflect the LLM-assisted terminology processing workflow. For instance, the mental demand (N1) item was framed as: “How much mental and cognitive activity was required to formulate prompts, comprehend AI outputs, and make professional judgements throughout the interaction?” Since a high score in self-reported performance (N6) originally represented high satisfaction (which is opposite to the direction of distress/load), this item was reverse-scored (computed as 8–original score) prior to statistics, ensuring that higher scores across all items uniformly indicate greater subjective cognitive load. Following the established protocol for the unweighted Raw-TLX ( Hart, 2006 ), the overall subjective cognitive load was derived by calculating the arithmetic mean of all six items. While the self-reported performance dimension captures subjective task outcomes rather than pure mental exertion, its reverse-scored inclusion is maintained in this study. This unified aggregation aligns with standard human-computer interaction practices, as the user's perception of poor performance and cumulative physical fatigue often directly exacerbates the overall psychological strain experienced during unpredictable AI interactions. Furthermore, to ensure the robustness of the cognitive load measurement, a sensitivity analysis was conducted by excluding the physical demand (N5) and self-reported performance (N6) items. analysis.results: Before hypothesis testing, this study first tested the reliability and validity of the core measurement tools. Preliminary sample suitability tests showed that the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) value of the total sample was 0.907, and Bartlett's test of sphericity reached an extremely significant level (χ 2 = 25591.08, df = 666, p < 0.001), indicating that the sample data were highly suitable for latent variable factor extraction. In terms of multicollinearity screening, the variance inflation factor (VIF) among independent variables was at 1.241 (for Perceived Output Quality), which is far below the conventional test threshold of 5.0 ( Hair et al., 2019 ). The measurement model of Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) showed good structural characteristics. Specifically, all standardized factor loadings for the measurement items ranged from 0.67 to 0.77 (all significant at p < 0.001), indicating strong indicator reliability. Combining the detailed test reports in Table 2 , it can be seen that the Cronbach's α and composite reliability (CR) of each core scale were far higher than the conventional standard of 0.70, showing excellent internal consistency; meanwhile, the average variance extracted (AVE) of most latent variables reached or exceeded the threshold of 0.50. Although the AVE for Task Complexity (T, AVE = 0.432) and Subjective Cognitive Load (N, AVE = 0.476) fell slightly below the 0.50 threshold, their Composite Reliability (CR) values (0.753 and 0.845) were well above 0.70, which justifies acceptable convergent validity according to ( Fornell and Larcker 1981 ). Regarding discriminant validity, Table 3 and Figure 2 demonstrates that the square root of each construct's AVE was larger than any of its longitudinal or transverse correlations, satisfying the ( Fornell and Larcker 1981 ) criterion. Furthermore, to provide a more rigorous assessment, the Heterotrait-Monotrait Ratio (HTMT) values across all latent variable pairs were evaluated. The maximum HTMT value obtained was strictly below the conservative threshold of 0.85 ( Henseler et al., 2015 ), providing robust confirmation of discriminant validity. Bold values on the diagonal are the square root of the AVE of each latent variable; off-diagonal values are the Pearson correlation coefficients between latent variables. * p < 0.05, *** p < 0.001. Structural correlation and path summary diagram of the latent construct model. Since the data in this study came from self-report questionnaires at a single point in time, common method bias may exist. Harman's single-factor test showed that the variance explained by the first factor in the unrotated principal component analysis was 17.96%, which is lower than the common threshold of 50%. Furthermore, to provide a more robust structural assessment beyond Harman's test, this study conducted an Unmeasured Latent Method Construct (ULMC) sensitivity analysis by introducing a common method factor into the CFA model. The comparison indicated that adding this method factor did not yield a significant improvement in model fit (Baseline model: χ 2 = 972.8, df = 608; ULMC model: χ 2 = 959.0, df = 607; ΔCFI = 0.003, ΔRMSEA = 0.002, both strictly below the 0.01 threshold). Meanwhile, all substantive trait factor loadings remained highly significant with negligible changes in their magnitudes (Δλ < 0.05). Therefore, common method bias does not pose a serious threat ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). To examine the group heterogeneity of terminology workers in prompt strategy usage, this study conducted a Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) on the 7 items of the prompt strategy preference scale. After comparing the 2-class, 3-class, and 4-class models sequentially, the results showed that as the number of classes increased, both AIC and aBIC decreased, with the 4-class model having the lowest AIC and aBIC. Although the 4-class model had the lowest AIC and aBIC, the 3-class model had higher entropy, clearer classification distinction, and better theoretical interpretability. Therefore, this study chose the 3-class model as the final classification scheme. According to the mean score patterns of the three classes of subjects on the 7 prompt strategy indicators, this study named them the low strategy use group, medium strategy use group, and high strategy use group, respectively.
