analysis.discussion: Based on cross-sectional data from 1,760 terminology workers, this study used structural equation modeling (SEM) and latent profile analysis (LPA) to examine the multidimensional structural relationship among prompt strategy preference, AI interaction self-efficacy, and subjective cognitive load in the context of generative large language model assistance. The data analysis results supported most of the theoretical hypotheses of this study and suggested that the role of traditional professional experience in mitigating cognitive load may be weakened when exploring experience boundaries. The results of this study provide quantitative empirical evidence for understanding the cognitive coping mechanisms of knowledge workers in the era of generative artificial intelligence. The path coefficients of the structural equation model indicate that structured and deep prompt strategy preferences are significantly and negatively associated with the subjective cognitive load level of workers. In actual terminology extraction and concept alignment tasks, the core challenge faced by practitioners is usually semantic ambiguity control in specific contexts. When users prefer to introduce explicit rules such as Chain-of-Thought or Few-shot in prompts, while requiring upfront working memory resources for instruction design, this strategic tendency ultimately exhibits a strong inverse association with the overall task-related cognitive load. This phenomenon reveals a mechanism of cognitive resource allocation during the interaction process: well-structured upfront instruction design acts to constrain the generation space of large language models (LLMs), thereby substantially lowering the reported burden of subsequent evaluation and error-checking phases caused by algorithmic hallucinations. Although the cumulative retrospective measurement adopted in this study objectively reflects the “net load” after the accounting for the psychological requirements in the two stages, the negative result of this cumulative effect strongly confirms that the cognitive resources saved in the later verification stage far exceed the extra effort in the upfront writing stage in terms of total volume. This negative association theoretically fits the “cognitive offloading” mechanism. In open-ended interactions lacking clear constraints, users must rely heavily on their working memory to compare machine output with professional standards in real time after each interaction. In contrast, pre-setting specific rules and boundary conditions in prompts essentially makes part of the implicit rule verification task explicit and “outsources” it to the algorithm's computational space as known parameters. Meanwhile, this study found that AI interaction self-efficacy plays a significant partial mediating role in the above structure. This means that the association between mitigation of cognitive load and prompt strategies is not only reflected at the physical operation level (such as reducing correction rounds) but also includes a psychological transmission mechanism: individuals who tend to use high-level strategies often possess a higher sense of system control; this belief in efficacy can act as an internal psychological resource that buffers the anxiety or frustration caused by model uncertainty, thus statistically corresponding to a lower overall cognitive load. This main effect perspective highlights another pertinent psychological attribute of prompt strategy optimization. Compared to examining the linear relationship of the overall sample, Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) reveals the heterogeneous distribution of strategy preferences among different types of users. The three classes of users extracted exhibited significant mean differences between groups: the “high strategy use group,” which accounted for about a quarter of the sample, scored the lowest on subjective cognitive load indicators and the highest on AI interaction self-efficacy. In response to this group differentiation, analysis can be carried out in combination with specific terminology work contexts. The “low strategy use group,” which remains at the primary instruction interaction level, often directly relies on the default response logic of the LLM. This shallow interaction mode allows the algorithm's “black box” to diverge freely ( Khosravi et al., 2022 ), resulting in highly unstable output quality, which in turn generates high cognitive costs in the later evaluation and error-checking stages. In contrast, the “high strategy use group” tends to implement strict formatting rules and persona framing at the starting stage. The process of using complex strategies essentially reflects the operator's behavioral tendency to implement predictive control over non-deterministic systems. By setting strict system boundary conditions, users not only converge the output framework of the model but also strengthen their sense of control over the task environment at the psychological level. The analysis of variance between groups confirms that this set of strategic behaviors aimed at enhancing environmental certainty corresponds to more positive psychological feedback levels and lower cognitive pressure on the user's part. The multi-group analysis of industry seniority involves a classic proposition in cognitive science and traditional occupational training. Traditional cognitive load theory usually holds that long-term domain schema accumulation gives senior experts a significant resource advantage when handling complex tasks, meaning they should exhibit lower mental depletion evaluations under equivalent task demands. However, in the cross-group equivalence test of this study, novices, intermediates, and seasoned experts did not show statistical differences in the overall core transmission paths of “strategy-self-efficacy-cognitive load.” This implies a broad structural invariance across different experience levels. While the overarching transmission framework remains statistically equivalent across seniority cohorts, observing the numerical coefficients within each group presents a subtle, exploratory trend regarding the direct pathway between prompt strategy and cognitive load. From a descriptive standpoint, this numerical trend can be interpreted through the lens of cognitive schema theory and the evolving role of external scaffolding. For practitioners in the earlier phases of their professional trajectory, domain schemata remain fluid and underdeveloped. In these cases, deliberate prompt structuring appears to serve as a supportive external proxy, being closely associated with lower perceived mental effort before the high-stakes output validation stage. abstract_text: The increasing integration of GenAI into academic writing has prompted renewed attention to how students engage with writing tasks in English for Academic Purposes (EAP) contexts. While existing research has focused on the capabilities and risks of GenAI, less attention has been given to the instructional conditions that shape how students use these tools. This paper proposes the Rigor–Commitment Alignment Framework (RCAF), a conceptual model that examines the interaction between academic rigor and teacher commitment as two dimensions of the pedagogical environment. reading.interpretation: The RCAF was developed to clarify how instructional environments shape students’ engagement with generative AI in EAP writing. The framework responds to a limitation in current discussions of GenAI in language education: the tendency to foreground either the technology itself or student misuse, while giving less attention to the pedagogical conditions under which particular uses of AI become more or less likely. This distinction is especially important in EAP writing. GenAI can substitute for some lower-level aspects of text production, including grammar, spelling, sentence formation, and surface-level fluency. This creates obvious risks if students use AI to bypass writing processes altogether. Yet it also creates pedagogical possibilities. When AI support reduces the burden of lower-level language production, classroom attention can shift toward higher-order academic literacy practices, such as argument development, source use, citation, logical progression, clarity, and disciplinary voice. analysis.methods: This study adopts a conceptual framework approach to develop the Rigor–Commitment Alignment Framework (RCAF). In applied linguistics and the social sciences, conceptual frameworks are used to organize and integrate existing knowledge into analytically coherent models that clarify relationships among key constructs and provide a basis for further investigation ( Jabareen, 2009 ; Ravitch and Riggan, 2017 ). Unlike theoretical frameworks, which apply a single established theory to a given context, conceptual frameworks draw on multiple theoretical and empirical sources to construct a new interpretive structure through systematic synthesis. The aim is not to generate empirical findings, but to develop a theoretically grounded model capable of explaining a complex phenomenon and guiding subsequent empirical work. Within this tradition, conceptual frameworks function as structuring devices that reduce complexity by grouping heterogeneous phenomena into analytically meaningful categories. As Miles et a.l (202 0 ), p. 15 note, conceptual frameworks may be “simple or elaborate, descriptive or causal, commonsensical or theory driven”, relying on a limited number of higher-order concepts that subsume a wide range of actions, processes, and experiences. These concepts operate as “intellectual ‘bins’” that organize disparate elements into coherent analytical units, derived not only from theory but also from empirical observation and the objectives of the study. This view underscores the interpretive and synthetic nature of conceptual framework development, in which abstraction is used to render complex educational phenomena analytically tractable. This approach is particularly appropriate to the present study, as the challenges associated with EAP writing instruction in the context of generative artificial intelligence span several largely distinct areas of research, including teacher effectiveness, student engagement, feedback, and AI-mediated pedagogy. No single theoretical perspective adequately accounts for the interaction between instructional conditions and student engagement in this context. A conceptual synthesis is therefore required to integrate these strands into a unified analytical framework. The development of the RCAF followed a structured, multi-stage analytical procedure adapted from Jabareen (2009) , involving the identification, mapping, and integration of key constructs across disciplinary domains. A purposive, conceptually driven synthesis of the literature was conducted using peer-reviewed sources indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC, covering the period from 2000 to 2026. Searches were conducted in December 2025 and January 2026. Seminal works published before 2000 were included through backward citation searching when they provided foundational definitions or theories required for the conceptual synthesis. This method describes a structured conceptual search rather than a systematic review. Searches were organized around three domains. The teacher and instructional conditions search combined terms such as (“teacher effectiveness” OR “teacher commitment” OR “instructional quality” OR “instructional responsiveness” OR “relational support” OR feedback OR “academic rigor”) with (EAP OR EFL OR “academic writing” OR “higher education”). The engagement search combined (“student engagement” OR “learner engagement” OR “cognitive engagement” OR “agentic engagement” OR motivation OR disengagement OR “approaches to learning”) with (EAP OR EFL OR “academic writing” OR “language education”). The GenAI search combined (“generative AI” OR GenAI OR ChatGPT OR “large language model*” OR “AI-assisted writing” OR “automated feedback”) with (writing OR EAP OR EFL OR “language education”) and (engagement OR assessment OR feedback OR pedagogy). Search syntax was adapted to the requirements of each database. Sources were retained if they contributed at least one of the following: a theoretically grounded construct definition, empirical evidence related to instructional conditions and engagement, an established account of academic writing or feedback, or evidence concerning GenAI-mediated writing, assessment, or learner behavior. Foundational theoretical works and major research syntheses were also included. Conversely, sources lacking sufficient conceptual or empirical grounding, or those that addressed AI technology without a meaningful connection to teaching, engagement, writing, or assessment, were excluded. A purposive sampling strategy was used to identify both foundational theoretical contributions and recent empirical studies relevant to the interaction between instructional practice, student engagement, and AI-mediated writing. Selection criteria prioritized theoretical relevance, methodological transparency and direct conceptual relevance, and contributions to understanding engagement under different instructional conditions. Preference was given to peer-reviewed journal articles and major syntheses, while non-scholarly and non-English sources were excluded. Key constructs from the three domains were identified and examined for conceptual compatibility and functional alignment. The analytical framework guiding this stage was Bandura's model ( Bandura, 1986 ) of triadic reciprocal causation (see Figure 1 ), which conceptualizes human functioning through the reciprocal influence of personal factors, behavior, and environmental conditions. In the present study, this model provides an organizing architecture for distinguishing learner-related characteristics, enacted engagement, and instructional conditions. Theoretical underpinning of the RCAF, adapted from Bandura’s (1986) triadic reciprocal causation. Personal factors comprise cognitive-affective learner characteristics, including goal orientation, motivation and task value, self-efficacy, affective states, language proficiency, and GenAI literacy. Behavior refers to observable or enacted engagement and GenAI-use practices, including planning, drafting, revising, verifying, participating, help-seeking, delegating, and avoidance. The instructional environment comprises the two central dimensions of the RCAF: academic rigor represents the cognitive demand, epistemic authenticity, and performance accountability embedded in task design and assessment, while teacher commitment represents the professional-relational orientation enacted through instructional responsiveness, relational support, and critical scaffolding. analysis.discussion: The RCAF was developed to clarify how instructional environments shape students’ engagement with generative AI in EAP writing. The framework responds to a limitation in current discussions of GenAI in language education: the tendency to foreground either the technology itself or student misuse, while giving less attention to the pedagogical conditions under which particular uses of AI become more or less likely. This distinction is especially important in EAP writing. GenAI can substitute for some lower-level aspects of text production, including grammar, spelling, sentence formation, and surface-level fluency. This creates obvious risks if students use AI to bypass writing processes altogether. Yet it also creates pedagogical possibilities. When AI support reduces the burden of lower-level language production, classroom attention can shift toward higher-order academic literacy practices, such as argument development, source use, citation, logical progression, clarity, and disciplinary voice. The central issue, therefore, is not whether GenAI is inherently harmful or beneficial, but whether instructional conditions direct students toward cognitive dependence or critical engagement. The RCAF reframes GenAI use as a function of pedagogical alignment. It asks how combinations of academic rigor and teacher commitment make particular engagement patterns more probable. In this sense, the framework shifts the analytical focus from isolated student behavior to the conditions that organize that behavior. The RCAF makes three conceptual contributions. First, it distinguishes academic rigor and teacher commitment as separate but interacting dimensions of the pedagogical environment. This distinction is necessary because high standards and high support do not always co-occur. A classroom may be demanding but weakly supportive, or supportive but insufficiently demanding. These asymmetries matter because they are likely to produce different engagement patterns and require different pedagogical responses. This dimensional logic has precedent in related literatures. Baumrind’s (1991) parenting styles framework crossed demandingness with responsiveness to identify qualitatively different developmental environments. Aelterman et al. (2019) similarly modelled motivating teaching through intersecting dimensions of need support and structure, with subsequent validation in higher education contexts by Vermote et al. (2020) . The RCAF extends this dimensional logic to AI-mediated EAP writing, where the interaction between cognitive demand and instructional support is intensified by students’ access to tools that can produce fluent academic prose. GenAI is not conceptualized as a separate instructional axis or an independent driver of engagement. Instead, it functions as an amplifying feature whose influence on the link between instructional conditions and engagement varies based on assessment design, process visibility, and accountability. Second, the RCAF synthesizes complementary perspectives of engagement drawn from related theoretical traditions. These traditions do not each supply a separate profile. Instead, the framework draws cognitive depth from approaches-to-learning research ( Biggs, 1987 ; Hattie and Donoghue, 2016 ; Marton and Säljö, 1976 ), motivational quality from self-determination theory ( Deci and Ryan, 2000 ), proactive learner contribution from agentic engagement ( Reeve, 2013 ), and cognitive, affective, behavioral, and social manifestations from ( Hiver et al., 2021 ; Hiver et al., 2024 ). The resulting profiles are prototypical configurations of motivational purpose, cognitive investment, agency, and GenAI use orientation. Their contribution lies in showing how these shared features combine in distinct patterns of AI-mediated writing engagement. Third, the RCAF embeds these relationships within a triadic reciprocal architecture adapted from Bandura (1986) . Academic rigor and teacher commitment jointly constitute the environmental component; learner beliefs, motivations, affective states, proficiency, and GenAI literacy constitute personal factors; and observable engagement and GenAI use practices constitute behavior. This architecture extends the RCAF beyond a static two-by-two typology by specifying how instructional conditions, learner characteristics and enacted behavior reciprocally shape one another. Consistent with Zhou et al.’s (2026) evidence of the reciprocal relationship between teacher motivational practices and student engagement, students’ responses may prompt changes in teaching and thereby shift the instructional configuration over time, although institutional conditions may constrain or enable such movement. Fourth, The RCAF's specificity is not only in its setting but in how rigor, commitment, and engagement are operationalized. EAP writing requires learners, many of whom are multilingual, to integrate developing linguistic resources with disciplinary genre knowledge, intertextual source use, citation, epistemic positioning, and authorial voice ( Hyland, 2019 ; Lea and Street, 1998 , 2006 ; Swales, 1990 ; Tardy, 2009 ; Wingate, 2012 , 2015 ). GenAI can perform parts of both the linguistic and rhetorical work involved, making textual fluency an increasingly unreliable indicator of academic literacy development. Accordingly, rigor in RCAF entails disciplinary-authentic, source-based reasoning and visible process accountability, while commitment entails responsive guidance and critical scaffolding attuned to students’ language proficiency and developing disciplinary participation. Engagement is therefore reflected not only in the quality of the final text but also in students’ ability to evaluate AI output, justify source and citation choices, revise claims, establish an authorial position, and retain responsibility for meaning. The practical value of the RCAF lies in its diagnostic specificity. It does not simply recommend “better teaching” or “AI literacy.” Instead, it identifies which dimension of the instructional environment requires attention. In Neglectful environments, both rigor and commitment are underdeveloped. In such contexts, GenAI may make low-investment completion easier because students receive neither strong cognitive demands nor meaningful instructional guidance. analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the RCAF is conceptual rather than empirically validated. Its quadrant predictions and engagement profiles are derived from theoretical synthesis and require empirical testing. Second, academic rigor and teacher commitment are internally complex constructs. Although they are treated as continua for analytical clarity, each contains multiple dimensions. Academic rigor includes cognitive demand, epistemic authenticity, and performance accountability. Teacher commitment includes instructional responsiveness, relational support, and critical scaffolding. Future work should examine whether these subdimensions vary independently and how such variation affects engagement. Third, the engagement profiles are prototypical engagement patterns rather than mutually exclusive or exhaustive learner categories. Students may display mixed patterns or move between profiles depending on task type, assessment pressure, time constraints, prior experience, and perceived teacher expectations. Their empirical distinctiveness therefore remains to be tested. Fourth, the framework is developed primarily for English-medium EAP writing in higher education. Its applicability to other contexts, including secondary education, community-based ESL, or EFL settings with limited access to GenAI, remains to be tested. Fifth, the RCAF foregrounds teacher-influenced instructional conditions and may underrepresent institutional assessment systems, disciplinary conventions, GenAI access and policies, socioeconomic differences, and learner factors such as language proficiency and prior GenAI literacy. These may constrain teachers’ enactment of rigor and commitment or moderate the predicted relationships. Moreover, Rigor with Support should not imply that greater demand is invariably beneficial: excessively demanding tasks may remain counterproductive despite substantial support, and the same level of rigor may be experienced differently according to learner readiness, proficiency, self-efficacy, and available resources. Rigor is therefore relational and context-dependent rather than a universal threshold. Finally, GenAI tools are changing rapidly. As these systems become more interactive and pedagogically specialized, the specific forms of AI use associated with each engagement profile may shift. The underlying logic of the framework, however, rests not on any single tool but on the relationship between instructional conditions and student engagement. Future research should first operationalize and test the framework's central constructs. Instruments are needed to measure academic rigor and teacher commitment in EAP writing contexts and to examine whether the predicted engagement patterns emerge across quadrants. Such studies should measure personal factors and enacted engagement and GenAI-use behaviors separately, rather than treating student engagement as a unitary variable, and should test the reciprocal pathways in Figure 1 . Student-centred analyses should examine whether the four proposed profiles emerge as empirically distinguishable configurations or whether alternate profile structures provide a better account of student engagement. Second, longitudinal research should investigate reciprocal movement over time. Such studies could examine whether disengagement leads teachers to reduce support or tighten control, and whether deep engagement reinforces sustained rigor and commitment. Zhou et al.’s (2026) dual-process methodology offers a useful model for this kind of work. Third, process-oriented studies are needed to examine how students actually use GenAI while composing. Think-aloud protocols, keystroke logging, screen recording, and revision analysis could show whether students use AI to bypass writing processes or to support planning, argumentation, source integration, and revision. Fourth, design-based research could examine whether the RCAF functions as a useful professional development tool. Teachers could use the framework to identify their current instructional configuration and design targeted shifts toward Rigor with Support. Tools could be developed and validated to examine and measure teachers’ reported orientations, observed practices, and students’ perceptions. Finally, comparative studies across EAP, EFL, ESL, and content-based instruction are needed to establish the framework’s boundary conditions and identify contextual factors that moderate its predictions.

analysis.discussion: In Study 1, trust in GenAI showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention ( β = 0.425, p < 0.001). This finding differs from patterns observed in general educational technology research, where performance expectancy is typically regarded as the primary driver of behavioral intention. Students’ willingness to integrate GenAI into their creative processes was associated not only with expected gains in productivity but also, and in this sample more strongly, with perceived trustworthiness ( Oc et al., 2024 ; Rana et al., 2025 ). The construct as operationalized here is primarily instrumental, supplemented by a modest art-value component. This strong association should not be read as evidence for a fully developed art-value trust dimension. The role of trust was not uniform across paths in the model. For all five antecedents, the indirect association through trust was significant (bias-corrected 95% CIs excluded zero), and the direct association with behavioral intention remained significant after trust was included. This pattern is consistent with partial mediation for each antecedent. Substantively, partial mediation means that trust is not the sole pathway connecting these antecedents to behavioral intention. Each antecedent is associated with behavioral intention both through trust and through pathways that do not involve trust. For facilitating conditions, the direct association was small but significant ( β = 0.092, p = 0.040; 10,000 bootstrap 95% CI [0.003, 0.179]). Thus, facilitating conditions are associated with behavioral intention partly through trust and partly through a direct association that is independent of trust. This direct association may reflect the possibility that resources, training, and support are associated with behavioral intention not only through their association with trust but also through their association with reduced perceived barriers to use. Because this direct association is close to the significance threshold, the partial mediation pattern should be interpreted cautiously. Overall, the mediation results suggest that trust is an important but not exhaustive explanatory pathway; the antecedents retain direct associations with behavioral intention that are independent of trust. Among the five variables associated with trust, social influence had the highest standardized coefficient ( β = 0.262, p < 0.001), and its indirect association with behavioral intention via trust was also the most pronounced among all indirect paths (indirect coefficient = 0.112), accounting for 42.1% of its total estimated association. In traditional information systems research, social influence is typically understood to operate through normative pressure or imitation mechanisms. However, in artistic creation contexts, its role may be more prominent because social influence may be closely tied to the standards used to evaluate the legitimacy of creative tools and outputs. Artistic value is not objectively given but is constructed through social negotiation and institutional recognition ( Wingström et al., 2024 ). When teachers, peers, and the broader arts community treat GenAI as a legitimate medium for artistic creation, students may perceive more than just social pressure to conform; they may update their normative beliefs about what constitutes authentic, masterful, and valuable artistic practice ( Garcia, 2024 ; Wu et al., 2026 ). This socially constructed legitimacy may be closely linked to trust in the technology. The prominent role of social influence is thus consistent with the findings of other scholars’ qualitative studies, which suggest that art students’ attitudes toward AI are deeply embedded in community norms and the process of professional identity formation ( Ursavaş et al., 2025 ). From a theoretical perspective, social influence may be more closely tied to students’ judgments of trust as a cognitive authority, rather than merely serving as a peripheral normative factor in this sample. The remaining three classic dimensions of the UTAUT model were significantly positively associated with trust in GenAI, all meeting the p < 0.001 criterion. While the strength of their associations with trust was slightly lower than that of social influence, together they may represent consistent technological and environmental correlates of trust. Educational attainment was significantly positively associated with behavioral intention ( β = 0.072, p = 0.041). This pattern suggests that, in this sample, art students with higher educational attainment reported stronger behavioral intention to use GenAI. In Study 1, metacognitive control was directly associated with behavioral intention ( β = 0.146, p < 0.001) and was also associated with trust ( β = 0.099, p = 0.042); the mediation results were consistent with an indirect association through trust. Taken together, this pattern is consistent with a dual-path process that may be involved in GenAI adoption in artistic contexts. This pattern suggests that metacognitive control may be associated with both greater trust in GenAI and greater willingness to use it. This finding is consistent with the metacognitive framework for creativity proposed by other scholars, which suggests that metacognitive monitoring and regulation are important for managing the inherent ambiguity and openness of creative tasks ( Lebuda and Benedek, 2023 ). Unlike structured problem-solving tasks with clear termination rules, artistic creation often requires continuous evaluation of whether the output is sufficiently original, aesthetically coherent, and aligned with the creator’s intent ( Green et al., 2023 ). Study 2 results converge with the survey findings on the role of metacognitive control. The pronounced association with visual style suggests that situational metacognitive guidance may be particularly relevant for outputs that deviate from the model’s default stylistic tendencies. However, this should be interpreted as greater output diversity within the feature space, not as direct evidence of enhanced creativity. It should be noted that these effect magnitudes are obtained within a tightly-controlled short-term laboratory setting and may shrink when transferred to authentic classroom contexts. Regarding computational feature-distance outcomes, larger within-group pairwise distances reflect higher heterogeneity among generated images within each experimental group. This metric captures statistical dispersion in semantic embedding, texture-style statistics, and edge-based compositional structure rather than artistic merit. analysis.discussion: This study, based on Social Cognitive Theory, focuses on vocational college students and examines the relationships among AI Literacy, self-reported Complex Problem-Solving Skills, Systematic Thinking Skills, cognitive load, and perceived school ICT support through a three-wave questionnaire survey. The findings indicate that (1) AI Literacy was significantly and positively associated with self-reported Complex Problem-Solving Skills; (2) Systematic Thinking Skills and cognitive load were involved in significant indirect relationships between AI Literacy and self-reported Complex Problem-Solving Skills; and (3) the associations between AI Literacy and the two cognitive factors varied across levels of perceived school ICT support. These findings should be interpreted as associations among time-separated self-report measures rather than as evidence that AI Literacy produces changes in cognitive processes or objectively demonstrated problem-solving performance. First, the findings showed that AI Literacy was positively associated with vocational college students’ self-reported Complex Problem-Solving Skills. This result is consistent with Promma et al. (2025) , who also reported a positive relationship between AI Literacy and Complex Problem-Solving Skills, while the present study extends this association to Chinese higher vocational education. More recent evidence likewise suggests that AI Literacy is associated with students’ use of AI for learning and that such engagement is related to critical-thinking and problem-solving skills ( Sultana et al., 2026 ). One explanation is that AI Literacy involves more than familiarity with AI applications. Students with stronger AI Literacy are better positioned to identify when AI may be useful, evaluate generated information, recognize the limitations of AI outputs, and integrate such information into their own judgment rather than relying on generated responses uncritically ( Long and Magerko, 2020 ; Wang et al., 2023 ). These capabilities are particularly relevant to complex problems involving incomplete information, interacting variables, multiple constraints, and changing decision conditions ( Dörner and Funke, 2017 ). This relationship has particular relevance to higher vocational education, where students are prepared for practice-oriented and increasingly technology-rich occupational contexts ( Chee et al., 2025 ). For students in technical programmes, for example, debugging a program may involve using AI to identify possible sources of an error while still judging which suggestion is technically appropriate and adapting it to actual operating conditions. In such situations, AI Literacy supports not simply access to AI-generated information, but the purposeful integration of that information with students’ own technical judgment. From a Social Cognitive Theory perspective, AI Literacy can therefore be understood as a personal capability associated with how students approach complex tasks. The contribution of this finding lies in showing that the AI Literacy–problem-solving relationship is also evident in a practice-oriented Chinese vocational context. This extension is relevant to broader higher-education research emphasizing transferable meta-skills in preparing students for changing professional demands ( Che et al., 2026a ). Second, systematic thinking constituted a significant indirect pathway linking AI Literacy with self-reported Complex Problem-Solving Skills. Students with higher AI Literacy reported stronger Systematic Thinking Skills, which were in turn associated with higher perceived complex problem-solving capability. This finding is consistent with Promma et al. (2025) , who identified a similar mediating relationship among Thai accounting students, while the present study extends evidence for this pathway to Chinese higher vocational education. The first part of this pathway may be explained by the cognitive activities involved in effective interaction with AI. Productive AI use rarely ends with accepting the first generated response. Students often need to clarify a problem, specify relevant conditions, compare alternative outputs, identify inconsistencies, integrate information from different sources, and revise their queries or decisions. These activities require problem structuring, reasoning, prioritization, and information integration, which closely correspond to the Systematic Thinking Skills examined in this study. Recent work on discipline-specific AI Literacy similarly emphasizes problem articulation, disciplinary reasoning, and evaluation of the consequences of AI-supported decisions ( Stolpe et al., 2026 ). This interpretation is also consistent with systems-thinking research emphasizing relationships among multiple elements ( York et al., 2019 ) and with work showing that meaningful AI engagement involves understanding and evaluating AI rather than using it only instrumentally ( Alamäki et al., 2024 ). Related research on GenAI-supported learning further suggests that AI-generated materials can provide opportunities for systems-oriented analysis when generated relationships and assumptions are critically evaluated ( Courchesne et al., 2026 ). The second part of the pathway concerns why systematic thinking is associated with complex problem solving. Complex problems typically involve incomplete information, interacting variables, competing constraints, and consequences that change as decisions unfold ( Dörner and Funke, 2017 ). Systematic thinking can help students form a more structured representation of these relationships, identify central elements, distinguish important constraints from less relevant information, and compare alternative courses of action rather than relying on isolated trial and error. This reasoning is consistent with research linking systems-oriented analysis with ill-structured problem solving ( Grohs et al., 2018 ) and with recent work emphasizing systems thinking in professional decisions involving feedback, uncertainty, and unintended consequences ( Pedraja-Rejas et al., 2026 ). In Chinese higher vocational education, this process may be especially useful in technical tasks involving several procedures, information sources, and constraints. When diagnosing a technical fault, for example, a student may need to distinguish relevant symptoms, examine possible causes, compare AI-generated suggestions with technical knowledge, and determine which solution fits the actual task conditions. Technology-acceptance models can explain whether teachers are willing to use AI, but they do not specify how teachers decide what to delegate, what to verify, when to override, what to document, or when to seek another human judgment. RADM therefore turns principle-level responsible-AI language into a decision-regulation problem aligned with educational psychology’s concern for cognition and self-regulation. Second, the model provides a psychological link between institutional AI expectations and teacher behavior. Governance research identifies transparency, human oversight, literacy, and accountability, but institutional arrangements influence behavior only after teachers perceive and interpret them. Perceived accountability specifies how clear rules and roles can become anticipatory answerability. The model deliberately avoids assuming that policy clarity removes substantive uncertainty in the learner case; instead, it treats uncertainty as a separate metacognitive state that teachers must monitor and regulate. Third, the framework connects decision uncertainty with metacognitive calibration. Educational psychology has long treated monitoring as a prerequisite for regulation, yet responsible-AI discussions often treat uncertainty mainly as a technical defect to be reduced. The present framework instead proposes that recognized uncertainty can be behaviorally useful when it triggers checking and consultation, while unwarranted certainty and unregulated uncertainty can undermine responsible action. AI literacy is positioned as a regulatory resource that helps translate monitoring into control. Fourth, the configurational extension recognizes that teachers operate in heterogeneous institutional environments and may reach responsible practice through different combinations of contextual clarity, accountability, uncertainty, and AI literacy. This extension is subordinate to the psychological process model: it is intended to test equifinality after the core constructs and directional propositions are validated, not to substitute set-theoretic results for mechanism evidence. Taken together, these contributions explain responsible GenAI use as regulated professional judgment rather than as compliance, trust, or technical competence alone. The model is intentionally bounded: it does not claim that governance clarity is sufficient, that uncertainty should always be increased, or that AI literacy can compensate indefinitely for weak institutional responsibility. The practical implication is not that schools need longer AI policies. They need psychologically usable governance: a small number of consequential boundaries that teachers can retrieve and apply while making decisions. Guidance should make clear which tasks may receive GenAI assistance, what student information may not be entered, which outputs require independent checking, where accountable human authority resides, and when additional review is required. Examples and counterexamples are likely to support cognition more effectively than broad exhortations to use AI ‘responsibly.’ Role clarity is equally important. Every consequential GenAI-supported workflow should answer four questions for the teacher: What am I allowed to delegate? What am I responsible for verifying? Where does accountable human authority reside? Who should I consult when uncertainty or risk exceeds my expertise? These questions convert abstract accountability into a decision architecture and make it less likely that responsibility diffuses across a teacher, school leader, vendor, and system. Professional development should focus on uncertainty calibration and metacognitive monitoring rather than prompt engineering or productivity alone. Teachers need practice distinguishing fluency from evidential strength, recognizing missing context, comparing AI output with authoritative sources, protecting sensitive student information, and deciding when to seek a second opinion. Scenario-based professional learning can make these skills concrete by asking teachers to state not only what decision they would make, but how confident they are, what they would verify, and why they accepted, modified, rejected, or escalated the AI-supported recommendation. Finally, documentation should be proportional to educational stakes. Routine low-risk use does not require bureaucratic logging of every interaction. Consequential uses should preserve enough process evidence to reconstruct the teacher’s reasoning: the GenAI contribution, independent evidence checked, uncertainty identified, and basis for the final action. Such traceability supports reflective practice and accountability without turning responsible AI into paperwork for its own sake. The psychological process model developed in this study has not yet been empirically validated. Its proposed relationships should therefore be interpreted as testable propositions rather than established causal effects. The calibration-sensitive prediction for decision uncertainty is especially provisional. It should be evaluated against objective task ambiguity, evidence quality, and decision accuracy so that warranted certainty can be distinguished from overconfidence and productive uncertainty from poorly regulated indecision. Direct evidence on GenAI in real, consequential teacher decisions remains limited in the literature examined here. Feedback-quality studies and pre-service teacher experiments inform possible assistance functions but do not establish effectiveness in referral, placement, or sustained student-support practice. reading.overview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in second-language writing, while translanguaging can serve as a pedagogical resource for mobilizing multilingual repertoires. Neither resource is inherently metacognitive.
reading.interpretation: This perspective addressed three questions concerning the integration of intentional translanguaging and GenAI within metacognitive EFL writing. First, the framework treats intentional translanguaging and GenAI as complementary resources that make different kinds of alternatives available for examination. Their potential metacognitive relevance lies not in resource use itself but in how learners monitor and evaluate resulting alternatives and regulate subsequent writing decisions. The author-developed heuristic—identify a purpose, examine alternatives, compare, judge, decide, and reflect—represents this recursive decision-making process rather than a fixed sequence. Second, teacher-mediated scaffolding is external support for learner regulation. It may establish purposes and boundaries, model comparison, provide evaluative criteria, prompt justification, and adjust support, while responsibility for accepting, modifying, rejecting, or further examining alternatives remains with the learner. Third, its application in Latin American EFL contexts requires adaptation to local linguistic repertoires, GenAI access, institutional policies, teacher preparation, and language ideologies. This regional orientation is contextual and prospective rather than evidence of empirical validation. Overall, the framework's contribution lies in the decision-making mechanism through which learners evaluate and act on alternatives while retaining regulatory and authorial responsibility. For minority learners, these decisions may also concern whether their linguistic and semiotic resources are recognized as legitimate and whether their voice remains visible in academic writing. analysis.methods: This study employed a cross-sectional design. An anonymous electronic questionnaire was distributed to university physical education teachers via the Wenjuanxing online survey platform between 1 June 2026 and 10 August 2026. Participants were recruited through a combination of convenience sampling and snowball sampling, both non-probability methods: the questionnaire link was first sent to teachers who could be reached conveniently, who were asked to forward it to other university physical education teachers they knew. The questionnaire link was initially sent to teachers at 18 universities in six provinces and municipalities (Sichuan, Guangdong, Chongqing, Beijing, Hainan, and Hunan; the universities are listed in Supplementary Table S1 ) and was then circulated through snowball referral. Because the link was circulated through personal and professional networks, the number of invited teachers could not be determined, so a response rate cannot be calculated; the effective rate reported below is the proportion of returned questionnaires that were valid. Because of snowball referral, the universities that the questionnaire ultimately reached cannot be determined; the questionnaire was also anonymous and did not record respondent-level institutional affiliation, so the distribution of participants across universities cannot be reported. Gender, age, and years of teaching experience were also recorded, but because of problems in the collection and compilation of these data they could not be used, and none of the analyses reported here includes them. In total, 981 questionnaires were returned. The questionnaire consisted of four sections: the Perceived AI Acceptance Scale, the Digital Well-Being Scale, the Innovative Work Behavior Scale, and the Job-related Affective Well-being Scale (JAWS). Prior to participation, all respondents provided electronic informed consent, and all data were anonymized to ensure confidentiality. Data cleaning excluded 174 questionnaires in three mutually exclusive steps applied in the following order, so that no case was counted twice. The questionnaire contained, in addition to the four scales, a screening item on professional identity, an item on whether the respondent teaches university physical education classes and an item on weekly class hours, a pair of positively and reversely worded items on the use of a teaching method, and one attention-check item. First, 30 questionnaires were excluded because the screening item showed that the respondent was not a university physical education teacher (981–30 = 951 remaining). Second, of these 951, 113 were excluded because the total completion time was outside the limits set on the Wenjuanxing platform: a minimum of 1 min (60 s) and a maximum of 30 min (1,800 s). Wenjuanxing offers several completion-time limit options (for the maximum, for example, 5, 10, 15, and 20 min), these two limits were selected from them, and questionnaires outside the limits were marked as invalid by the platform and removed (951–113 = 838 remaining). The limits were platform settings and not empirically derived criteria. Third, of the remaining 838, 31 were excluded for internally inconsistent responses, defined as failing any one of the following checks: (a) answering “no” to whether the respondent teaches university physical education classes while reporting weekly class hours greater than 0; (b) answering “agree” or “strongly agree” to both the positively worded item “I often apply this teaching method in class” and the reversely worded item “I rarely apply this teaching method in class,” or, after reverse-scoring the negatively worded item, an absolute difference of 2 or more between the scores of the two items; and (c) not selecting the instructed option on the attention-check item (“Please select ‘somewhat agree’ for this item”). A total of 807 valid questionnaires (807/981 = 82.26%) were retained for analysis. The anonymized dataset will be retained in accordance with institutional data-management practice and made available to qualified researchers upon reasonable request, subject to a formal data-sharing agreement that protects participants’ privacy. This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. It did not involve invasive procedures, and all research methods complied with relevant guidelines and regulations. Ethical approval was obtained from the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of Hunan Normal University (approval no. LSK2026-472) prior to the commencement of the study. The author, who is the project leader and the applicant, is affiliated with Sichuan Film and Television University; the ethical review was conducted by the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of Hunan Normal University, which accepted the author’s entrustment to review the project (letter of acceptance of entrusted ethics review). The approved protocol specified online recruitment of university physical education teachers by convenience and snowball sampling in 18 universities in six provinces and municipalities (Sichuan, Guangdong, Chongqing, Beijing, Hainan, and Hunan) between 1 June and 10 August 2026; because of snowball sampling, the questionnaire reached universities across these provinces and municipalities. Data were collected anonymously and kept strictly confidential. All participants provided electronic informed consent and voluntarily agreed to participate; they retained the right to withdraw from the study at any time without penalty. The Perceived AI Acceptance Scale was adapted from Davis (1989) , with item wording modified to refer to AI tools used in university teaching. The Digital Well-Being Scale is a researcher-developed instrument: Gui et al. (2017) offer a theoretical framework and indicators of digital well-being but no ready-made item set, so the 12 items were compiled, translated, and reworded by the research team on the basis of that framework, and the scale should not be regarded as a previously validated instrument. The Innovative Work Behavior Scale and the JAWS were based on the original instruments ( Janssen, 2000 ; Van Katwyk et al., 2000 ). The English items of the three published scales were translated into Chinese by one bilingual researcher, and a second bilingual expert who had not taken part in the translation checked the Chinese version against the original scales; disagreements were resolved through discussion in the research team. A pilot test with cognitive interviews was then conducted with 30 university physical education teachers, and the items were revised accordingly before the final version was set. analysis.discussion: This study constructed and tested a serial mediation model examining whether perceived AI acceptance is associated with university PE teachers’ occupational well-being through the sequential mediating roles of digital well-being and innovative work behavior. The data were consistent with all four hypotheses, and the pattern of results is compatible with a resource-based interpretation of how favorable technological appraisal may be linked to occupational adaptation in a digitalizing higher-education context. Given the cross-sectional, single-source design, however, the results describe statistical indirect associations and not established psychological mechanisms or temporal processes. This study found that perceived AI acceptance was significantly and positively associated with university PE teachers’ occupational well-being, supporting Hypothesis H1 and aligning with a growing body of evidence documenting positive associations between favorable technology appraisals and occupational adjustment among teachers ( Yi et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ). The association between perceived AI acceptance and occupational well-being was accompanied by indirect associations through both digital well-being and innovative work behavior, which were themselves intercorrelated. From the perspective of Conservation of Resources theory, perceived AI acceptance can be interpreted as a favorable appraisal of a potential job resource, which is consistent with lower anticipated resource loss and with higher levels of resources in digital and behavioral domains ( Hobfoll, 1989 ; Hobfoll et al., 2018 ) (these resource states were not directly measured). Higher levels of such resources are, in turn, associated with more favorable affective experiences of work, consistent with the Job Demands–Resources proposition that job and personal resources are linked to engagement and well-being ( Bakker and Demerouti, 2017 ). Notably, similar to prior chain-mediation research on teacher occupational well-being ( Nong et al., 2022 ), the serial indirect pathway identified in the present study, while statistically reliable, represented a modest proportion of the total effect (11.66%), indicating that the sequence from digital well-being to innovative work behavior accounts for only a modest part of the association between perceived AI acceptance and occupational well-being, and that other factors not measured here are likely to be involved. Given that prosocial and occupational outcomes are typically shaped by numerous factors beyond any single technological appraisal—such as institutional support, professional identity, and workload—the magnitude of the present associations is consistent with the broader literature’s understanding of teacher well-being as a multiply determined outcome, while still carrying meaningful implications for how institutions introduce and scaffold AI tools for PE faculty. This study also found a statistically significant indirect association between perceived AI acceptance and university PE teachers’ occupational well-being through digital well-being, consistent with Hypothesis H2. This result indicates that perceived AI acceptance is not only directly associated with occupational well-being but also shows an indirect association with it through digital well-being (in a statistical sense). One possible interpretation, which these data cannot test directly, is that when AI tools are appraised as useful and easy to operate, teachers may be less likely to experience the technology as an additional demand and may be more likely to adopt selective, adaptive strategies for managing digital information and communication flows ( Gui et al., 2017 ). Consistent with this reasoning, prior organizational research has shown that workplace digitization is associated with reduced digital anxiety, which in turn is linked to enhanced employee well-being ( Han Z. et al., 2025 ). Within a COR framework, a favorable technological appraisal is theoretically linked to a lower anticipated resource cost of digital engagement, which may be related to higher digital well-being as a personal resource that is, in turn, associated with broader occupational well-being ( Hobfoll, 1989 ; Diener et al., 1999 ). Thus, the emotional and cognitive experience of digital demands may be one relevant correlate linking PE teachers’ appraisal of AI and their overall occupational well-being. The results showed that innovative work behavior had a significant indirect association linking perceived AI acceptance and university PE teachers’ occupational well-being, consistent with Hypothesis H3. This finding is compatible with a role for proactive, resource-investing behavior in linking technology appraisal and occupational adaptation, although the cross-sectional data do not establish this role. When PE teachers regard AI tools as beneficial and easy to use, they appear more willing to invest cognitive and behavioral resources in generating, promoting, and realizing novel ideas in their work, consistent with recent evidence that generative AI use is associated with employees’ innovation performance through resource acquisition and integration mechanisms ( Wang et al., 2025 ). Innovative work behavior is, in turn, associated with occupational well-being, plausibly because the successful promotion and realization of novel ideas is linked to experiences of competence, recognition, and positive affect at work ( West and Farr, 1990 ; Janssen, 2000 ). This finding is consistent with prior literature indicating that innovative behavior is associated with individual well-being outcomes ( Amabile, 1988 ), and adds evidence on this association in the domain of AI-related technology appraisal among university PE teachers. Note that innovative work behavior was measured with Janssen’s general scale, which captures idea generation, promotion, and realization in one’s work role; it does not specifically capture teaching or pedagogical innovation. The instructional examples given above are therefore illustrations of how general innovative behavior might appear among PE teachers and not features of what was measured. This study further found a statistically significant serial indirect association through digital well-being and innovative work behavior in sequence, consistent with Hypothesis H4. This pattern is compatible with a cumulative, resource-based sequence: from a favorable technological appraisal, to digital resource sufficiency, to proactive behavioral resource investment, and then to occupational well-being. A key contribution of this study is the use of RI-CLPM to disentangle between-person stability from within-person fluctuations, revealing that the CAS-SABA relationship operates primarily at the trait level, with worry uniquely emerging as the core domain most consistently associated with both stable comorbidity and dynamic change. This study systematically examined the associations between CAS, including total score and domains, and SABA using a multi-wave longitudinal design with multiple analytical approaches. analysis.methods: The baseline data for Phase 1 were collected from students enrolled at a medical university in China. A total of 1025 medical students (399 male, 626 female) completed the survey, with ages ranging from 16 to 24 years (M = 19.41, SD = 3.207). They were recruited from Sojump, a Chinese online survey platform, for a study titled "A Research of Your Opinions on Smartphone Use." After reading an information sheet describing the study procedures, participants completed the survey in accordance with the provided instructions. All procedures were approved by the Scientific Research Ethics Review Committee of Shanxi Medical University (approval No. 2025038; approval date: January 8, 2025). All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation. For minors (under 18 years), additional written consent was obtained from their legal guardians, along with participant assent directly from the minors themselves. Participants were informed of their right to withdraw at any time without penalty. All data were collected anonymously and stored securely. In Phases 2 and 3, the final longitudinal sample consisted of 668 medical students (61.68% female), with a mean age of 19.64 years (SD = 1.11; range = 17-24). All participants were invited to complete a battery of online self-report measures at two follow-up time points: 4 months (T2) and 8 months (T3) after T1. Of the initial 1025 participants at T1, 668 participants (65%) completed all three waves of data collection and were included in the primary longitudinal analyses. Retention rates were 69% (n = 705) at T2 and 65% (n = 668) at T3. All assessment sessions could be completed from any smartphone with internet access.
analysis.discussion: The present study provides a comprehensive examination of the relationship between CAS and SABA using a multi-method approach that integrates cross-sectional, longitudinal, and machine learning analyses. The results support the proposed metacognitive model of SABA, which was developed by extending and modifying Wells' (2009) S-REF framework of obsessive-compulsive disorders (OCD) to the context of behavioral addictions, demonstrating that CAS is associated with SABA across multiple analytical approaches. A key contribution of this study is the use of RI-CLPM to disentangle between-person stability from within-person fluctuations, revealing that the CAS-SABA relationship operates primarily at the trait level, with worry uniquely emerging as the core domain most consistently associated with both stable comorbidity and dynamic change. This study systematically examined the associations between CAS, including total score and domains, and SABA using a multi-wave longitudinal design with multiple analytical approaches. The findings provide empirical support for the proposed metacognitive model of SABA, demonstrating that CAS total score is primarily associated with SABA at the between-person level, indicating a stable trait-level comorbidity rather than a short-term dynamic process. Among the seven CAS domains, worry uniquely emerged as the most consistent predictor for SABA: it showed the strongest between-person association with SABA and the largest within-person cross-lagged association, with a directional path from worry to SABA. This within-person association remained significant even after controlling for comorbid anxiety and depression, supporting worry as a prospective within-person correlate of SABA. Methodologically, the integration of LCGM, Random Forest, and SHAP analyses provided convergent evidence across person-centered and variable-centered approaches, which extended the RI-CLPM findings by indicating that the relative influence of CAS domains differs across SABA trajectories. Machine learning analyses consistently identified worry as the most influential CAS domain in relation to SABA, ranking first in predicting both high-stable and moderate-decreasing trajectories of SABA, and further suggested a synergistic interaction between worry and substance use, corresponding to a higher likelihood of belonging to the high-stable SABA trajectory. Clinically, the dual-pathway pattern of worry observed in the RI-CLPM suggests worry can serve different functions depending on the target population and time frame. At the trait level, its strong betweenperson association with SABA supports its potential use as a screening marker for identifying high SABA-risk medical students who may benefit from early prevention for SABA. At the state level, its significant withinperson association with SABA suggests that worry fluctuations may serve as a dynamic indicator for monitoring short-term changes in SABA risk. For medical students who have already developed SABA, whether worry represents a candidate target for future intervention research, and whether reducing worry could potentially influence the maintenance of SABA requires confirmation in future experimental studies. Given that the within-person association of worry remained significant after controlling for anxiety and depression, future research could examine whether interventions targeting worry are effective regardless of individuals' current anxiety or depression levels. Future research could employ experimental designs (e.g., randomized controlled trials targeting worry) to further test whether worry prospectively predicts SABA, and whether abbreviated metacognitive therapy is effective in reducing worry and, consequently, alleviating SABA among medical students at both short-term and long-term levels.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the reliance on self-report measures and the specific sample of medical students in China may limit the generalizability of these findings. Future research could replicate these findings using more diverse populations and multimethod assessments (e.g., objective measures such as actual smartphone usage data) to reduce this potential bias. Second, the 35% attrition rate over the three waves needs to be considered when interpreting the findings. Although attrition analyses suggested limited bias (|d| = .168-.196), the reduced sample size may have limited statistical power to detect small effects, particularly at the within-person level. Future research with larger samples and lower attrition rates is needed. Third, although anxiety and depression were controlled as covariates in the RI-CLPM, they were not controlled for in all analyses of this research. Future research could systematically include these covariates across all analytical levels. Fourth, the entropy values for the LCGM (.69-.74) indicated moderate trajectory classification precision, suggesting that the trajectoryspecific results, particularly those involving the low-stable group (n = 84, 12.50%), warrant careful interpretation. Future research with larger samples and more waves of data is needed to replicate and refine these trajectory classifications. Fifth, the SABAS uses a single item per addiction criterion, which may limit measurement precision. The use of a 6-point Likert format for both the SABAS and MCASS, while intended to reduce neutral midpoint bias, may have influenced response distributions and warrant consideration when interpreting the findings. Although the SABAS has been validated as a brief screening tool, future research could employ multiitem measures for greater reliability. Sixth, the two-step factor-score sensitivity analysis partially accounted for measurement error in CAS. However, the CAS latent measurement model showed relatively poor fit, and the factor loadings for substance use (λ = .29-.33) and worry (λ = .46-.50) were relatively low, suggesting these domains were less well represented by the latent factor. Furthermore, the strict one-step latent RI-CLPM did not converge, and SABA remained a unidimensional construct represented by an observed total score. Estimating a fully latent RI-CLPM with seven indicators across three waves involves a large number of parameters, which may have contributed to the estimation difficulty. Therefore, measurement error was not fully addressed, and the factor-score analyses represent limited, exploratory sensitivity checks. Future research with larger samples and more stable measurement models may be needed to estimate fully latent RI-CLPMs that better account for measurement error in CAS. Seventh, the measurement invariance results warrant consideration, as the configural models for SABAS and MCASS showed relatively weak fit, and SABAS achieved partial rather than full scalar invariance. Therefore, these results provide qualified, rather than definitive, evidence of measurement equivalence across time. Eighth, the three-wave longitudinal design constrained the precision of growth trajectory estimation. Future research with more frequent assessments (e.g., ecological momentary assessment) could further clarify the short-term dynamic relationship between worry and SABA. Ninth, although RI-CLPM provides a more stringent test of temporal precedence than traditional CLPM, it does not establish causation. Future research could employ experimental designs, such as randomized controlled trials targeting worry, to further test whether worry prospectively predicts SABA, and whether abbreviated metacognitive therapy is effective.

abstract_text: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in daily life, ascertaining whether an agent is human is critical. Here we systematically benchmark AI's ability to imitate humans in three language tasks (image captioning, word association and conversation) and three vision tasks (colour estimation, object detection and attention prediction), collecting data from n = 636 humans and 37 AI agents. We also conducted 72,191 Turing-like tests with 1,916 human judges and 10 AI judges. Current AIs are approaching the ability to convincingly impersonate humans and deceive human judges in both language and vision. analysis.methods: A total of 9,342 responses were collected from human judges. We collected gender and education level for each participant (Fig. S2M , O for online participants and Fig. S4M -P for in-lab participants). The performance of the human judges was reported in Fig. S15C . Turing-like test, machine judges. As the images were the same for humans and AI models, we used solely the text embeddings for the AI judge to classify a given response as human or AI. We concatenated the three responses into a sentence and collected textual features for the sentence using BERT [33] . These features were passed into an SVM classifier to classify responses into humans versus AI, with 90% / 10% split cross-validation. The performance of the AI judge was reported in Fig. S15D . We followed the same procedures as in the three language tasks to introduce two judge variations: (1) To compare with the results of the experiments where human judges received feedback (Fig. S9S ), we trained SVM-based judges on the same number of trials with feedback for human judges (Fig. S9T ). (2) We used a large language model, ChatGPT [13] , as a zero-shot judge by feeding the image and the three keywords as inputs and outputting a binary label: "human" or "AI-generated". The text prompt was: You will be shown a scene image along with 5 object detection results. Each result consists of 3 identified objects. Your goal is to determine whether each estimation was generated by a human or an AI model. Instructions: Please present answers as pairs consisting of the classification (either 'Human' or 'AI-generated') followed by a brief justification for your decision. At the end, include a section titled 'Summary of Classifications' that lists all classifications in order as a bullet list. Detections: [THREE OBJECTS] where [THREE OBJECTS] refers to the actual object responses in the test set. All data and code are made publicly available See Data Availability Statement one designated as the human judge and the other as the human agent. Each participant was limited to joining one Turing test at a time, although they had the option to participate in additional tests once their current test was concluded. In such cases, the server would randomly pair them with the remaining available human partners. Ultimately, we gathered a total of 10 conversations with an average of 2.5 exchanges per conversation. Of these, 3 conversations were from condition 1, involving deceitful human agents, while the remaining 7 were from condition 2, involving deceitful AI agents.
