analysis.discussion: We first introduce a dataset of human answers in 6 common language (Fig. 1 ) and vision (Fig. 3 ) tasks to evaluate the ability of algorithms to imitate humans. The dataset also includes answers from state-of-the-art AI algorithms (Table S1 ). Using the human and machine answers, we conducted Turing-like tests, showing that current algorithms are not far from being able to imitate humans in these tasks (Fig. 4A-C , G-I , Fig. S5A , C , E , Fig. S15A , C , E ). In contrast to human judges, even simple machine judges can distinguish human from machine answers (Fig. 4D-F , J-L , Fig. S5B , D , F Fig. S15B , D , F ). The Turing test has been extensively discussed, and contested, as a means to assess general intelligence. Our work is not intended as an evaluation of intelligence or to contribute to the discussion of Turing tests to quantify intelligence. Imitating humans can benefit humanity in many situations where we want to align machine and human outputs, such as in emulating expert decisions. However, imitating humans can also be used for evil, as in the dissemination of fake information, phishing attempts, or other scams. Regardless of whether Turing tests are good or bad metrics of intelligence, it is of high practical importance to assess whether algorithms can imitate humans or not. In some cases, we summarized results using the overall imitation detectability metric. It is important to emphasize that this summary metric does not differentiate between the two types of classification errors: (1) False Negatives -A human response misclassified as machine-generated. (2) False Positives -A machine response misclassified as human-generated. Understanding the distinction between these two error types is important for interpreting decision-making by human and machine judges. Moreover, in real-world applications, these errors may have different consequences. For example, misclassifying a machine as a human might be more problematic than misclassifying a human as a machine if the goal is to reliably detect AI-generated content. We present confusion matrices throughout to complement the imitation detectability scores and quantify the two types of errors. One approach towards mitigating the risks from evil human imitators is to build AI judges that can distinguish true human answers. The results presented here show that even simple AI judges like the ones introduced here can generally do a better job than human judges in detecting machine answers for the current tasks. There will likely continue to be an arms race between the development of better imitators and better detectors. In most of the Turing-like tests presented here, AI judges were explicitly trained to classify responses from humans versus AIs, while human judges received no explicit training. However, we also presented results using ChatGPT-4o, a state-of-the-art, off-the-shelf, multimodal model. We evaluated ChatGPT-4o in zero-shot Turing-like tests across all six tasks. This unified, multi-modal model can distinguish between human and machine-generated responses with above-chance accuracy, even without any explicit training. These observations also raise the possibility that humans may be trained to better recognize machine answers. In support of this hypothesis, when human judges received training in the form of trial-by-trial feedback, they showed improved accuracy in identifying human-generated responses. By and large, humans have lived in a world without good human imitators and did not have to worry too much about the possibility of machines emulating humans, other than in famous works of fiction. This situation is changing rapidly and may lead to the need to educate human judges. An algorithm's ability to imitate humans does not necessarily correlate with traditional performance metrics like accuracy. Consider a simple scenario of an image with a highly occluded dog that is hard to see, and both machines and humans interpret the object to be a wolf. Both would be wrong, but the machine would be adequately imitating humans. Conversely, the example in Fig. S14C for the Image captioning task. This example shows that both machines and humans can provide correct answers, but the algorithm does not fully imitate how humans interpret the image. Thus, M and H can be wrong, and M can adequately imitate H; M and H can also both be right and M fail to adequately imitate H. Being right or wrong is not the same as imitation. Turing-like tests provide a complementary assessment to existing benchmarking frameworks for AI algorithms. Comparisons between models in Turing-like tests also provide insights helpful for developing future AI models that can better align with humans. We refer to the evaluations in our study as "Turing-like" to emphasize that they are not identical to Turing's original description [44] . Turing did not spell out the implementation details of his tests, perhaps because he did not imagine at the time that these tests could be truly implemented, barely a few decades later. The datasets and evaluations introduced here are extensive (72, 191 Turing-like test trials, 636 humans contributing to the dataset, and 1,916 human judges). Yet, these evaluations barely scratch the surface of what needs to be evaluated. There are essentially infinite possible Turing-like tests. Each algorithm and each task can be evaluated in terms of imitation capabilities. Even within a particular task, there are multiple ways of instantiating a Turing-like test. The results of a Turing-like test depend on the task, the algorithm, how the question is formulated, the demographics of the human agent, the characteristics of the human judge, and many other variables. Such variations are particularly evident in the context of conversation tasks where the topic, medium, length, format, instructions, agent and judge expertise, and agent and judge demographics, can lead to different results [32] , [34] , [37] , [38] , [39] , [40] . For example, the conversation topic and participant expertise can be critical: one could conduct the conversation focusing exclusively on medieval history, string theory, or basketball games as conversation topics and agents/judges with or without domain-specific knowledge may perform differently. However, the topic-agnostic formulation is relevant to many (but certainly not all) real-world scenarios. The results presented here further emphasize the importance of integrative benchmarks. The current work is not intended as an exhaustive assessment of every conceivable task. We do not believe such a complete characterization is even feasible in practice. Instead, we focus on a subset of task formulations that arise naturally in everyday contexts. For instance, in conversational tasks, one might imagine an exchange between two agents on a social media platform, with an observer attempting to determine whether both, one, or neither of the participants is human. We also implemented and evaluated an online version of the conversation task that is closer to the original formulation of the Turing task. The results from the online test with adversarial prompting differ from those of the offline, non-adversarial formulation. These are distinct experiments based on contrasting formats and underlying assumptions, which naturally lead to different outcomes, further emphasizing that the details of how the Turing tests are defined matter. The findings underscore that Turing-like test results can vary widely

verified_article_review.discussion: The caption results show why mistaking a model for a person and recognizing a person are separate judgments. Letting judges choose a follow-up question also gives them a way to probe an answer that is unavailable when they see only a finished caption.
verified_article_review.limitations: The tests used particular tasks, models and rules for what a judge could see or ask. The perfect score in the live comparison describes that experiment with one chatbot. It does not establish how well people would identify other models in everyday conversation.

title: Focus Filters — Apple Developer Documentation
evidence: Product documentation; no independent effectiveness assessment
preview: Apple's Focus APIs allow apps to adapt their behavior or notification handling to an active Focus state. These affordances are relevant to the technical feasibility of a privacy-conscious attention app.

editorial_notes.argument: Apple documents mechanisms through which apps respond to system Focus configurations and filter notifications.
editorial_notes.design_relevance: A prototype could coordinate with system-selected focus states rather than inferring users' mental states or monitoring all applications.
editorial_notes.caveat: Product documentation is a description of features, not independently established evidence of effectiveness.

reading.provenance: Apple Developer published product documentation
reading.overview: Apple's Focus APIs allow apps to adapt their behavior or notification handling to an active Focus state. These affordances are relevant to the technical feasibility of a privacy-conscious attention app.
reading.notice: Original synopsis of product features. This is not a tested intervention or a claim about its effectiveness.

digest.idea: Focus settings let apps adjust their behavior to a user's preferences and chosen context.
digest.explain: Apple lets people choose which parts of a participating app belong in a particular Focus, such as which email account can send alerts during work.
digest.interpretation: A prototype could coordinate with system-selected focus states rather than inferring users' mental states or monitoring all applications.
digest.limitation: The developer has to implement the filter. The available choices depend on what the particular app exposes when someone configures a Focus.

longform.thesis: Apple lets people choose which parts of a participating app belong in a particular Focus, such as which email account can send alerts during work.
longform.reasoning: When someone turns on a Focus, the system calls the filter the developer has built into the app. The app uses the configuration for that Focus to change its behavior and decide which incoming notifications to show.
longform.examples: Apple gives the example of personal email or messages during a Work Focus. Account-specific filtering lets work communications still get through while alerts from a personal account stay quiet.
longform.implications: A prototype could coordinate with system-selected focus states rather than inferring users' mental states or monitoring all applications.
longform.qualification: The developer has to implement the filter. The available choices depend on what the particular app exposes when someone configures a Focus.

plain_reading.lead: Apple lets developers change what an app shows when a Focus is on. The choices a person sees depend on which filters the app supports.
plain_reading.detail: Apple gives the example of separating email accounts during a Work Focus. An app with the right filter can let work alerts through while keeping personal ones quiet.
plain_reading.limit: The documentation explains what app developers can support. It does not test whether filtering alerts improves anyone’s concentration.

title: Android Focus Mode and Digital Wellbeing
evidence: Product documentation; no independent effectiveness assessment
preview: Android describes system-level features for pausing distracting apps, managing screen time and notification habits, and configuring focused periods.

editorial_notes.argument: Android presents Focus Mode and Digital Wellbeing controls as user-directed tools for reducing digital interruptions.
editorial_notes.design_relevance: Use the platform's existing pause, schedule, and limit features as a baseline when testing whether a proposed attention tool adds value.
editorial_notes.caveat: Product documentation is a description of features, not independently established evidence of effectiveness.

reading.provenance: Android published product documentation
reading.overview: Android describes system-level features for pausing distracting apps, managing screen time and notification habits, and configuring focused periods.
reading.notice: Original synopsis of product features. This is not a tested intervention or a claim about its effectiveness.

digest.idea: Device-level focus controls can pause apps and manage interruptions without guessing how attentive someone is.
digest.explain: Android users can pause selected apps during a focused period. They can also see which apps use the most time or send the most notifications before deciding where to set a limit.
digest.interpretation: Use the platform's existing pause, schedule, and limit features as a baseline when testing whether a proposed attention tool adds value.
digest.limitation: Time spent in an app and the number of alerts describe phone activity. The guide gives no measure of how well a person concentrated during that time.

longform.thesis: Android users can pause selected apps during a focused period. They can also see which apps use the most time or send the most notifications before deciding where to set a limit.
longform.reasoning: Focus Mode changes what is available on the phone while it is active. Digital Wellbeing also shows how time and notifications are distributed across apps, so a person can choose which apps warrant a daily limit.
longform.examples: Android lists games, social media and communication apps as things a person can pause. Someone who wants to understand repeated interruptions can instead check which app sends the most notifications before choosing a limit.
longform.implications: Use the platform's existing pause, schedule, and limit features as a baseline when testing whether a proposed attention tool adds value.
longform.qualification: Time spent in an app and the number of alerts describe phone activity. The guide gives no measure of how well a person concentrated during that time.

plain_reading.lead: Android’s Focus Mode lets you pause selected apps. Its activity records show time spent on the phone and how many alerts arrived.
plain_reading.detail: Android’s guide describes using the activity view to choose a daily limit, or scheduling a period when particular apps should pause. Someone concerned about interruptions can start by looking at which app sends the most alerts.
plain_reading.limit: Time spent in an app tells you how long it was open. It does not tell you whether you were concentrating on the task you meant to do.
